project.title: The Salt-Iron Road
project.author: Neve Aubermont
project.subtitle: A Novel of the Saltreach
project.premise: Every autumn the Verdigris Company runs a salt-caravan across the Saltreach, the only land bridge between two crowns that hate each other. This year its disgraced quartermaster is bribed to smuggle one unlisted crate the length of the road — a Salt-Iron Ledger that proves the mute drover travelling with the caravan is the exiled heir the regent declared dead. As a succession war kindles and zealot rebels ride to burn the proof, she must decide what the truth is worth.

ch1.body:
In Oststrand a woman was worth what she could carry, and Sable Coyne had spent the whole grey winter learning exactly how little that came to.

She stood at the mouth of the Verdigris Yards with her entire estate on her back — one salt-stiffened coat, a bedroll cinched with fishing-twine, and her father's tally-knife riding the hip where an officer's sword had ridden for eleven years — and she counted the coins in her palm again, because counting was the last trade the city had left her. Four grey salt-pennies and a thumb of rock-salt too foul to season soup. Two days' eating, if she ate like a woman doing penance. Not enough to leave the city. Not enough to stay in it. Not enough, in the plain Meridian arithmetic that governed everything under the Kept Flame, to matter at all.

Behind her Oststrand climbed its harbor in black tiers, basalt and salt-bloom, the raked masts of the salt-fleet scratching at a bruised autumn sky. Above them, on the Throne-hill, the Kept Flame burned its thin gold thread — the sacred fire the priests swore had never once gone out, tended by men who had never in their lives gone thirsty and who set, from that comfortable height, the price of every swallow of water in the reach. Each of those masts had been a road home once. Her name was struck off all of them now. Struck off the fleet-rolls in red the morning they broke her, so that no salt-captain from the Oststrand mole to the reefs of Lowmarch would sign Sable Coyne aboard so much as a bilge-scow.

A blacklist was a cheap and a permanent thing. It cost the Throne nothing and it cost her everything, which she had decided, over the course of the winter, was the whole Meridian notion of justice rendered small enough to hold in one hand.

The Verdigris Yards did not care about fleet-rolls. That was the single virtue of the caravan trade and the entire reason she had swallowed what was left of her pride and walked the length of the mole to stand here: the Company weighed a soul by the load it could shift and the tally it could keep, not by the name a regent's clerk had crossed out. Salt was salt whoever hauled it. Coin did not remember your disgrace.

She went in under the verdigris-green arch — the copper gate-plate gone the pale sick colour that gave the Company its name — and into a churn of noise and dust and the huge, patient reek of camels.

A boy came across the yard at a dead run with a tally-board hugged to his chest and very nearly put himself face-down in the muck stopping short of her. He righted himself, went red to the ears, and stared at her the way a novice stares at a relic he has read about but never expected to touch.

"You're her," he said. "You're Coyne. Quartermaster Coyne, off the salt-fleet. I read your loading-tables — everybody read your loading-tables, they still teach the water-split out of them, the one where you brought a fleet-tender home across the Glare on half a ration and didn't lose a soul—" He ran clean out of air.

Sable let a beat go by, the way you let a camel settle before you cinch it. "And you are?"

"Ino. Water-clerk. I keep the tally." He hoisted the board an inch, as evidence, then remembered something enormous and inconvenient. "Master Voss said if you came I was to bring you straight in. He said — he said you'd come."

That last landed under her ribs and sat there. He said you'd come. Of course he had. Adder Voss had always been able to read a manifest, and she was a manifest anyone could read this winter: one broke, blacklisted quartermaster, assets nil, options nil, arriving on foot at the one gate in Oststrand that would still open to her. She hadn't come to the Verdigris Yards. She'd been counted to them.

"Lead on, then," she said.

Ino towed her across the yard talking the whole way, because it seemed to be the only speed he had. The Company was loading for the autumn crossing, he told her, the last west-run before the road closed for the season — forty-one camels, nineteen souls, bound over the Saltreach for the salt-markets of Lowmarch. The water was already going into tally, three hundred and some skins, every one counted twice and sealed with the Company lead, and was it true, was it really true, that she could reckon a string's daily draw in her head to the half-swallow—

"Ino."

"Quartermaster."

"Breathe."

They passed a knot of teamsters throwing knuckle-bones in the lee of a fodder-stack, and one of them unfolded from the game as she went by: a long grey man with a drooping soldier's moustache and hands like cured harness-leather. Marsh. He'd teamed for the fleet in the old days, before the fleet decided it had no further use for either of them.

"Coyne," he said.

"Marsh."

"Heard you was dead."

"Working on it."

He almost smiled, and went back down to the bones — which over the years had taken more off him than the fleet ever paid on, and would take more again tonight, by the grim, patient set of the men waiting to win it. Some debts a man just kept feeding. Sable knew the type. She'd have said she wasn't it, but then she was the one walking into Adder Voss's tent with four salt-pennies to her name, so perhaps a person didn't get to grade her own honesty.

She stopped outside the black tent at the heart of the yard, because her legs had halted without consulting her, the way they still did sometimes. Past the yard-wall the fleet-masts stood up hard and black against the harbor, and she made herself look at them the way you press a bruise to be sure it is still yours. Eleven years she had given the salt-fleet, and she had been good at it — better than good; they had made her a loading-officer at an age when most of her year were still learning to coil a wet rope — and it had all run out at last in a fleet-court and a scaffold and her name struck through in red. Under the whole black sum of it, at the bottom of every column, was Petar. Her brother had shipped under her because she had promised their mother she would keep an eye to him, and instead she had kept the tally. When the Throne priced a hold of storm-season salt above the crew it took to run it, she had done the sum she was given and sent the boats out into weather she had argued against and lost the arguing, and the sea had given Petar back drowned and kept the rest. The court that followed had needed a name to carry the loss and found hers already written at the head of the manifest. They would have hanged her for the salt. Adder Voss had paid, at the foot of the scaffold, whatever a broken loading-officer went for that season, and cut her down, and never once said what it had cost him. Four years on she still could not make that column come even. Some numbers didn't. And here she was, going in to shoulder a cargo she was forbidden even to weigh. The road had a sense of humour. It had never once been a kind one.

Adder Voss kept his counting-office in a black tent at the heart of the yard, and he was bent over a manifest when she came in — spectacles down his nose, a stub of tallow-pencil in a fist that had once hauled her up out of the dark by the collar and not let go. He'd gone heavier in the years since the fleet, grey through the beard, slower to stand. But he still read a page the way the Flame-priests read the fire: as though the numbers were the only honest thing in a lying world, and he meant to hold them accountable.

"Sable," he said, not looking up. "Shut the flap. You're letting the good air out and the flies in, and I've paid for neither."

She shut it. She did not sit, because sitting was a thing you did when you'd agreed to stay.

"You're loading short a quartermaster," she said.

"I'm loading short a quartermaster." He set the pencil down and looked at her over the spectacles, and there it was, the old weighing look, the one that had followed her out of a fleet court and into a condemned cell and had cut her down off the rope at the end of it. She hated that look. She owed everything she was standing in to that look, and she hated it the way you can only hate a thing you cannot pay back. "Belfry took the coughing sickness at the Weeping Rocks two runs ago and never shook it. I've been keeping the tally myself since, which is theft of my own time. I need someone who can split three hundred skins nineteen ways across a crossing and make every ration come out even at the far side."

"You need someone the Throne will let you hire."

"I need someone who's the best water-tally between here and the reefs." He said it flat, a fact off a page. "The Company doesn't answer to the Throne's red ink, Sable. Out on the road there's no red ink. There's what's in the skins and what's in the ledger and whether the two agree. You were always good at making them agree." A pause, weighted precisely. "It's one crossing. West to Lowmarch, sell the salt, come home light before the road shuts. The berth pays a full share and a quartermaster's premium on top, in milled salt, weighed out at Lowmarch scales. It's more coin than you've seen since they took your coat."

It was. It was a great deal more, and both of them knew to the penny how little she had, which was the trouble with Adder: he never had to threaten you with what he knew. He simply let you feel him knowing it.

She thought about the four salt-pennies in her pocket. She thought about the winter behind her — the doors that had shut, the slow humiliating schooling in exactly what a struck name was worth on the Oststrand mole, which was nothing, which was less than nothing, which was a grown woman counting a thumb of foul rock-salt in her palm at a gate that would not open. And she thought, because she could not help thinking it, about a plain grey crate she had not yet laid eyes on, sitting somewhere out in the loading, being heavier than it had any right to look. A wise woman would ask more questions. A wise woman would also still have a coat.

"There's a catch," she said. "You've got a face on you like there's a catch."

Adder took off the spectacles and rubbed the red marks they'd left, and for a moment he looked less like a caravan-master and more like a tired old man who had been carrying something heavy for a long time and would carry it a while yet.

"One thing," he said. "There's a piece of private freight going west on this run. A crate. It's not yours to weigh and it's not yours to log. When you close the manifest it'll come up one short of the truth, and you'll leave it one short, and you won't ask me or anyone whose it is or what's in it. That's part of the wage. The premium's for that as much as the water."

"Whose is it?" she asked, which was the one thing he had just told her not to.

"Sable."

"I'm not asking to log it. I'm asking whether I wake up at Ninefold with the Guild's irons on my wrists for hauling some lord's unpaid toll — or worse than a toll. A quartermaster who doesn't know what rides in her own train isn't careful, Adder, she's just blind, and you didn't spend good coin cutting a blind woman off a rope."

That reached him. She had aimed it to. For a moment the old thing came up in his face — the fleet-deck look, the one he had worn telling frightened men to hold a line while the sea came over the rail — and then he folded it away, and what was left underneath was only an old man who was tired in a place sleep did not reach.

"It's not contraband the Guild will weigh you for," he said. "It's not weapons and it's not poison and it's not a person" — and there the smallest hitch went through him, a hairline crack across a flat wall, gone before she could be sure she had seen it — "and it will not get you hanged. That I'll swear to, on the Flame or on anything colder you like. The rest of it isn't mine to hand you. And if I did hand it you, it would be a weight you'd carry the whole width of the reach whether you wanted the carrying or not. Let me keep this one on my own book. You've hauled enough that was mine."

It was the nearest he had come, in four years, to naming the thing that stood between them, and it went in harder than the salt-iron had. He was doing it again — lifting a weight off her and setting it on the pile she could never pay down, and doing it so gently that she could not even find the edge of it to be angry with. That was the whole cruelty of Adder Voss. He never made you carry anything. He simply carried you, quietly, and let the owing do the rest.

Sable was quiet. A quartermaster's whole religion was the balanced tally — the terrible, simple faith that if the ledger and the world disagreed, someone was going to die of it out where there was no forgiveness. Adder Voss knew that about her better than any living soul, had built his own career on that about her, and he was sitting there asking her to carry a lie across the Saltreach with her name on the book.

"Since when does the Verdigris Company run cargo off its own manifest," she said.

"Since it started paying better than salt." He put the spectacles back on. The tired old man folded away and the caravan-master came back up over him like water over a stone. "Don't make it a question, Sable. I'm doing you a kindness by not letting it be one."

And there it was — the debt, laid on the table between them without a word, the way he always laid it. He was doing her a kindness. He had done her the largest kindness one person could do another, once, at the end of a rope, and he had never asked her for a single thing on account of it, and that was the worst of it. Sable Coyne could bear being owed. It was owing that itched under her skin like salt worked into a wound, that kept her awake, that had put a knife of resentment through the middle of every good thing the man had ever done for her. She would rather cross the Glare with a lie on her book than spend one more season owing Adder Voss her life and doing nothing whatever to work it down.

So she said yes. She told herself it was the four salt-pennies, and the coin at Lowmarch scales, and the road under her again instead of the black stones of a city that had struck her out. All of that was true and none of it was the reason, and she knew the difference even as she reached out and took his hand on it, and Adder knew it too, and neither of them said so. It was, she thought, walking back out under the green arch into the last of the loading, a fine thing to be back at work. She had said yes for every wrong reason there was, and there was a certain freedom in that. A woman with nothing left to protect could at least stop pretending to be wise.

ch2.body:
By the grey of first light the Verdigris Yards had become a machine for turning salt into distance, and Sable stood at the dead centre of it with a tally-board and did the one thing left in the world she knew how to do without a flaw.

Forty-one camels knelt in their strings while the loaders built the panniers up their flanks block by white block — milled salt out of the Oststrand pans, wrapped in reed matting, sealed with the Company lead. Each block was worth its own weight over again in the tide-markets of Lowmarch, and worth a man's life anywhere in the middle of the reach, where you could neither eat it nor drink it nor trade it to the sand. That was the joke the whole road was built on, and Sable had never once found it funny. The most precious thing a body could carry across the Saltreach was salt. The one thing that could not keep a body alive out there was salt. You could die of thirst lying on a fortune, your mouth full of money.

She built the load the way her father had taught her and the fleet had drilled into her: weight low and even, no string carrying its own ruin, the water spread across the whole caravan so that no single loss — a foundered camel, a burst skin, a raider's lucky arrow — could take out the margin between the crew and a dry death.

The camels she had learned by name before she learned half the drovers, because the camels were the ones who would kill you by dying. There was Old Ката at the head of it all, the grey camel-mother, who led the first string and whom the drovers approached the way sappers approach an old and temperamental mine. There was Bittern, splay-footed and sweet, who would carry a third again her share and never once grumble of it. There was Thief, who would have the glove off your hand if you gave her the opening, and Salt-Widow, who had outlived three of her own calves and every driver but one, and a gangling ill-made two-year-old the crew had named Toll because he ate like a Guild factor and gave back about as much. Sable set the heaviest panniers on the steadiest backs and the water across all of them, and she went down the strings with her palm running along their flanks, feeling for the hitch in a stride or the sick heat of a girth-gall, because a caravan-master counted crates and a quartermaster counted heartbeats, and the difference, out on the road, was the whole difference between arriving and not. Down the water-line Ino trotted at her heel with the tally-board, calling the count, and she made him call it twice, because water was not salt and could not be reckoned in your head and trusted. Salt you could always buy more of. Water was the number that killed you, and it was tallied to the swallow, every skin weighed full and sealed and its seal checked, three hundred and eleven of them, nineteen throats and forty-one thirsts to carry to Lowmarch and — the sums ran cold and clean behind her eyes — no margin at all for a foolish day.

"Three-eleven, sealed and split," Ino said, glowing, when the last skin went up. "Even to the far side, Quartermaster. I checked it against your split three times."

"Check it a fourth on the road," she said. "The desert unchecks things."

There was a rhythm to the last hour of a loading that Sable had missed the way you miss a language you were raised speaking. The drovers went down the strings tightening and testing; Doria's cook-wagon took on its own smaller tally of flour and oil and the bitter road-herbs she doctored with; the beasts groaned up onto their feet one string at a time, towering, and stood chewing at the morning with the vast indifference of animals who had crossed the reach more times than the people leading them. Somewhere down the line a flame-priest was going with a censer of hot salt, blessing the crossing in the name of the Kept Flame — touching each camel's brow, each sealed water-butt, asking the fire that had never died to see them dry-shod to Lowmarch and safe home before the road closed. Sable did not hold with priests. But she noticed she had stopped where the low drone of the blessing carried, and she let it carry, because whatever a person did or did not believe, three hundred and eleven skins was a thin enough wall that you took your luck wherever it was offered and paid it no mind at all if it happened to be wearing a robe.

The crate came in near the end, when the light had gone from grey to a hard flat white and her list was all but closed.

It came on a hand-barrow pushed by two porters she did not know — sweating, both of them, in the morning cold, and struggling with the thing as though it weighed three times what a crate that size had any business weighing. Plain grey wood, the size of a seaman's chest. No chandler's mark. No Company brand. Roped twice and sealed at every knot with grey lead.

She went to log it out of eleven years of reflex — hand to the board, pencil coming down — and a voice at her shoulder said, "Not that one."

He had come up on her without a sound, which was a trick, in a yard, past camels. A spare grey man, ageless in the way clerks and undertakers went ageless, with a meek stoop and clean, soft, careful hands and a pair of eyes that did not match the meekness at all. He put something into her palm and folded her fingers shut over it before she could look, and the weight told her before her eyes got the chance. Cold. Far heavier than its size. When she opened her hand there were three coins lying on it, black as basalt and dense as sin, struck with the salt-star of the Meridian mint — salt-iron, the old throne-metal, each one worth more milled salt than a drover earned across a whole season.

Nobody paid a bribe in salt-iron. That was the thing that snagged, even then, even with three fortunes cold in her fist. Salt-iron was what crowns paid armies in. It was throne-money, ledger-money, treasury-metal, the sort of coin that remembered every hand it had passed through. Smugglers paid in salt or in favours or in the promise not to cut your throat. They did not reach into a pocket and come out with the Throne's own iron.

She looked up from the coins to the man who had given them, and gave him the read she gave a manifest that would not foot, and got almost nothing back. He was made to give nothing back. Everything about him had been sanded smooth — no rings, no accent she could place, no callus but the writing-callus riding the second finger, boots a shade too good for the coat thrown over them. A messenger, then, and a careful one: not the purse but the hand the purse had hired to keep itself clean. Whoever had struck this bargain wanted three walls between themselves and a quartermaster's memory, and had paid, in cold Throne-iron, for every one of them.

"The crate isn't weighed and isn't logged," the grey man said, in a voice as soft and level as his hands. "It rides west, it comes off at Lowmarch, and until then you never saw it. Master Voss has explained the terms. That"—a flick of the meek eyes at her closed hand—"is the courtesy on top of them, from someone who would rather you were content than merely paid."

"You'll want to say the threatening part now," Sable said. "About what becomes of me if I do log it after all."

"No," the grey man said, mild as milk. "People remember threats. I would very much rather you forgot me entirely."

"And who's that," she said. "This someone who'd rather I was content than paid."

"Someone who is not here." He was already stepping back, already folding himself into the churn of the loading the way clerks did, present one moment and simply absent the next. "Safe road, Quartermaster."

Then he was gone, and the crate sat there on its barrow, unlogged, waiting for her to make it disappear off her own book.

When she was sure the grey man was well away, she crouched and put her hand flat on the lid, the way she'd lay a hand on a fevered animal to feel what was wrong under the hide. The wood was ordinary. What was under it was not. Cold came up through the grain into her palm — a deep, mineral, patient cold that had no earthly business in a yard warming fast toward noon. And when she tipped the crate a finger's width to feel how its ballast rode, it did not shift like packed salt, or slosh like water, or grind like a chest of tools. It sat. It had the total, dead, single weight of a thing that was all one solid piece the whole way through. Iron, she'd have said, if she'd had to say. Except that no honest man crated iron, sealed it with grey lead, and paid in the Throne's own coin to keep it off the road's books.

She set it down soft. She wrote nothing. And her tally — for the first time in her working life — went west one crate short of the truth, and the truth sat cold and heavy under a mat of reed on a Company barrow, and it had paid, she thought, a very great deal to stay a secret.

The new drover was down at the water-line when Sable came along it, and Sable noticed her the way she noticed any figure that did not foot the sum.

The girl was young — nineteen, twenty — brown enough, but the wrong brown, a fresh brown laid over a skin that had lived indoors. She had a stillness to her that no real drover ever had, drovers being the twitchiest, most weather-nagged people alive. When Sable said, "You're the new water-drover," the girl only looked at her, and did not answer, and instead lifted her hand to a small bronze bell strung at her throat on a plaited cord and rang it once — a single clear note — and turned her other palm up and open. Empty. No words in it.

"Mute," Ino supplied, hovering, unable not to. "Master Voss took her on this morning, cheap. She came down the mole with nothing but the bell and the clothes on her. She's better with the strings than men who've teamed ten years, though, honest, you should see her with—"

Sable lifted two fingers and Ino swallowed the rest of it.

She had spent eleven years learning to read a person the way she read a manifest — for what was declared on the face of it and what rode heavy and unlisted underneath — and this girl did not balance. The hands on the lead-rope were wrong: too fine under their new blisters, a scribe's hands or a lady's-maid's, not a drover's horn-palmed paws. She stood too straight, in the way of people who had been taught how to stand. And her eyes had gone, once, quick and cool, to each of the yard's three gates and counted them and come back — the private arithmetic of someone who wanted, always, to know the way out.

But when Old Ката swung her ancient head around and bared a mouthful of yellow teeth — Old Ката, the lead camel-mother, forty years of foul temper packed into one moth-grey hide, who had already put two loaders into Doria's surgery that season — the girl did not flinch, and did not back off, and did not reach for a stick. She set her knuckles against the huge working jaw and leaned her whole weight in and rang the little bell, low and slow, by the animal's ear. And the old killer gentled under her hand like a pot lifted off the boil.

"Huh," said Ino, in a voice of pure reverence.

Sable did not share the boy's wonder. Two wrong things before noon, then. A crate that weighed like solid iron and paid its way in Throne-coin, and a mute drover with a scribe's soft hands who could talk the caravan's worst-tempered animal quiet without a single word.

The girl felt the weight of Sable's attention and turned, and for half a breath the two of them only looked at one another across the kneeling animal — and Sable watched the drover see her seeing, watched the quick private recalculation move behind the young face and the careful flattening of it back into a servant's blank. It was very well done. It was too well done. Nobody learned to empty a face like that hauling water; you learned it in rooms where the wrong expression cost you something, and Sable had learned it herself once, in a fleet-court, watching men price her life across a table. She knew the craft of it when she saw it worn by somebody else.

"She likes you," Sable said, and nodded at the lead-rope, because a question you couldn't ask was still worth the asking for the way a face answered it. "Keep her at the head of your string. Lose her and you'll spend the whole crossing chasing forty spooked animals across the flat." The girl inclined her head and rang the little bell once — a small clear note that might have meant yes, or thank you, or nothing whatever — and gave Sable back precisely the blank she had put on, and not one grain more than that.

On any other run in her life she'd have pulled the loose thread on each of them until something came unravelled, because the loose thread was the whole of her trade and the desert killed the people who let threads run.

But she had three salt-iron coins riding cold in her kit against a full share and a premium, and a berth she had taken for every wrong reason there was, and the entire art of keeping that berth, she understood now, was going to be the fine and unfamiliar art of not noticing precisely this. So she noticed it, and filed it, and wrote nothing down, and moved on down the line to check her seals. The seals were her one honest thing; she checked them the way other people prayed — twice, and then once more for the doubt — and found them whole, three hundred and eleven small grey lozenges of Company lead, every one a promise she could actually keep. She was getting, she thought, a great deal of practice at that lately. She wondered how much of it a person could get before the not-noticing stopped being a skill and started being a way to die.

ch3.body:
The bell at her throat was the whole of her voice now, and in eleven days Wren had learned to say a surprising amount with it.

One clear note to turn a camel. Two to still it. A soft shake muffled in her closed fist for yes; the bell pressed silent to her palm for no. It astonished her, how little a person truly needed to say aloud — and how much other people would rush to say for you, if you only let a silence sit there long enough to make them nervous of it. Silence, she had discovered, was the safest country she had ever lived in. No one could catch you out in a lie you never spoke. No one could hear, in the shape of your vowels, the schoolroom and the sea-view and the four hundred years of Meridian blood you were pretending you had never had. She meant to stay inside that silence for as long as it kept her breathing, and she had begun — and was uneasy at how easily she had begun — to find it almost restful.

She had spent eleven days learning to be no one, and it was harder work than anyone had warned her. The bell she had taken to at once. It was the rest of it — the walk that had to come up out of the hip and not the spine, the way a servant lets her eyes rest on the middle distance and never on a face, the trick of eating fast and without pleasure, of being always a little cold and a little hungry and never once remarking on either — that snagged at her a hundred times a day. Her grandmother's people had drilled her in it for a month in a shuttered room in the Pickle-Yards before they sewed her into these clothes and walked her down to the Verdigris Yards in the dark. Hold your tongue, hold your water, hold your name; and if all three should fail you, run for the old camel, because a beast will hide a girl when a person won't. She had thought it playacting, in the shuttered room. She had thought a great many things were playacting, in the shuttered room, that had since turned out to be the plain hard furniture of staying alive.

They marshalled at the edge of the world in the last of the dark, where the black grit of Oststrand's hinterland gave over all at once to the white. Wren stood at Old Ката's shoulder and watched the caravan pour itself into its order of march — the shape the drovers called the crossing-serpent, the same shape, she supposed, that caravans had poured into on this ground since before there had been a Throne to declare her dead. Adder Voss and the outriders at the head. The pack-strings behind in their long roped file, camels nose to tail. The water in the guarded belly of the column, where a raider would have to cut through the whole caravan to reach it. The tail-guard, the loose beasts, the cook's wagon. And, somewhere back along that file, nine camels behind her under a mat of reed and salt-block, the crate.

She did not look at it. She had gotten very good, in eleven days, at not looking at things.

Before the off, the cook found her.

Doria Fenn was a broad, unhurried woman with a face like a kind fist and forearms gone pale and shiny with the scars of decades of fires and knives, and she moved through the waking caravan the way a shepherd moves through a flock at dawn — touching, counting, mending, missing nothing. She took Wren's hands into her own without asking leave, and Wren nearly bolted out of her skin; but the cook only turned them palm-up and looked, unhurried, at the blisters the lead-ropes had torn and the soft skin splitting under them.

"You've not done this before," Doria said. Not a question, so it wanted no bell. She dug a little clay pot from her apron and worked a grease that smelled of tallow and bitter herbs into the raw places, with thumbs that were gentle and entirely without hurry. "There. Wet them tonight — never mind with what, you'll learn — it keeps off the rot. Don't pull that face, girl, you'll do a deal worse than that before we see Lowmarch." She held on a moment longer than the mending needed, her eyes going up to Wren's face, resting there — on the cheekbones, on the line of the brow, on some old sum she seemed half to be working and half to be refusing to finish. Something crossed her, a shadow of a thought, and did not settle. Wren rang the bell once, soft — thank you — and made herself breathe slow, and after a moment Doria let go.

"Aye," the cook said, to no one, and shook herself. "Stick by the old lady there. Ката'll teach you more than I've got time to." And she went on down the line, and Wren stood with her greased and stinging hands and her heart going like a struck bell that no fist could quiet, and understood that she had just been very nearly seen.

She turned into Old Ката to hide her face, and put her forehead against the great warm slope of the animal's neck, and breathed in the enormous smell of her — dust and lanolin and something almost sweet underneath — and let the fear come. It was better to let it come now, here, in the last of the dark, leaned up against a beast that would carry the knowledge of it to no one, than to have it lie in wait and ambush her later in the pitiless white light.

Eleven days ago she had been Wrenna Sarthe. Before that, for four years, she had been a dead girl.

Dead by the word of her own uncle. Halloran Sarthe sat the Meridian Throne "in trust" and had held it in trust the whole four years since he had put it about that the old blood was ended — that the Dowager's granddaughter had taken a southern fever and died of it, poor child, such a waste, and now there was no one steady left but Halloran to keep the salt and mind the reach. It was a good lie. It was, Wren had come to see, a far better lie than the truth, which was only that Halloran had needed her dead, and had very nearly, twice, managed it, and that the sole reason he had failed was an old woman under house-guard in Oststrand who was cleverer than the whole of his court together — a grandmother who had spent four years and every hidden coin and every last loyal servant she still commanded on the slow, patient work of turning a lie back into a living girl, and then pointing that girl west across the Saltreach with the one thing in the world that could make a court believe her.

That thing rode nine camels back, under the reed and the salt. Wren could feel it there the whole time, like a second sun at her spine, heavy and cold and waiting. She had been told never to look at it, never to go near it, never to let her face change when it was spoken of. She had not been told what it would cost the people around her if it were found — but she was learning to do sums out here, and she could reckon that one well enough. Every soul in this caravan had signed on to haul salt to Lowmarch for a season's wage. Not one of them had signed to die for a girl's name. She looked down the waking line of them — Ino with his tally-board, the grey teamster losing at bones even now, the sharp-eyed quartermaster moving through it all — and felt the weight of what they did not know settle onto her, and did not know what to do with it except carry it, silently, the way she carried everything now.

They went out onto the Saltreach with the sunrise, and Wren saw the desert whole for the first time and understood, in her stomach and not just in her schooling, why men out here priced water the way soft southern lords priced gold.

It was not sand. She had imagined sand. It was salt — a cracked white plain of it running clean to the round edge of the world, hexed and buckled into plates by ten thousand years of sun, so bright already that the drovers had wrapped their eyes to slits and so flat that the caravan cast its long dawn shadow out across the crust like the shadow of something far larger than itself. There was no green. There was no shade but the shade a body carried. There was only the white, and the enormous washed-out sky, and the far shimmer at the world's rim where the heat had already begun to lift false silver lakes off the crust and hang them, trembling, over nothing at all. The first mirage of the crossing. Wren's whole parched soul lunged toward the water of it before her mind caught up and named it a lie, and she thought: so that is how it kills you. It shows you the thing you want and lets you walk to it.

She had grown up on the near edge of this desert without once understanding it. In Oststrand the Saltreach had been a fact on a map, a white margin the salt-fleets skirted and the caravans dared, a place her tutors had named to explain why the two crowns hated each other across it and never once to explain why anyone crossed it at all. Now she walked upon the thing itself and understood that the map had been a lie of comfort. There was no skirting this. It went down, the drovers said, further than any well could reach — dig for a day and you found only more salt, drier and older and whiter, the bones of a sea that had died before there were kings to quarrel over its floor. Every league of it had to be carried across on the strength of what you loaded at the rim, and what you loaded was tallied to the swallow, and the tally was the only wall standing between the whole shuffling caravan and a death so clean and so complete it would leave them sitting up in the crust like salt-pickled saints for the next crossing to find.

The caravan found its rhythm within the hour, and the rhythm was slow, and the slowness was its own kind of terror, because you could see how far it was and how little you closed of it. The drovers walked. Camels' feet crushed the crust with a sound like a fire eating dry grass, a constant soft ruin underfoot. The water went out at the mid-morning halt in tallied measures, and Wren watched the whole grave ritual of it — the sealed skin, the marked cup, the clerk's board, every swallow set against a name, salt-cheap and water-dear, the true coin of the road counted out one throat at a time. She drank her measure and it was warm and tasted of the skin and it was the best thing she had ever had in her mouth.

By the second halt she had the shape of a caravan-day by heart, the way you learn a prayer before you understand a word of it. They walked in the cool and lay up through the worst of the heat under stretched awnings, the camels couched in a rough ring with the water in the guarded middle of them; they walked again into the long evening; they set a night-watch in three turns and burned a fire of dried dung that smelled of the very animals it came from, and someone always sang, low, so that the sound would not carry across the flat. Wren took her turn at the beasts and kept the bell shut in her fist through the dark hours, and learned the desert's one mercy, which was the cold — the same sun that would kill you by daylight letting go all at once at nightfall, until the salt ticked and cracked as it shrank and the stars came out so thick and low they looked like frost furred over a black window. She had never in her life seen so many. In Oststrand the Kept Flame washed the whole sky orange the night long, so that a person forgot there was anything behind it. Out here nobody kept any flame but the small one they could carry in their own two hands, and the dark was honest, and enormous, and did not care in the least who she was, and she found that in it she could breathe.

And she watched the quartermaster.

She could not help it. Sable Coyne moved through the crossing-serpent the way a good steward moves through a house she does not own but understands better than its master — up and down the file, into every string, her hand on ropes and seals and the necks of beasts, her eyes doing sums that never seemed to stop. Wren was afraid of her, cleanly and specifically, in a way she was not afraid of the others. The zealot pilgrim with his warm voice frightened her differently, in the gut; the desert frightened her in the throat. But the quartermaster frightened her in the mind, because Wren had felt those eyes go over her in the yards, once, and had felt them read her hands and her spine and her counting of the gates, and had felt them stop just short of the answer and choose, deliberately, not to take the last step to it. Wren did not know why she had chosen not to. She did not trust the choosing. A woman who could see that much and say nothing was a woman keeping her own accounts, and Wren had learned, in a court that ran on exactly such women, never to mistake a closed mouth for a friendly one.

Only Old Ката asked nothing of her. That was the whole of why Wren loved the animal already, eleven days in — not the way you love a pet, but the fierce cornered way you love the one thing in a strange country that does not need you to be anybody at all. The old camel did not care whose blood ran under the borrowed brown of Wren's skin. She cared that Wren's hands were steady on the rope, and that Wren had learned quickly where the sweet place was under her jaw, and that Wren rang the bell low and never sharp. In return she carried Wren's fear without comment, and set a pace the younger beasts could trust, and turned, now and then, to breathe her enormous grassy breath into Wren's face as if to tell her the one thing no person on the caravan could be trusted to hear: still here, still walking, still alive. It was not much of a confidant. It was the only one Wren had, and she had begun to tell it everything, in the single language out here that cost her nothing and gave nothing of her away.

And yet. When the false silver lakes swam up off the Glare-white distance and her heart failed her, it was to the quartermaster's straight back that Wren's eye went for its bearing — that unbothered, unhurried, unfrightened back, moving down the line as though the desert were merely another ledger that would, in the end, be made to balance. Wren fixed on it. She rang her bell soft against Old Ката's flank to bring the old camel up into the file, and buried the dead girl a little deeper under the mute one, and pointed herself, and her secret, and her impossible name, out into the white after that back, west, toward a throne she was not sure she wanted and a road that did not care either way.

ch4.body:
By the fourth day out the caravan had become a single long animal, and Sable Coyne was the part of it that counted the water.

She had forgotten, over the black wasted winter, how much she loved it — not the thirst and not the glare and not the way the salt got into every crack of a body until you tasted the road in your own sweat, but the work of it, the clean cold arithmetic of keeping nineteen souls and forty-one beasts alive across a plain that wanted them dead by simple indifference. On the fleet she had commanded men. Out here she commanded a number, three hundred and eleven skins dwindling by a reckonable amount each day, and the number did not care about her disgrace or her name or the red ink across the fleet-rolls. The number only asked to be told the truth and kept even. She could give it that. It was, she had begun to think, the only relationship in her life that had never once let her down.

Four days had worn the crew into its shape. Marsh had the tail-guard and a slow-burning dice-feud with two of the drovers that Sable pretended not to see, so long as the losses stayed inside the caravan and off the water; Doria fed them twice a day from the wagon and stitched what wanted stitching and asked, in her flat unhurried way, after everyone's water and everyone's bowels, which out here amounted to the same question. The mute drover kept Old Ката at the head of her string and did her work well and silently and drew, Sable noticed, no more notice than she strictly had to — which was itself a kind of notice, if you were the sort of woman who watched people trying not to be watched. And nine camels down the file, under its mat of reed and salt-block, the grey crate rode as it had ridden since the yards, giving off, when Sable passed it in the blue cool of the morning tally, the faint patient cold she could have sworn she felt come up through the soles of her boots. She did not touch it. She had three salt-iron coins to remind her not to, and a berth she meant to keep.

Each dawn she and Ino ran the tally before the off, in the blue cold, by lamp. He called the sealed skins and she checked her split, string by string, throat by throat, salt-cheap and water-dear, and it was the boy's great daily happiness and she would sooner have died than let him see her know it. On the fourth morning the sums came up two measures light.

"Recount," she said.

"I did. Twice." Ino's face had gone stricken, because a light tally in the Saltreach was not a clerk's error, it was a coffin with the lid not yet on. "Two measures short on the pilgrim's string, Quartermaster. I sealed it full myself, I swear it on the Flame, I—"

"I believe you." She was already walking.

She found the pilgrim at his morning devotions, which was to say she found Brother Kest kneeling in the white with an empty water-cup upturned in the salt before him and the last bright bead of a measure of tallied water soaking away into the crust at his knees. He was a big, soft-spoken man with a face made for gentleness, weather-creased around eyes that were the warmest she had met on the whole caravan, and he was smiling as he watched two full measures of the crew's survival drink into the ground that would give not one drop of it back.

"You poured off your ration," Sable said. It was not quite a question. She had a talent for saying the appalling thing flatly, and it had cost her, over the years, most of the friends she'd started with.

"I gave it back," Kest said, and rose, unhurried, dusting salt from his knees. His voice was a low warm current; you wanted, against all sense, to drift on it. "A measure to the ground, that the road might remember it is not owned. And a measure this morning to the little killing-tempered camel your drovers all fear, because she is old and she carries more than her share and no one had thought to tally her thirst against her worth." He said it without a scrap of reproach, which was somehow worse than reproach. "You keep a very fine ledger, Quartermaster. I have watched you keep it. Every swallow set against a name, every name against a price. I only wonder, sometimes, who set the prices, and whether they ever crossed this ground themselves, and whether the salt agreed to belong to them, or was simply told that it did."

"The salt doesn't agree to anything," Sable said. "That's rather the point of salt."

"No." He smiled, delighted, as if she'd handed him a gift. "But we agree, don't we, on its account. We agree that a block of it is worth a man's day, and a skin of water worth his week, and a life"—the warm eyes held hers, perfectly kind—"worth whatever the last person to weigh it decided it should fetch. You of all people know how those weights are set, and by whom, and how little the truth is consulted when they set them. You wear the fleet in your shoulders still. Somebody weighed you once, and struck your name, and here you are hauling salt for a wage. Did that price feel just to you? Or only enforced?"

It went in cleaner than she liked, the way only a true thing could. She let the silence do its work, because she had learned that trick too. "Out here your principle costs two measures of water," she said at last, evenly, "off a string that's carrying an old woman and a sick teamster among others. You didn't give your ration back to the ground, Brother. You took it off them. The road doesn't send the bill to the man who feels holy pouring it out. It sends the bill to whoever's throat comes up dry first at the Glare." She crouched, righted his cup, turned it in her fingers. "You want to make an offering, make it of your own thirst on your own time and don't touch my tally. Believe me or don't — I've buried people who believed prettier things than you're saying, and they died just as thoroughly."

For a moment something moved far back behind the warmth in his face, quick and cold and gone, like a fish turning under still water, and Sable — who had spent eleven years learning to see exactly that, the thing under the thing — marked it and said nothing and felt the small hairs rise along her arms. Then Kest bowed his head, gentle again, all pilgrim. "You are a hard woman and a just one," he said, "and I think the road has not finished with either of us. I'll take my water off my own tongue hereafter, Quartermaster. You have my word on the Vow— " a breath, a smile, a smooth correction, "—on my vows."

She let it go. She docked his string's ration back to even, entered the loss in red, made Ino watch her do it so the boy would learn that you wrote the wound down and did not hide it, and carried the small cold snag of that word he had not quite finished with her the rest of the morning. She had known warm men before who went cold underneath. She had generally been right to.

Ino fell into step at her elbow when it was done, subdued, the tally-board hugged to his chest. "He gives me the creeps," the boy confided, low, as though the pilgrim might hear it across the whole length of the caravan. "And he's the kindest man aboard. He remembered my mother's name off one telling. He gives me the creeps and I can't say why, and that's worse, somehow, than if I could."

"You can't say why because he hasn't given you a reason yet," Sable said. "That's the trick of him. A man who is all warmth and no reason is a man saving his reasons for later." She did not yet know what Brother Kest's reasons were. But she had felt that cold thing turn over once behind his eyes, at the word he had swallowed and smoothed away, and she had spent eleven years learning that the desert and men were alike in the single way that counted: the thing that killed you was almost never the thing on the surface. "Enter the loss in red and let him be," she said. "And Ino — the day he does give you a reason, you come and tell me before you tell your own two feet to run."

The wool-wagon came up on their dust in the flat gold of late afternoon, and it was, from the first glance, a lie about itself.

Sable saw it while it was still a shape shivering in the heat-haze off the eastern crust, and she knew the shape was wrong before she could have said why. It was a wagon where a wool-buyer this deep into the crossing had no business having one — high and lacquered and running on good iron-shod wheels, drawn by a matched four of desert-bred camels that had cost more than the whole Verdigris string, with a striped awning and shuttered windows and two outriders whose ease in the saddle had nothing of the wool-trade in it. A wool-buyer travelled light and cheap and haggled over water. This travelled like a small mobile court that happened to have wool painted on the door as a courtesy to the credulous.

By the time it drew even, Adder had already sold it escort-right — of course he had; road law let any traveller buy shelter under a caravan's guns for a fee, and the fee this one paid, Ino reported, wide-eyed, was salt enough to reprovision the whole crew at Ninefold. Which meant the wool-wagon was now Sable's problem: its water to fold into her tally, its place to fix in the order of march, its owner to reckon with.

The owner was waiting for her in the lee of the wagon with two cups already poured, as though she had known to the quarter-hour when the quartermaster would come to arrange her ration.

"You'll be Coyne," the woman said. "They say you count better than anyone west of the Throne, and that you were cashiered for it, which I find I like enormously. Sit. I've a wine that survived the heat better than I did — a small miracle, and I intend to profit from it before it changes its mind." She was perhaps forty, dark and quick and elegant in the way of someone who has decided elegance is a form of armour and worn it into a second skin, with a mouth built for amusement and a pair of eyes that were doing to Sable, unmistakably and unhurriedly, precisely the thing Sable did to a suspect manifest. "Ysolde Marrin. I buy wool for the Coral Seat's clothiers. You needn't believe that, but I'd take it as a courtesy if you'd pretend to, at least until we know each other better."

"I don't drink another traveller's wine on the first day," Sable said. "It's a bad habit to teach the crew."

"Then teach them a worse one another day, and drink it with me privately." Ysolde smiled up at her, entirely unoffended, and lifted her own cup. "The Drowned Mother forgives most things, Quartermaster, but never a wasted vintage. Now. I'm told you're carrying a great deal of salt west, which is unremarkable, and a very great deal of care about it, which is not. A quartermaster who checks her seals four times a day is either the finest on the road"—the eyes flicked, once, mild as milk, out over the crossing-serpent, over the strings, over one particular grey crate riding under its mat nine camels down—"or a woman who has been given something to worry about. Which are you? You may lie. I'll enjoy it either way."

"You've a Lowmarch tongue on you," Sable said, not answering, buying the half-second she wanted, "and Lowmarch manners, and a wagon that cost more than the wool in three good seasons would ever clear. If you're a wool-buyer, I'm a flame-priest."

"Then bless me, Mother, for the road is long." Ysolde's smile widened; she had beautiful teeth and used them the way a card-player uses a good hand. "I am a wool-buyer the way you are a drover, Quartermaster — which is to say, entirely, for the whole length of this crossing, and we shall both keep our other trades folded up small and dry where the salt can't reach them. There. That's honest, and it's more than you'll get from most. I'm told the Meridian find honesty a little indecent, but I was raised under the Drowned Mother, and she teaches that everything comes out in the wash in the end, so one may as well start the wringing early." She tipped her head, studying Sable with an open and unhurried pleasure. "You didn't sit. You didn't drink. You corrected my cover inside a minute and did it bone-dry. I think I am going to enjoy you enormously, and I think it is going to be inconvenient for the both of us, and I find that I don't much care. Do you play at anything, Coyne? Bones, cards, kings-and-toll? A crossing is very long, and I am poor company sober."

Sable had a great many things to worry about, all of them cold and heavy and unlisted, and she had just watched this wool-buyer count them at a glance the way Sable had counted the gates in a mute girl's eyes. Trouble, then. Elegant, funny, salt-rich, court-trained trouble, riding under the Company's guns with a painted door and a sharper knife than either of them was showing.

"I'm the finest on the road," Sable said, and did not sit, and did not touch the wine. "You can put that in your book. And you'll fold your four camels' water into my tally at the morning halt, by measure, sealed, same as every throat out here — the wine's your own affair, but the water's mine, and out here the water's the only thing I'll ever argue with you about." She turned to go, and then, because the woman's mouth had curved at *argue* in a way that had put an unexpected and unwelcome warmth up the back of Sable's own neck, she added, over her shoulder, "There's a common table at the cook-fire after the beasts are down. Doria feeds anyone who'll eat off a tin plate. Come sit at it, if your vintage can bear the company. You'll get further asking your questions where I can watch your face."

"Oh," said Ysolde Marrin, delighted, raising her cup to Sable's retreating back, "I'll come. I always come to dinner, Quartermaster. It's the only place people ever tell the truth by accident."

ch5.body:
The caravan made camp the way Sable liked a ledger kept — in straight lines, everything accounted for, nothing left where the dark could take it.

She walked the lines at dusk with Ino a half-step behind, the tally-book braced on his forearm, and named the count as they went. Nine head to the first string, hobbled nose to tail; eight to the second; the water-butts lashed upright on the sledge-wagons, bung up, each chalked with the day's draw. And the salt — forty-one crates of block and one of ground, the Company's whole fortune for the season — roped under waxed canvas and counted twice, because salt was money, and money walked off in the dark if you let it believe you weren't watching.

"Two hundred and eight cups drawn today," Ino read off. "Against the tally I set at dawn. We're three over."

"Three over is three stolen," Sable said, not slowing. "Or three spilled, which is the same sin done by a clumsier man. Find me the mouth by morning."

"Yes, Quartermaster." He wrote it down. Ino wrote everything; he was seventeen and still believed the world could be made to sum if you only kept a good enough book. Sable had believed that once, in a black-basalt city, in another life with a uniform in it. She let him keep the faith a while yet.

At the tail of the second string plodded the crate that was in no book at all.

She let her eye slide over it the way you slide over a card you don't want the table to know you hold. A plain deal box, roped to the pack-saddle of a placid gelding named Bittern, no larger than a foot-locker — and yet Bittern walked under it the way a camel walks under true weight, hips dropped, each foot set down like a man choosing where to stand in a fight. A stranger had counted forty coins of salt-iron into her palm at the Verdigris Yards to keep that box off her tally and her mouth shut over both. Forty coins was a year of a quartermaster's wage. She had taken it because she was broke and blacklisted, and because, she'd told herself, a thing you were paid not to see was a thing that was no longer your problem.

Three days into the Saltreach she was learning that this was not how her mind worked. Her mind wanted to know what it weighed. Her mind always wanted the number.

"Coyne."

Adder Voss stood at the head of the camp, where a caravan-master stood, watching the west go from white to the color of a healing bruise. He was a broad, weathered slab of a man with a voice he never troubled to raise, because in twenty years no one had made him. Sable had served under that voice in the salt-fleet, had been broken by another man's order and hanged in all but the drop, and it was Adder who had bought her down off the rope with Company coin, for reasons he had never once named. She owed him her neck. He had never let her forget it by mentioning it, which was worse.

"Master."

"The wool-buyer's asked you to supper." He said it to the horizon. "Marrin. The one who bought escort-right off me at the last well."

"Buyers feed masters," Sable said. "Not quartermasters."

"This one asked for the quartermaster by name." A dry pull at the corner of his mouth. "Go and be fed. Be charming, if you've got any left in the barrel. And while she's charming you back — because she will — ask yourself why a wool-buyer pays caravan rates to cross the Reach going east, in autumn, when every fleece worth buying is being sheared behind us in the west." He finally looked at her, pale eyes in a brown face. "I like her coin. I don't like a sum that won't add. You're good with sums that won't add."

"I used to be good at a lot of things."

"You're good at owing me, too," Adder said, without heat, and turned back to his horizon, and that was the end of it.

Marrin's wagon did not smell of wool.

That was the first thing, and Sable was a quartermaster; first things were her trade. The wagon was drawn a little apart from the Company's honest square, curtained in oiled canvas dyed a deep sea-green that no working teamster would waste the money to dye, and it smelled of beeswax, of clove, of some warm resin that had never been within a hundred leagues of a sheep. A boy took her at the step and drew the curtain, and inside it was another country.

Lamps — real oil lamps, hung on gimbals so the road couldn't spill them — threw a honeyed light on a folding table laid for two. There was a cloth. There was a dish of olives glistening like wet jet, and white cheese, and a loaf still warm from a covered stone, and a green bottle sweating cold in a cradle of sand that someone had carried a long dark way to keep cool. In a desert where Sable measured a man's life out in cups, here was water enough to chill a wine.

"You're counting my sins already," said Ysolde Marrin, from a low chair, delighted. "I can see you doing it. Sit down and count them where I can watch — it's the only entertainment out here worth the fare."

She was perhaps forty, dark-haired, with a clever unhurried face and rings on both hands that she wore too plainly to be as valuable as they were. She poured without asking, two fingers of pale wine into two horn cups, and Sable noted the horn — silver would have been a boast, horn was a courtesy, a woman meeting a road-worn quartermaster on the road's own terms. Everything in the wagon was chosen. That told her more than the wagon's contents: this was a woman who chose.

"Lowmarch white," Ysolde said, watching her drink it. "From the terraces above the tide-market. My grandmother would say the Drowned Mother spits the sweet grapes up onto the rocks for her daughters, and I say the grapes grow where the men plant them, and we've never once agreed, she and I." She smiled. "Do you pray, Quartermaster?"

"I keep books," Sable said. "It's steadier. The Kept Flame never once put out a fire I paid to have lit."

"A Meridian, then. Oststrand in the mouth, under all that road-dust." Ysolde said it lightly, but the light was aimed. "I did wonder. A Verdigris quartermaster with the fleet in her spine. You stand a caravan the way you'd dress a deck."

There it was — the first cast of the line, easy, a fly laid soft on the water. She wants to know what I was, Sable thought, so she'll know what I am. Sable ate an olive and gave her nothing but the stone.

"You're a long way to buy wool," she said.

"And you're a long way to haul salt for a Company that hanged your reputation in the square," Ysolde returned, pleased, as if Sable had played a good card and she wanted her to know it was seen. "We're both a long way from where we're supposed to be. It's what makes the food better." She tore the bread, offered half across the cloth — a Lowmarch manner, Sable knew, bread from the hand meaning a truce for the length of the meal. Sable took it. It would have been a discourtesy the crew would hear about not to. "Tell me about your load."

"Salt."

"Salt," Ysolde agreed. "Forty-one and one. Block and ground. Consigned to the tide-market factors at Lowmarch, tolled through Ninefold on the Company's standing writ." She recited it like a woman reading Sable's own book back to her, and Sable kept her face a shut drawer while her pulse did something she disliked. That was not buyer's knowledge. That was the manifest. Someone had shown a wool-buyer the Verdigris manifest, or the wool-buyer had bought a look at it, which came to the same and cost more.

"You've done your reading," Sable said.

"I always do my reading." No apology in it. "It's why I'm poor company and good dinner. Here's what my reading tells me, Quartermaster, and you'll correct me, because you can't help it." She leaned forward into the honey light. "A salt-caravan rides at a known weight. Forty-two crates of salt, so many butts of water drawn down so many cups a day, so many head of camel eating their heads off — a caravan is a sum, and a good quartermaster is a woman who has the sum in her sleep. And your caravan," she said, gently, "rides three hundredweight over its sum. I watched your camels come off the last well. I've bought a great deal of freight in my life. I know the walk of an animal carrying more than the book admits."

For a breath Sable said nothing, because the honest answer — I don't know what it weighs, someone paid me not to ask — was the one answer she could never give. So she did what the fleet had taught her to do with a question that could sink you: she stood up inside it and made it small.

"You've bought a great deal of freight," she said, "and never once found a teamster's private grief roped under the canvas? A man's mother's dowry chest he'd sooner die than declare to the toll? A widow's press of tools? People carry their lives across the Reach, envoy. Not everything that weighs is worth your reading." She turned a horn cup slowly in her fingers. "You know the manifest to the crate. So you already know it isn't on the manifest. Which means you're not asking me what it is. You're asking me whether I know what it is." She let that sit. "That's a better question. I'll trade you for it. Answer mine and I'll weigh answering yours: what does the Coral Seat want on the Meridian road badly enough to send its wool-buyer this far east with silver rings she's too clever to be wearing?"

The lamps swung, gentle, on their gimbals. And Ysolde Marrin laughed — a real laugh, low and surprised out of her, the first thing all evening she plainly hadn't chosen — and sat back, and looked at Sable the way a duelist looks at a stranger who has just, without fuss, turned her own blade.

"Oh," she said softly. "There you are. I'd been talking to the quartermaster. Now I'm talking to you." She refilled Sable's cup though it wasn't empty, an excuse to lean near, and this near Sable could smell the clove-warmth of her over the wine, and was annoyed to find it worked. "I'll tell you what I want, since you asked so prettily. I want to go home to Lowmarch having earned my keep. That's all any of us out here want, isn't it — you, me, the boy with the tally-book, that grey pilgrim who won't take water from a woman's hand. To come off the Reach owing no one and owed a little." She tilted her head. "You told me true, before. You keep books because it's steadier than faith. But a book only balances, Sable Coyne, if both sides are honest. And you're carrying one side you haven't read."

"So are you," Sable said. "You just think you've read further."

"I usually have." Ysolde's smile stayed, but her eyes had gone to work, and Sable saw the whole shape of her then, the way you see the reef under still water when the light finally comes right: not a buyer at all. A weigher. A woman sent to find the Company's over-weight and price it in something other than salt.

She should have hated it. She had spent three years hating everyone who wanted a thing off her. What she felt instead, with a small internal disgust at herself, was the old fleet pleasure of a well-matched hand — the wish to keep playing, to see what the woman across the cloth would do next, played across a nerve she'd thought long dead. That was a debt too, she thought. Wanting something. The most expensive kind. You always paid it back with interest.

"Thank you for the supper," she said, and stood, because standing was the only sure way to leave.

"You'll come again," Ysolde said, not a question, warm and certain, and did not rise, and let her go.

Outside, the cold had come down hard the way it did on the Reach, the day's white furnace flipped clean over into a black bowl of salt-bright stars, and Marsh was waiting for her at the edge of the lamplight with his hands jammed in his coat and his laconic face doing the small tight thing it did when he'd rather not be the one to say.

"Rider," Marsh said. "West ridge. Doria saw it first, made me look."

Sable's warmth went out of her all at once. She followed his chin.

On the long dune to the west, black against the last stain of dusk that clung there after the rest of the sky had let go, a single horseman sat his mount and did not move. Not a camel — a horse, and only one people crossed the Reach's edge horsed instead of on the good sensible camel: soldiers who meant to be quick. Even at this distance, in this light, Sable's fleet-trained eye read the cut of him, the lance socketed at the stirrup, the pale surcoat that would be, in daylight, the grey-and-salt-white of the Meridian dune-cavalry. An outrider. A scout. He sat there long enough to be certain he'd been seen — that was the message, that was the whole of it — and then he turned his horse without haste and went down the far side of the dune and the desert took him.

"Escort," Marsh said, unconvinced, because escorts announced themselves and were paid for and did not sit on ridges at dusk counting your fires.

"Escort," Sable agreed, meaning the opposite, and behind her she heard the sea-green curtain draw, and knew without turning that Ysolde Marrin had come to her wagon's step to watch the same rider go, and was already, behind that clever unhurried face, re-pricing every sum the evening had shown her. The Meridian crown had put a horseman on their trail. The wool-buyer had seen it too. And somewhere in the dark at the tail of the second string, Bittern stood hipshot under a plain deal box that weighed three hundredweight more than Sable's honest world could account for, and Sable stood in the cold between all of it and did the only thing she knew how to do with a night that wouldn't balance.

She started, in her head, to count.

ch6.body:
They came to Dead-Drover's Waystation on the third night, in the blue hour when the salt still held the day's glare like a held breath, and Sable understood at once why no one made a joke of the name.

It had been a stage-post once, in the years the two crowns still pretended the road was a road and not a knife they both held. Now it was four courses of black-basalt wall standing open to the sky, a fallen arch, a cistern gone to a green scum you wouldn't water a dying man from, and the long low mound behind the wall that the crews called the drover, because a drover was in it. The story ran that a Company man had cut his string loose in a mirage-storm a generation back and walked out into the white to bring them home and never came home himself, and they'd found him in the spring sitting up against the wall, wind-cured, salt-kept, perfect, as if he'd only sat down to wait. The Saltreach kept its dead the way it kept everything else. It pickled them and held the account open.

"Cheerful," said Ino, at her elbow, too loudly, the way a boy is loud when a place has got into his chest.

"Water the animals first, then the people, then yourself," Sable told him, which was the order of things and also a kindness — give a frightened boy a tally to keep and you gave him a wall to stand behind. "And chalk the butts before dark. I don't want a single cup drawn in this place off the book. A haunted well is where an honest crew learns to steal."

They made the camp inside the old walls, out of the wind, the fires small and mean because the dead wood out here was two days behind them and every stick was carried. Doria set her cook-pot on the one blackened hearth the post still owned, and the smell of her lentils and dried mutton went around the ruin like a promise, and the crew's talk came back up out of its boots by degrees, the way it did, because people are people and a hot bowl is louder than a ghost. Sable did her rounds. She always did her rounds. She had learned in the fleet that a quartermaster who walked her lines at the same three hours every night bought a kind of luck you couldn't put in the book but could feel go missing the night you skipped it.

It was on the second round, past moonrise, that she saw the rider come in to Adder.

She would not have seen it if she'd kept to the walls. But she'd cut wide to check the west picket, where the mute drover kept her string, and so she was out beyond the fallen arch in the blue dark when a horse came up soft out of the flats — a horse, again, ridden by a man in no colors at all, a hood and a road-cloak and a good animal ridden quiet — and Adder Voss walked out from the wall alone to meet him, having known, plainly, that he was coming.

Sable stopped where she was and made herself part of the ruin.

She could not hear the words. She could see the shapes of it: the rider not dismounting, which meant not staying; Adder's big still head bent to listen; something passed down from the saddle to Adder's hand, small, a fold of something, a message or a token or a coin, and Adder's hand closing it away into his coat with a quickness that did not match the rest of him. Then the rider was gone, back the way he'd come, no more ceremony than the outrider on the ridge two nights past, and Adder stood a moment in the flats alone with his hand pressed flat to his own chest over whatever he'd put there, and Sable, who had followed this man's back through worse dark than this, knew the set of a man's shoulders when a thing has just cost him something he'd hoped not to spend.

And the fleet-officer she'd been before the rope, the part of her that read a night the way Ino read a column of figures, filed the whole of it against Adder's account and did not like the sum. A Guild factor rode the road in daylight, under a writ, with a lantern and a name, and dunned you for the toll to your face; a Guild factor did not come hooded and horsed across the dark flats to a ruin, pass a fold of something down from the saddle, and turn for home without a word or a light. That was not a factor. That was a man being reached — quietly, on a schedule, by people who did not want to be a name in anyone's book. Sable had seen that particular grammar of the dark before, in the fleet, worn by men who'd sold a course or a signal to the other crown and told themselves it was only ever the once.

She could have stepped out. She thought about it, the way you think about touching a blade to see if it's hot. Instead she was three strides back inside the arch, unhurried, a quartermaster on her rounds, when Adder came in through it and near enough walked into her.

"Coyne." Not startled. Adder did not startle. But a beat slow, and Adder was never slow.

"Master. You've a visitor."

"Guild factor." He said it easily, and that was how she knew. A true thing came off Adder flat and bored; a made thing came off him easy, oiled, ready. "Riding ahead of the toll. Ninefold's raised the water-price again — the Tollwright smells the season's short and he's pricing his neighbors' thirst. Wanted us warned so we'd not draw down too hard before the fort." He clapped her shoulder, once, the old commander's weight of it. "You'll want to tighten the tally the next three days. I'll leave the how to you."

It was a good lie. It was a good enough lie that a woman who did not know him would have written it down and slept on it. Everything in it could be true — the price did rise, the Tollwright was exactly that grasping, a warned caravan did draw down soft. It explained the rider, it explained the message, it explained the hand to the chest, and it gave her a task to keep her mind busy chewing. It was, Sable thought, the lie of a man who had lied to good people for a long time and had grown careful and kind about it, which was the worst kind to catch, because you had to want to catch it.

He clapped her shoulder as he said it, the old commander's weight of the hand, and when it lifted she saw the smudge on his fingers — a pale grey-white dust worked into the creases of them, on the pads and under the nails, where he'd handled the thing from the saddle. Salt, she thought. Of course. It was a salt road; everything on it was white; you woke with salt in the seams of your own hands. She thought salt, and let herself think it, because the other thought had nowhere yet to stand — a finer, greyer white than salt, soft as a moth's wing, the pale ash a man's fingers keep after they've touched a thing that has been marked with fire. She would remember the smudge later, in the Glare, when it was far too late to be worth the remembering. Tonight it was only salt.

"I'll tighten it," she said.

"Good girl." He went to his fire. And Sable stood in the cold arch of Dead-Drover's Waystation and felt the thing she owed him shift in her like ballast in a hold — because you cannot easily call a man a liar to his face when that same face once looked up at you on a gallows and paid the coin to bring you down. A life-debt was the heaviest freight on the road. It rode three hundredweight over every honest sum. She had spent three years learning to hate being owed, and had never once thought to be careful about owing, and here it was, the bill, come due in a ruin at midnight: Adder Voss had lied to her, plainly, and she was going to let him, because he had bought her breath and she had not yet finished paying it back.

She told herself she would watch. Watching cost nothing. That was the other lie of the night, and it was hers.

The scream, when it came, was a camel's, and it came from the west picket.

Sable was moving before she'd finished naming it — a camel down, or a camel gone, either a wound in the caravan's living purse — and the camp came up around her in the ragged way a camp does at night, shapes and sparks and Marsh's voice cursing for a light. Out at the picket the second string had bunched and shied, a wall of alarmed animal in the dark, and at the center of it a young cow named Skerry had gone to her knees in a fright with her lead fouled around a fallen block, hauling back against it, strangling herself on her own panic, and the whole string ready to catch it off her and bolt into the flats where the dark and the ghost would have them.

And the mute drover was in among them.

Wren — Sable had the name off the hire-book, one flat word, a drover paid the same morning as the silence Sable had been paid to keep — was down the throat of it where a wiser hand would not have gone, one shoulder set against Skerry's heaving neck, working the fouled lead with both hands by feel, her body a small still point the frightened animals were, unaccountably, beginning to gather themselves around. That was drover's craft of an order Sable didn't often see for hire. But a mute drover has one tool the rest of the trade leans on and she does not: the voice. You steadied a spooked string with your voice, low and level and endless, a river of nonsense sound that told the animals the world had not ended. The girl couldn't. What she had instead was the little brass bell every mute drover carried at the wrist, to be a voice — a tap for come, a shake for hold, the string trained to it as other strings were trained to a name.

Sable saw the bell come off her wrist.

It was nothing — the strap old, the panic hard, Skerry's shoulder catching the girl's arm as she leaned in — but the little bell tore loose and went down under the churn of feet, and Sable heard the one small crush of it, the flat dead cluck of brass going to shapeless metal under a camel's pad, and in that instant the drover had no voice at all, spoken or rung, nothing between her and a bolting string but two hands.

And Wren's mouth opened.
