Sable was near enough, by then, to see it — pushed in through the shying bodies with her own hands on hide and halter, near enough in the leaping light of Marsh's finally-lit lantern to see the girl's face turn up and her mouth come open on the word every drover in the world shouts at a moment like this, the word that was already shaped, hold, the breath already under it —

"HO," Sable roared, over her, into the string, the fleet-deck bark that could carry over a gale and a hundred panicking men, "HO, now — hold — HOLD," dropping her own weight onto Skerry's lead, throwing the whole authority of her lungs across the moment like a tarp thrown over a spark, "steady, you great fools, steady —" and the string, wanting only a voice, any voice, took hers, and shuddered, and held. Skerry came off her knees blowing. The dark did not get them.

It was over in a breath. It always was. Sable stood in the settling animals with the lead burning her palms and her heart going like a teamster's dice, and she did not look at the drover. She made herself not look. She looked at Skerry's fouled leg, at the fallen block, at Marsh coming up with the light and Ino behind him white to the lips clutching the tally-book to his chest as if the ghost had reached for it, and she said, in the flat bored voice of a woman for whom nothing at all had just nearly happened, "Cut that block out of the picket line before it does that again. Ino — a cow named Skerry, note her lamed, we'll look at the leg by daylight." And only then, last, as if it were the least of it, "Drover. You're bloodied. See Doria."

She let herself look then, for exactly as long as an order took.

Wren stood in the churned salt with her chest heaving and her empty wrist held against her, and she was not looking at the string or at her own torn hands. She was looking at Sable, and her mouth was shut now, shut hard, and her eyes above it were doing a thing that no hired drover's eyes should do to a quartermaster who had only bawled an order across a picket: they were afraid, and they were reading, and they were saying as plain as any bell what the mouth would not — you heard. Sable held the look a beat past comfort. Then she turned and walked her rounds, because a quartermaster on her rounds sees nothing that isn't in the book, and there is no line in any book for a mute girl who had, for half a held breath, been about to speak.

Later, past the last watch, Sable found the crushed brass in the churned ground where a camel had made it nothing, and she stood turning the flat ruined little thing in her fingers a long time. A drover with no bell was a drover the whole crew would notice — a silence with a hole in it, a question anyone might trip over the way Sable had. That was a loose end. A quartermaster hated a loose end. That was all it was, she told herself; that was the whole of the reason; it had nothing to do with the girl's afraid reading eyes.

She had a second bell in her kit by morning, the spare off a dead man's harness she'd carried three years and never spent, and she left it where a drover would find it and no one would see it left. And she did not, when she'd done it, examine why. Some sums you didn't run. That was a thing the road taught you too, though it took longer, and cost more, and Adder Voss had known it the whole time, out there in the flats with his hand pressed to his chest over the thing he'd been paid to carry and never say.

ch7.body:
Ysolde Marrin had been raised in a city that stood in the sea, and so she had never once, in forty-one years, feared the sky. In Lowmarch the danger came up at you — from the tide, from the reef, from the green weight below the stilts where the Drowned Mother kept her patient house. You watched the water. No sensible person watched the air.

The Saltreach was teaching her, at some length, to watch the air.

It came out of the west a little after noon on the fourth day, and at first it was only a wrongness in the light — the white flats going a curdled pewter, the far dunes lifting off the ground on a shimmer of false water and floating there, unmoored, like a fleet at anchor in a harbor that did not exist. She had thought it beautiful. She had, Drowned Mother forgive her, taken out her little book to make a note on the color of it for the report she'd never let anyone read, and it was the boy Ino who came pelting down the line crying the word the whole caravan then took up in a dozen throats — mirage-storm — and Ysolde looked up from her book and could no longer find the front of the caravan at all.

The air had filled with salt. Not wind as Lowmarch knew wind; a dry, luminous, blinding rush of ground salt lifted off the pan, and with it the light broke into pieces and lied. The camel six feet from her wagon-step became two camels, then a grey wall, then a shining lake with a camel drowning in it. Sound went strange and near and far at once. She heard Sable Coyne's fleet-bark somewhere ahead — close the line, hold your neighbor's tail, no one walks off after a well that isn't there — and Ysolde understood, with the small cold clarity that had kept her alive in three courts, that a mirage-storm did not kill you with its violence. It killed you with generosity. It showed you water. It showed you the way home. It showed you a companion beckoning, and you stepped off the line to take the kindness, and the desert closed over the place where you had been and kept you, wind-cured, perfect, sitting up against nothing at all.

So when her own wagon's off-wheel dropped into a brine-soft seam and canted, and a lashing gave, and one of her water-butts — one of only three she carried, a wool-buyer's honest ration — bounded off the bed and rolled away shining into the murk, Ysolde Marrin did the correct thing, the diplomat's thing, the thing that valued the self above the asset. She let it go. Water was replaceable at Ninefold. She was not replaceable anywhere.

And then, because the storm made liars of everyone, she watched a figure go past her canted wheel at a dead low run after the rolling butt — road-cloak, cropped hair, a quartermaster's tally-knife bright at the belt — and Ysolde heard herself say a word she had not chosen in twenty years of choosing all her words, and went after her.

"You," Sable said, when Ysolde caught her, both of them bent into the blind rush with a wool-buyer's water-butt finally run to ground between them in a hollow of salt, "are the stupidest clever woman I have ever met. Get behind me. Hold my coat. Do not let go of my coat if the Kept Flame himself walks up out of that light and offers you a chair."

"It's my water," Ysolde said, absurdly, into the wind.

"It's four cups a day for eleven days and it isn't worth your bones." Sable had the butt up on its end and was working it, and Ysolde saw the moment the quartermaster understood what Ysolde had already understood: that in going twenty strides after it they had put the storm between themselves and the line, and that the line was gone. Not near. Gone. The great sounding animal of the caravan, four hundred head and a hundred souls, had been swallowed as cleanly as a dropped coin, and the two of them stood alone in a shining nowhere with one water-butt and the light lying to them from every side at once.

Ysolde watched her not panic. That was the thing she would remember, after, out of a night she remembered too much of: Sable Coyne stood in the mouth of the thing that had killed the drover in the wall, and she got smaller and colder and more exact, and she did not once look at the beckoning water or the false road or the grey shapes that offered themselves. "We don't walk," she said. "Walking is how they find you sitting up in the spring. We dig in, we get low, we wait for it to blow through, and we do not trust one single thing the light tells us until the sun's back in one piece. Give me your hands, we build a wall." And she began, with a quartermaster's flat economy, to make the two of them a small mean shelter of the water-butt and a salt-scarp and both their cloaks, a shelter that valued survival over dignity absolutely, and Ysolde — who had bought her way out of every hard place she'd ever been, who did not, as a rule, do things with her hands — got down in the salt and dug.

The hours in it were the longest Ysolde had ever spent. The salt got everywhere, into the eyes, the teeth, the folds of the body, a fine bright grit that scoured you clean the way she imagined the desert had scoured the drover in the wall. The light never stopped lying. Twice she saw, with perfect clarity, the caravan not thirty strides off — the wagons, the fires, her own sea-green curtain — and twice Sable's hand closed hard over her wrist without the woman even turning her head, as if she could hear Ysolde's faith failing, and said, flatly, into the roar, "It isn't there. Nothing that far off is there. If you can see it, it's lying." And Ysolde, who had spent a life being the one who knew which things were lies, put her knowing into a stranger's hands and believed her, and the caravan wavered and dissolved and was only ever more salt and more light. In Lowmarch, when the tide-fog came in off the reef and hid the stilt-walks, you did not walk; you sat where you were and you sang, so your neighbors could find you by the sound and you would not step off the edge of the known world into the green. She had thought that the hardest discipline a person could keep, sitting still inside a fog that wanted to move you. The Reach asked worse. The Reach put your own salvation six feet away and made a virtue of refusing it.

She was not, she would admit only to the salt, entirely brave about it. There was an hour, deep in, when the wind's voice came apart into other voices — her grandmother's, a dead man's she did not name even to herself — and her breath went short and quick and useless, and it was the quartermaster's back against her own, the plain animal fact of another spine holding the cold off hers, that she steadied against. Not the words. Sable gave her no comfortable words. Only the weight, and the count under her breath, and once, when the worst of it passed, "There. That's the top of it. It always sounds like the whole sky's coming down just before it goes." As though the sky's coming down were a thing on a list she'd already priced.

The storm blew through at dusk and left them the cold.

They did not die, which Ysolde had privately rated a nearer thing than she let her face say. They came out of the salt at full dark under a sky scoured to a violence of stars, two small figures in a white waste with a horizon in no direction, and Sable took one look at the sky and said the caravan was that way, the Reach ran east-and-west and Ninefold's beacon would show at the third watch if the air stayed clean, and until the third watch they would sit still and burn nothing and share the butt by the cup, because water was tallied even between two, especially between two, and a night was survivable and a lost bearing was not.

So they sat in the lee of the butt with their backs together for the warmth two bodies made, which was not nothing and which Ysolde declined, with some effort, to make into more than it was, and they passed the cup between them by strict half-measures, and Ysolde Marrin, who was never off duty, discovered that she had walked off her own line too, out here — that a woman with salt in her hair and a stranger's warmth at her spine and no audience anywhere under the whole indifferent sky was a woman it was very difficult to keep being a diplomat about.

"You had a brother," she said, into the dark, because it was the truest cruel thing she knew about Sable Coyne, and because out here the truth was warmer than the lie. "In the salt-fleet. Before Oststrand hanged your name in the square."

She felt Sable go still against her back. "You did your reading."

"Petar Coyne. Junior officer. Lost off the flats the same season you left the service and the Company took you on with a rope-burn round your good name." Gently, now, because she had learned — a spymaster's discipline and, she was uneasy to notice, something warmer under it — where the reef lay under this still water. "You didn't leave the fleet, Sable. You were driven off it. And the man who drove you is still wearing a Meridian uniform and calling it order, and you crossed a desert to haul another crown's salt sooner than breathe that city's air again. I don't have to be clever to see that. I only have to have lost something myself."

For a long time the only sound was the salt ticking as it cooled. Then Sable said, in a voice with all the flatness gone out of it, worn down to the plain grain of the wood: "He was owed his life. By the man over him. A signal, a boat, a half-hour's care — nothing, a line in a book, a debt any decent officer pays without blinking. And the man didn't pay it, because paying it would have cost him a reprimand he'd sooner drown a boy than take. So my brother went into the flats owed, and the Reach kept him, and when I said out loud in the wrong hall exactly what I've just said to you, they broke me for it. Not for lying. For counting. For saying the debt out loud where the man who owed it had to hear the number." A breath. "That's what I know that you don't, envoy, for all your reading. Everything out here is priced. Salt, water, a girl's silence, a night like this one. Everything's got a number and I can find it. Except the one thing. The thing a man owes and doesn't pay and no scale in the world will make him. That's the only sum I've never been able to run, and it cost me my brother, and I have been very careful ever since to owe as little as I can and be owed even less."

For a while Ysolde said nothing, which was itself a kind of confession, from her. Then, because the woman had given her a true thing and the desert made a debt of an unanswered truth: "I serve the Coral Seat because the Coral Seat is the only mother I was left. Did your reading get that far? — no, of course not, mine's the better-kept book." A thin thread of the old wit, and under it something she had not meant to spend. "There was a house of us, once, on the third tide-terrace. The reef took the terrace in a spring flood when I was nine — the Drowned Mother's own hand, my grandmother said, which is a fine thing to tell a child about the water that ate her family. The tide-court fed me after. Housed me, schooled me, made me useful, and useful is not the same as loved, but a drowned girl learns not to be particular. So I am the Coral Seat's, the way you were the fleet's, except no one ever hanged my name, they only made very sure I'd never have a name that wasn't theirs to spend." She turned her head; Ysolde felt the movement more than saw it, in the dark, spine against spine. "You asked me across the cloth what the Coral Seat wanted so badly it sent its wool-buyer east. I gave you a diplomat's answer. Here's the true one, since we're being kept alive by each other's backbone and it seems poor manners to lie: the Coral Seat wants leverage on Oststrand it can't get with ships, because ships can be counted and answered and this cannot. It sent me to find the one thing on this road worth more than the road. And I have spent four days deciding it must be roped somewhere under your canvas."

"You don't know that," Sable said, too quickly.

"No," Ysolde agreed, gently, "I don't. And neither, I begin to think, do you. Which is the most interesting thing you've told me all night, and you didn't say a word of it." She let the cup pass between them, half-measure, strict. "There we are, then. Two women who were spent by the only houses that ever kept them, sitting in the one place on the Reach where nobody's spending us. It won't last past the beacon. Enjoy it. I find I am."

And Ysolde Marrin, spymaster of the Coral Seat, sent east with silver rings and a false wagon to find the Verdigris Company's over-weight and price it into a treaty that would ruin the Meridian crown, sat with her back against the back of a woman who owed nothing and wanted nothing and had just, unknowing, told her exactly what she was — and understood, all at once and far too late to do anything sensible about it, two things she could not afford at the same time.

The first was that the caravan's three hundredweight of over-weight was not a smuggler's private grief. A woman this careful about owing did not take forty coins of salt-iron to smuggle a dowry chest. Someone had made Sable Coyne owe a silence, and had paid a year's wage for it, three days into the road, going east; and the only cargo worth a year's wage and a lifelong silence on the Meridian road, in an autumn when the whole of Oststrand was whispering that the Regent had at last done something quiet and permanent about the succession — was proof. Ysolde did not know yet what shape the proof took. She was a weigher; she knew the weight of a thing before she knew its name. And this thing weighed like a crown.

The second thing she understood was that she was going to have to take it from this woman. And that she no longer wanted to.

"You're very quiet," Sable said. "That's a first. It's almost restful."

"I'm counting," Ysolde said, and felt Sable's short surprised breath of a laugh go through both their spines, and hated, with a clean unfamiliar completeness, the report she was going to have to write.

The beacon of Ninefold came up out of the east at the third watch, a low steady red star that did not float or lie, and they went toward it through the cold together, sharing the last of the water by the cup, the diplomat and the quartermaster, each of them carrying a weight the other hadn't yet been shown, each of them — for one honest night in a country that kept everything — carrying it a little less alone.

ch8.body:
Wren had learned to hold her whole self behind her eyes, and so she watched, and did not speak, and knew more than any of them guessed.

She knew the camels first, because the camels were the only ones who had never once asked her a question. She had come to the string a hired silence, a name off a book, a girl with a bell at her wrist and a fear behind her teeth so old and so large it had stopped feeling like fear and started feeling like weather; and Old Ката had turned her great deliberate head down out of the dawn and breathed the whole story of her over with one long green-hay breath and made, apparently, no objection. That was three mornings back and a life ago. Old Ката was the caravan's lead camel-mother, twenty seasons on the Reach, worth more salt than the girl who tended her, and she suffered Wren to sleep against her flank in the cold and walked the young cows straight because Wren walked at her shoulder, and Wren, who had been Wrenna Sarthe in another country and was learning at some cost not to be, loved the old cow with the flat total love of a person who has been given exactly one thing she is allowed to keep.

She did not love the quartermaster. Love was the wrong word and Wren had grown careful, out here, about words, having so few she was permitted. But she watched Sable Coyne the way you watch weather off the sea, because two nights back in a dead man's ruin the quartermaster had roared a stranger's word over the top of Wren's own opening mouth and thrown a caravan's whole authority across the half-breath in which Wren had nearly, nearly, spoken — and had then looked at Wren with a face like a shut drawer and said see Doria and walked away as though nothing had happened, as though a mute drover's mouth had not just come open on hold in a voice no drover was supposed to own. And in the morning there had been a bell in Wren's kit. Not her bell; her bell was brass paste under a camel's foot. A second bell, older, good, off some dead harness, left where a drover would find it and no one would see it left.

Wren had turned it over and over in the grey light and understood none of it. She had spent her whole hunted life learning the two shapes people took around her: the ones who wanted the reward on a dead girl, and the ones who didn't yet know there was one. She had no shape at all for a woman who heard your secret and covered it and then armed you against being caught at it, and asked nothing, and looked at you as if you were a loose figure in her book she'd rather not have to explain. It frightened Wren more than a raised hand would have. A raised hand she understood. Kindness with no bill attached was a language she'd never been taught, and she did not trust a thing she couldn't read.

"You favor that old cow like she's your mother," said Doria Fenn, coming up the line with her surgeon's satchel over one shoulder and two cups of something warm, and Wren went still all over, the stillness that had kept her alive, because Doria Fenn was the one aboard she watched even harder than the quartermaster.

Doria was the cook and the crew's unlicensed bone-setter and, Wren had decided, the crew's conscience, the one they brought their small guilts to over the pot; a broad, unhurried, grey-cropped woman with burn-scars old and silvered on the backs of both hands and a way of looking at a person that took the whole of them in one pass and filed it without comment. She handed Wren a cup. Wren took it — a drover does not refuse water, water is tallied, a refused cup is a thing people remember — and made the small bob of thanks a mute girl makes, and did not meet the eyes, and felt the eyes on her anyway, filing.

"You've a highland seat on a camel," Doria said, conversational, watching her drink. "Did you know that? Most drovers ride slumped, save their backs. You ride like you were taught upright and never got the straightness beaten out of you." A pause exactly long enough to be nothing, or to be everything. "I knew a family once rode like that. Off the black coast. Long time gone." She let it sit in the cold air between them, gentle, terrible, and Wren looked at the salt and made her face a drover's face — tired, blank, a little slow — and felt the old cold pour down her spine, because Doria Fenn had walked away from a life before the Company, everyone said so and no one said which, and there was only one family off the black coast a woman might mean, and it was the family in the crate at the tail of the string that everyone thought was salt.

She could not answer. That was the whole architecture of her survival, that she could not answer, and for once it saved her — a mute girl cannot be trapped into the wrong word. She only shook her head, slow, no, a stranger's family, and drank her tallied water, and Doria Fenn looked at her a moment longer with something in her broad face that was not suspicion and not quite pity and was, Wren thought, the very worst thing it could have been: recognition, held back out of kindness. Doria knew. Or Doria half-knew, and was choosing, for reasons of her own, not to finish the knowing out loud. And that too was a kindness with no bill on it, and Wren stood between two women who had covered for her without being asked and understood neither of them and trusted the camels, still, more than either.

"Drink up," Doria said, and moved off down the line, and did not look back, and that was its own mercy.

The crust broke under Skerry a little before the noon halt, where the pan went from honest white to the pale grey-glass sheen the drovers called false floor.

Wren felt it before she heard it — the wrongness coming up through her own soles, that hollow give the Reach hid under its hard skin where old brine had eaten the salt out from underneath and left a lid over nothing — and she was already lunging, already three strides wrong-footed, when the young cow's near foreleg went through the crust to the knee, and then the shoulder, and then the whole grey lid gave way in a slab and Skerry went down screaming into a brine-sink to her chest.

It was the fear that killed a camel in a sink, not the brine. Wren knew this the way she knew her own pulse. A camel that thrashed drove herself deeper, fouled her legs, cracked a bone against the crust-edge, drowned herself in a hole she could have stood in; and Skerry was thrashing, was hauling her own weight down onto her trapped foreleg, was one hard wrench from a snapped cannon-bone and a mercy-stroke, and the rest of the string was catching the terror off her and starting to shy back down the line toward more false floor, toward putting a second cow and a third through the crust — and there was no time, none, to run for the quartermaster, no time for the one thing Wren was not allowed, which was to shout.

So she used the bell.

Sable's bell, the dead man's bell, off her wrist and into her fist, and she did the thing Old Ката had spent three mornings and twenty seasons teaching her to trust: she turned her back on the drowning cow and rang hold to the rest of the string, three flat shakes, the sound cutting through the panic small and certain, and she walked — did not run, walked, because a run is a shout too — walked to Old Ката's head and set her hand on the old cow's jaw and looked into the great dark eye and asked her, with nothing but a hand and a look and the total trust of a girl who had one thing she was allowed to keep, to hold. And Old Ката held. Twenty seasons of lead-cow authority, the whole weight of the camel-mother, planted four feet in the good salt and stood, and the string, wanting a certainty, took hers over Skerry's terror, and stopped, and stilled, and did not put another cow through the floor.

Then Wren went into the sink after Skerry.

She went in the way you go to a foundering animal and not a moment before you've stilled the rest, low along the crust where it was still sound, spreading her own weight, talking with her hands the way she could not talk with her mouth — flat pressure on the heaving neck, hold, hold, I have you — and she got the leg. That was the whole of it and it was everything: she got her arm down through the cold brine along the trapped foreleg and found where the crust-edge had it pinned and worked the slab of it away by feel with her fingers going numb, and she took Skerry's terror into her own small still body and gave back stillness, and the cow, feeling one calm thing in a world of terror, stopped fighting the hole long enough to be gotten out of it. That was the craft. Not strength; a camel outweighed six of her. Stillness, lent. The one thing she had endless supply of, having spent her whole life learning to hold everything behind her eyes.

She was aware, distantly, of the caravan arriving around her — of Doria in the brine beside her with the satchel, splinting a barked foreleg with quick scarred hands, of Marsh and two teamsters on the ropes, of Ino somewhere counting cups of spilled water in a shaking voice because counting was his bell — and she was aware, last and most, of the quartermaster.

Sable Coyne stood at the crust-edge and did not give an order.

That was the thing. Wren felt it even down in the brine with her arm gone dead to the cold: the quartermaster, who had a flat bored order for every moment of the world, stood over the worst thing to happen to the string in a hundred leagues and gave no order at all, because the order was already being given, cleanly, by a mute drover with a dead man's bell in her fist and a lead-cow held to stillness at her word. Sable only watched. And when they had Skerry up out of the sink at last, blowing and splinted and alive on the good salt, and the string breathing, and the false floor marked with a cairn so the next crew would go around — only then did the quartermaster come and crouch at the crust-edge over the exhausted girl still kneeling in the drying brine, and look at her, and say, quiet, so only Wren could hear it under the noise of a saved caravan:

"That was mine to do. And you did it better than I would have. With a bell you shouldn't know how to use half so well." A pause, in which the whole shut drawer of her face came open the width of a crack. "Who taught you camels, drover?"

Wren looked up at her out of the sink, salt-caked, dead-armed, her heart going, and could not answer, and for the first time did not want the not-answering to be a wall. She held the tally-knife-bright grey eyes and let her own say the thing her mouth couldn't — someone who loved me, before all this; someone in a workshop by the black coast; someone who is dead or worse — and saw Sable Coyne read it, the way she'd read the near-word two nights back, the way this woman read everything, and file it, and not, this time, look away.

"Old Ката," Sable said finally, not to Wren, to the great cow standing planted and patient in the good salt with her ward's whole life apparently in her keeping. "You picked her." It was almost, from a woman who owed nothing and wanted nothing, an accusation. It was almost a blessing. "You picked her out the first morning and you've walked her straight ever since, and I stood here and watched a hired silence hold my string when a shout would've cost me three cows and a boy's nerve, and I am going to have to start wondering, drover, exactly what I hauled up onto this road the same morning as a crate I'm paid not to weigh."

She stood. The drawer shut. "Get warm. See Doria for that arm. And ring my bell if the floor goes soft again — I'll come." And she walked back up the line to her count, and did not look back, and Wren knelt in the brine of a country that kept everything and understood, with the cold coming up her dead arm and Old Ката's shadow falling over her like a roof, that the quartermaster had begun, at last and against every instinct in her careful hoarding soul, to see her.

It was the most dangerous thing that had happened to Wren since the night they told the black-basalt city she was dead. She pressed her numb hand flat to Old Ката's warm jaw, and held her whole self behind her eyes, and watched Sable Coyne go, and did not know yet whether being seen by such a woman was the thing that would save her or the thing that would get them all kept, wind-cured and perfect, sitting up against the wall of some ruin in the spring.

Behind her, down the line, ropes creaked as the teamsters righted a shifted load, and a plain deal crate no bigger than a foot-locker rode on toward Ninefold at the tail of the string, cold and patient and heavy as a crown, and waited, the way iron waits, to fall.

ch9.body:
The Saltreach did not sleep so much as hold its breath. By the third watch the wind had lain flat, and the cold came up out of the pan the way cold comes off standing water, so that the caravan moved through it in a hush of hoof-pad and harness-creak — four hundred camels and eleven wagons strung out beneath a sky so thick with stars that they threw a grey shine on the salt. Sable Coyne walked the line because she could not have slept if Adder had paid her in Oststrand's own minted salt to do it, and because the tally was hers, and a tally left overnight was a tally already wrong.

She had the numbers by heart the way other people had prayers. Nine hundred and forty measures of water in the butts and skins at dusk; less the crew's night ration, less what the camels drew, less the two skins Marsh had signed for and the one he had not. Every drop on the Saltreach was owed to somebody, weighed against the distance still to walk, and a quartermaster who lost the thread of it lost the caravan a week later, out where losing killed you. Salt was money and water was blood. Sable trafficked in both and trusted neither.

She passed the water-wagons first, laying a bare hand on each butt to feel for the sweat of a seep, then the meal-carts, then the long picket where the camels stood couched in the cold with their necks folded like put-away rope. Old Ката lifted her great head as Sable went by and made the low door-hinge sound she made at everyone she had decided to allow. Beside her, small and swaddled against the chill, the mute drover sat her nightwatch with her knees drawn up and her broken bell dead-silent at her belt.

Sable had been noticing the girl for days now, and had not troubled to ask herself why. Two mornings back the drover had gone into a foundering camel's panic bare-armed and talked it up out of the crust with nothing but the flat of her hand and a patience that no seventeen-copper hire had any business owning. Doria had watched her do it with an expression Sable hadn't liked. Sable filed it under things to weigh later, the way she filed everything, and walked on. The girl's eyes followed her the length of the picket. That, too, went into the ledger of the unaccounted.

The unlisted crate rode third wagon, portside, lashed under the meal-sacks where Sable had stowed it herself in the dark of the Verdigris Yards, off every manifest, paid for in a coin she still carried in her boot because she could not make herself spend it. She knew its place the way she knew the water. She was, in fact, walking abreast of the third wagon and turning the coin over in her mind — that odd cold weight of it, dark iron struck with the Meridian salt-mark, too heavy for its size — when the salt gave way under the offside wheel.

It went with a sound like a jaw breaking. Somewhere beneath the white crust the Saltreach kept its old brine-pockets, roofed over with a hand's-breadth of salt and nothing under it but dark water and dark air, and the offside wheel found one and dropped through to the axle. The wagon slewed. The near camel screamed and lunged in its traces, the lashings jumped their cleats, and two hundredweight of meal-sacks and the thing they hid slid grinding to the low side and went over the rail into the dark.

Sable was already moving. "Hold the line!" she called, low and hard, the voice that carried without waking a caravan, and heard Marsh take it up ahead of her. She got a shoulder to the tilting bed and let the sacks come, riding them down, and when the crate came with them she took it against her ribs and folded around it and they hit the salt together.

The crust broke under her hip. Cold shot up her side. For a moment she lay half in the brine-pocket with the crate crushed to her chest and her legs kicking at nothing, and then she got a heel onto something solid and heaved them both back onto the flat, and lay there in the star-shine with her heart going and her breath smoking and the crate against her like a second, colder body.

Its corner had split.

She felt it before she saw it — the pine had staved along one edge, and through the wound in the wood her fingers found not the straw or the oil-cloth or the pickled hide she had half expected of somebody's smuggled fortune, but iron. Flat iron. A stacked edge of it, leaf on leaf, cold as the brine, colder, cold the way only worked metal is cold at the bottom of a desert night.

She knew that cold. She had been carrying it in her boot for six days.

"Marsh," she called, without turning her head. "Wheel's through a pocket. Chock it, unhitch the near camel before it drags the axle off, and hold the march till I've counted the water for spill. Nobody touches the third wagon's load but me. It's my count."

"It's always your count," Marsh said, from the dark, laconic as a closed door, and went to do it.

Sable got the crate up under her arm and carried it out past the picket-line into the flat where the wagons' shadow couldn't reach, and set it down, and knelt over it, and made herself breathe. A quartermaster's whole worth was in not wanting to know things before she had decided it was safe to know them. She had been paid, and paid well, precisely not to know this. The wise thing, the paid-for thing, was to bind the corner with a strap and log a broken crate and forget her fingers had ever found what was under the pine.

She pried the staved board back until it cracked off in her hand.

The Ledger came out of its ruined shell the way a blade comes out of a sheath, heavy and final. It was the size of a large hymnal and it weighed like a cannon-shot, and it was made all of iron — a spine of riveted bands and, hung on rings through that spine, page after page of hammered iron leaf no thicker than good vellum, each one etched edge to edge in a close ruled hand. Sable had seen sheet-iron worked thin in the Pickle-Yards when she was a fleet-girl, seen the vats where they bit the metal with brine and acid until the letters stood, and she had never once thought about who paid to have it done or what got written that was worth writing in a thing that would not burn.

She turned a page. It rang, softly, a struck-bell note, and lay over against its neighbours with a weight that was its own argument. She tilted it to the starlight and read.

The etching had been bitten deep and then pickled, and the brine had left its ghost in every stroke, so that the letters stood up white with dried salt in a field of black iron — you read a salt-iron page not by ink but by the salt caught in the wound of it, and the salt did not lie and the iron did not burn and the weight could not be forged. That was the whole point of the thing, she understood now, kneeling in the cold. Paper could be written twice. Paper took whatever a regent's clerk chose to give it and then took fire. This took nothing. This only kept.

It kept the Meridian succession. She read the top leaf and it was a genealogy of the Sarthe line, generation on generation, each name struck and salted and weighed, the crown's own bloodline rendered in a metal that could be neither rewritten nor denied nor thrown on the Kept Flame's own altar-fire and lost. She read the hand at the foot of the last full page — a maker's mark, an old woman's cramped and beautiful strokes, the letters LADY SARTHE, DOWAGER OF OSTSTRAND, HER TRUE ETCHING — and something turned over in her chest, because she had been in the Pickle-Yards as a child and knew whose workshop had held the last of the brine-vats.

She turned to the final leaf, the one that mattered, because a succession is only ever an argument about its last line.

There it was struck and salted and cold: that Halloran Sarthe held the Meridian Throne in trust and by no blood-right of his own. That the trust fell void upon the coming-of-age of the true heir of the body of the elder line. And that the true heir, living, not dead, whatever any counting-hall or grave-marker or crier at the Oststrand gate might say — the true heir was named on the iron in letters of standing salt: Wrenna Sarthe.

Wren.

Sable knelt in the dark a long time with the cold of it going up through her hands and into her arms and settling somewhere behind her breastbone that no fire had warmed since Petar died. She was a woman who priced things. It was the one gift the fleet had left her when it took everything else. And she knelt there and could not price this — could not put a figure on a book that made a mute water-drover into a crown and made the man in the Counting-Hall into a thief who would want, very badly, every witness to it drowned in the Glare and every leaf of it fed to the flame it could not feel.

She had been paid to carry a stranger's crate the length of the road, no questions. She saw now that she had not been paid nearly enough, and that the difference was going to be measured out of her in some coin she had not agreed to spend.

Behind her the salt whispered under a light foot, and she knew without turning who it was, because there was only one person in the whole strung-out sleeping caravan whose count she had already made and could not make come right.

The drover stood at the edge of the wagons' shadow with her broken bell held still against her belly to keep it from betraying her, and her eyes were fixed on the open iron in Sable's hands, and her face in the star-shine was the face of someone watching the one wall of the house she has left come down.

Neither of them moved. On the picket a camel shifted and blew. Marsh's chocks knocked home under the stove wheel, wood on wood, ordinary as breathing, and the ordinary sound only made the space between the two of them stranger and thinner.

Sable had put men over the side of a fleet-barge for less than what she was holding. She knew, coldly, what it was worth and to whom, and she knew that the girl in front of her knew that she knew, and that this was the exact hinge of the night — the moment where a quartermaster with a fortune in her hands and a debt at her back either closed the crate or called out for the caravan-master.

She looked at the girl. The girl looked back and did not run, though every muscle in her small body was strung to run, and did not beg, though her hands had started to shake, and did not make a single sound, because silence was the one coin she had left and she was spending it the way Sable spent salt — carefully, to the last grain, because it was all that stood between her and the grave the crown had already dug her.

And that, Sable thought, was the thing she could not get around. Not the crown. Not the fortune. That the girl had ridden six days in the string of a woman she'd watched run a hard tally and dock a lazy drover and fence with a Coral-Seat spy over dinner, and had chosen, out of nothing but the reading of her, to gamble that when it came to it Sable Coyne would rather be owed something than take the easy coin.

"You'll want to breathe," Sable said, quietly, into the dark. "You've stopped."

The girl breathed. It came out of her ragged.

Sable closed the Ledger. The pages rang down against each other one last time, that soft struck note, and then the weight of it was a dumb dead thing in her arms again, iron and cold and worth a war. She wrapped the split corner in the oil-cloth from the crate, and bound it with a strap off her own belt, and stood, and got the whole of it up against her chest, and it settled there like something that had decided to stay.

"I don't know a thing," she said. "Do you understand me? A crate cracked on a bad wheel. I bound it and logged it broken and stowed it dry. That's the count. That's the whole count." She heard how her own voice had gone rough and did not try to mend it. "I don't know your name. I've never read a page of iron in my life. And you're a drover I'd trade for two who'd shovel without arguing, and if you make me regret one hour of this I will put you off in the flat myself. Are we counted?"

The girl's throat worked. For one reckless instant Sable thought she would break the whole six days of silence and answer, and something in Sable — the fleet-officer, the sister, the part that had learned the hardest lesson a mouth can teach — leaned toward it and dreaded it at once.

The girl did not speak. She lifted one small chapped hand and laid it flat against the wrapped iron in Sable's arms, once, the way she'd laid it on the foundering camel, the way you touch a thing to tell it you have it now and it can stop being afraid.

Then she took her hand back, and turned, and went to sit her nightwatch beside Old Ката as though nothing at all had come out of the salt.

Sable stood in the cold with the Throne of the Meridian in her arms and did the only sum she had left. She was owed nothing. She had agreed to nothing but a crate. And she was going to carry a war the length of the road anyway, for no coin she could name, because a girl who had every reason in the world to run had chosen instead to lay a bare hand on the thing that could get them both killed and trust her not to drop it.

Adder had bought her out of a noose once. She knew exactly what it cost to be owed a life you never asked to keep. She had spent five years hating it.

She carried the Ledger back to the third wagon, and stowed it dry, and logged the crate broken in Ino's fair round hand at first light, and told no one, and went on walking the line as though the count still came right.

ch10.body:
They raised the second ruin at the grey end of the night's march, and Adder called the halt there because water is water and walls are walls and the Saltreach did not give you many of either.

It had been a waystation once, long before the Company's grandfathers, a squat stone toll-house and a fallen stable-yard now half-swallowed by the pan, its threshold drifted level with salt so that the whole ruin seemed to be sinking very slowly out of the world. No name that anyone still living had a use for. The crew called it the Widow, for the black lean of its one standing gable, and were glad of it, because a wall at your back was a wall the wind couldn't get around, and the sick certainty of open desert lifted a little when there was worked stone to couch the camels against.

Sable did not like it. She had not liked anything since the third watch two nights gone, when she'd learned what she was carrying and stopped being able to un-know it, but the Widow she disliked in the older, plainer way of a quartermaster looking at ground. It sat low. The dunes came up close on the west side, three of them shouldering together into a ridge that a rider could sit behind and never be seen till the sun found him. She said as much to Adder and Adder heard her out, which he always did, and posted the watch heavy on the west, which he always did, and neither of them said the thing that had grown quietly between them since the night at Dead-Drover's when he'd taken a private rider's word and lied to her face about it. She had stopped bringing that to him. She was learning, page by cold page, what it cost to trust the man who held your leash.

The crew took the false comfort the way crews do. Marsh got a fire going in the lee of the toll-house and a pot of the grey road-porridge over it, and men who had walked all night came and crouched to it and let the wall pretend to be a roof. Somebody found a bone-dice cup, and Marsh — who had come out of Oststrand owing money to the sort of men who do not forget a marker, and had been quiet and careful with his wagers the whole road because of it — sat in on one hand, and then, uncharacteristically, on another. Sable marked it: the small wrong note of a careful man reaching for a comfort he could not afford. She meant to speak to him about it, and did not, because the morning came first.

Dawn on the Saltreach was the cruelest hour, and the men who came out of the west knew it. They came with the low sun at their backs, so that the light stood off the salt in a white blaze that put a man's hand up in front of his own eyes, and out of that blaze the dune-riders came at a dead run with the glare behind them turning them to blots and blades. Sable was at the water-wagons when the first of the picket-camels went down screaming with a fire-arrow in its flank, and the whole grey morning tore open at once.

"Ashen Vow!" someone shrieked — Ino, she thought, high and cracking, the boy's voice going up the octave it went up when he was frightened — and then there was no more shouting words, only the flat awful noise of it, hooves and the hiss of oil-fire catching, the camels lunging screaming against their hobbles, a wagon-cover going up in a sheet of flame that turned the dawn orange.

They wanted the wagons burned. That was the whole of their creed rendered into fire: the salt belongs to no house, and so no house's goods should cross it, and what the Vow could not free it fed to the flame. She saw one of them wheel his mount broadside to the meal-carts and fling a clay fire-pot that burst and ran liquid flame down the boards, and she saw, briefly, terribly, the mark on the round hide shield slung at his back — a spread hand, brand-black, the ash-brand they burned into everything they took, into stone and beast and, the road said, into people. Then he was past and she had stopped looking at his shield because she was looking at the third wagon.

The fire was three wagons up the line from the crate. Sable did the sum without deciding to. She would not reach the crate in time to move it and she would not draw a single eye toward it by trying, and so she did the one thing a quartermaster could do that was worth doing in a burning: she went to the water.

"Marsh! The butts, cut them loose, roll them clear!" She had her tally-knife out — her father's knife, quartermaster's steel, as good for a strap as a throat — and she was slashing the lashings that held the water-butts to the burning wagon and shouldering the great casks down off the bed while the flame walked toward them along the rail. Water was the caravan's blood and the Vow knew it as well as she did; burn the wagons and you might kill a season, but burst the water in the deep of the road and you killed every soul on it. She got two butts clear and rolling and a third, and the heat came off the cover-fire like a hand pressed to her face, and somewhere in it Marsh was doing the same at the far end, laconic even now, cursing in the flat even voice of a man reading a bad hand of cards.

She priced it even as she fought, because that was the one gift the fleet had left her that still worked. A wagon of covers gone — forty measures of pitch-cloth. The near string's lead camel down and screaming and worth a teamster's year. A butt splitting its staves as the fire found it, forty measures of water hissing away into steam and stink, and every lost drop a step nearer the Glare with nothing in the skins to cross it. The arithmetic ran under the terror like a millstream under ice. A caravan did not die all at once in the Saltreach; it died by subtraction, one butt and one beast and one boy at a time, and the Ashen Vow knew that sum as well as she did and had come out of the sun to work it on her by hand.

Then Ino was beside her, seventeen years old and white to the lips and utterly where he should not have been, wrestling at a butt-lashing with his little clerk's hands. "I've got the tally, Sable, I brought the tally—" the water-ledger, the boy had run into a burning to save the count because the count was hers and he loved her the graceless way the young love the people they mean to become — and she had half a breath to shout him back before the rider came out of the smoke.

She saw the camel's chest and the man's arm going up and the short curved cavalry sword catching the fire-light, and she got her shoulder into Ino and put him down under the wagon-bed where the blade meant for the both of them couldn't follow, and the edge of it took her across the meat of the shoulder instead, a line of cold that became a line of fire a heartbeat later. The rider wheeled to come again. Sable came up off the salt with her father's knife reversed in her fist and no plan in the world but to make herself expensive.

She never learned whether she'd have managed it, because that was the moment the Meridian came.

They came from the north in a disciplined line, dune-cavalry in the salt-white surcoats of Oststrand with the Kept Flame worked in gold at the breast, and they came not at a mad run but at the long ground-eating canter of soldiers who have done this a hundred times and mean to do it right, and they hit the Ashen Vow's scattered charge in the flank and folded it. It was, Sable thought later, the difference between a brawl and a trade: the Vow fought like men on fire with God, and the crown's riders fought like men doing a day's brutal work, and the work won. The rider who had cut her went down with a lance through him before he'd finished his turn.

On the ridge to the west, behind the three shouldered dunes, a single figure sat a tall pale camel and watched the crown's line come, and did not move to meet it, and did not run. Even at that distance and in that light Sable felt the weight of him the way you feel a scale-beam tip — a big man, still, patient, reading the field the way she read a manifest. Ottlength. It could be no one else; the road knew the Highwarden's name the way it knew the Tollwright's. He sat and he counted and when the count came right for him he lifted one arm, and the Ashen Vow broke off all at once and streamed away west into the glare that had carried them in, and the last of them fired the standing gable of the Widow as they went so that the caravan's one wall burned at their backs like a struck match.

Then it was only the crown's soldiers, walking their blown camels down the line of the wrecked caravan, and the Company's people coming up white and shaking out of whatever holes had held them, and the two of them looking at each other across the smoking salt like the two halves of a snare a bird has only just understood it stands inside.

The captain of the dune-cavalry put up his sword, dismounted at the head of the burning caravan as though he had all the morning in the world, and pulled off his salt-veil, and he was younger than his rank and older than his face, with the flat scoured calm of a man who had made his peace with obeying and not with what he obeyed.

"Captain Roan Ferrough," he said, to the line generally, in the carrying voice of an officer. "Of the Meridian dune-cavalry, on the Throne's commission." His eyes went down the caravan, unhurried, cataloguing — the burned covers, the dead camel, the water-butts rolled clear in the salt, the crew, Sable standing there with her shoulder running red into her sleeve and her father's knife still live in her hand — and came to rest on Adder Voss, who had appeared, as Adder always appeared, only once the outcome was settled. "Verdigris Company. You'll be Voss."

"I'll be grateful," Adder said, spreading his big hands. "You've saved my season, Captain. Whatever the Throne wants of me for it—"

"The Throne wants the road kept," Roan said, "and this caravan escorted to Ninefold under the Crown's escort-right, for its safety." He let the word sit in the smoke where all of them could look at it. Escort-right. The same road-law that let a Coral-Seat wool-buyer's wagon ride under a caravan's protection let the crown fold its arm around a caravan whether the caravan wished it or no, and every soul in the yard old enough to shave knew the difference between an escort and a leash was only which end of it you held. "You'll not object to your safety, I think."

"Never in my life," said Adder, and smiled, and Sable watched him smile and thought about a private rider in the dark at Dead-Drover's, and said nothing.

His gaze had gone back to Sable once while Adder talked — to the knife still live in her fist, the blood soaking her sleeve, the water-butts she had rolled clear of the fire instead of running from it — and something in the flat soldier's calm of him shifted a degree, the way a man's face shifts when a sum comes out other than he had reckoned. "You saved your water before your goods," he said to her, not quite a question. "Water's the count," Sable said. "Goods you buy again." Roan looked at her a moment longer, filing it somewhere he kept things that might matter later, and then turned back to his men. He did not ask her name. She noted that, because a man who does not ask a name is often a man who already has it.

Behind Roan, his soldiers were watering their camels — from the crown's own skins, punctiliously, a captain who would not so much as drink a caravan's water uninvited — all but one, a lean trooper who had walked his mount up alongside the third wagon and sat looking down at the meal-sacks and the strapped, oil-cloth-bound corner of a crate that had been logged broken, with an idle, professional interest that stopped Sable's heart for the length of a breath before he moved on. She made herself look away from the third wagon. She had had two nights' practice now, and was getting better at it.

All down the burned line she watched the same understanding arrive on face after face, slow as the light. An hour ago the caravan had known one shape of danger — the fanatics who rode the dunes and burned what dared to cross the salt. Now it knew two, and the second wore the crown's own gold and had just saved every life in the yard, and would ride at their flank the whole way to Ninefold being unfailingly, immovably helpful. There was not a soul in the Company who could say aloud what all of them now understood in the gut: that they were not a caravan under escort but a thing being carried, carefully, somewhere to be opened. The Vow wanted them burned and the Throne wanted them kept, and a woman with a war logged broken in her third wagon was the hinge both sides had ridden out to seize — and only she, and a silent girl at the camel's head, knew that the hinge had a name.

Doria came and got her by the good arm and sat her on a fallen stone and cut her sleeve away to look at the shoulder, working with the swift ungentle competence of a woman who had dressed worse in worse places, and while she worked Sable found the one face in all the smoke that she had been half-consciously counting the whole time and had not yet placed.

Brother Kest stood at the edge of the burning gable with his pilgrim's staff in his hand and his back to the flame, and he was not shaking, and he was not staring, and he was not doing any of the things that the rest of the crew were doing with the leftover terror in their hands. He was watching the west, where the Ashen Vow had gone, with an expression Sable could not read at all — not fear, not the ordinary awe of a pious man who has seen God's fanatics ride down out of the sun. Something quieter. Something that looked, for one heartbeat, before he felt her eyes and turned it off and became again the warm mild pilgrim who had argued scripture at her over the water-tally, almost like grief. As if he had watched his own people ride away and leave him.

Then he came and knelt to help Doria hold the bandage, gentle as a nurse, murmuring the Vow's own comforts he had no business knowing over the crew's wounded, and Sable let him, and marked it, and put it in the ledger of the unaccounted with all the rest, and hurt too much to add the sum.

ch11.body:
They gave the dead to the salt at noon, because you cannot carry the dead across the Saltreach and you cannot burn them for want of wood and would not if you could, and because the pan does the one kind thing it knows how to do, which is to keep.

Two teamsters and four camels had died at the Widow. The men they laid in a scrape in the crust with their faces to Oststrand and their debts, Ino murmured, "settled by the road, which cancels all accounts" — a drover's rite older than either crown — and Doria packed them round with salt scraped up in the cook's own kettles, so that they would lie there white and unspoiled and unrobbed under a cairn of stones prised from the Widow's fallen wall until the world ended or someone came who loved them. Sable stood the tally at the graveside because the dead were on her manifest too, and read their names off Ino's ledger in a voice she kept level by main force, and thought that this was the first cost, and that it had been paid in the one coin the Saltreach could not give back.

The salt would keep them. That was the Saltreach's one mercy and its cruelest joke at once — that a land which would kill you for a cupful of water would then hold your body perfect and unrotting for a hundred years. The road ran its whole length between the salt-kept dead of every caravan that had ever miscounted: drovers and toll-cheats and lost children lying white and calm a hand's breadth under the crust, waiting on a rescue that had stopped coming before their grandchildren were born. Sable had walked past them all her working life and priced them the way she priced everything. Only now, standing over two of her own with the iron war lying cold in the wagon at her back, did she let herself feel what the pan truly was: not a road at all but a ledger of everyone who had ever tried to cross it and come up short, each of them kept forever at the exact weight of their last mistake.

Ino himself she had nearly lost. The blade that took her shoulder had clipped him going down, a long shallow rip along the ribs that Doria had stitched with forty of her small furious stitches by lamplight while the boy tried to be brave and mostly succeeded, and he had a fever coming now, the wound-heat, and rode the meal-cart wrapped in every spare blanket the crew would give up, which was all of them. He kept the tally-ledger on his knees even so. When Sable came to check the water — six hundred and ten measures now, and the arithmetic of that number was a cold room she made herself walk through twice a day — he tried to sit up and give her the count before she asked, and she pressed him flat with her good hand and took the ledger and read it herself and told him he'd kept it fair, which he had.

"You shouldn't have come into the fire," she told him.

"You'd have come in for the tally," Ino said, through chattering teeth, with the terrible clear-eyed certainty of the young. "I've watched you. You'd have come in for it."

She had no answer to that, because it was true, and because the boy had learned it from her, and she sat with him a while longer than the water strictly required and did not tell him he was a fool, because he had done a brave stupid thing for the reason she would have done it, and that was hers to have taught him and hers to grieve.

She thought of Petar then, because the fever-flush on the boy's cheek was the same colour, and because she had sat a watch like this once before, over someone younger than herself who had followed her into the salt-fleet on the strength of loving her and believing she knew the way out. She had been wrong about the way out. She had carried the weight of that up and down the road ever since, like a butt that never emptied no matter how she poured. She had left the fleet over it, and sworn — in the flat unwitnessed way you swear the oaths that actually hold — never again to let a child spend himself on the credit of her competence. And here was Ino, seventeen and fevered and quietly proud of the wound he had taken to keep her count; and here she was again; and there was no page in any ledger she knew that told you how to stop being the thing the young decide to become.

Doria found her there when the boy had gone under into the shivering half-sleep of the feverish. The cook washed her hands in a bare palmful of the day's ration — a thing Sable would have docked anyone else for, and did not dock her — and sat down heavily on the cart-rail and looked at Sable with the level ex-Ashen-Vow eyes that had once, she now knew, watched people burned for less than a caravan carried tonight.

"That pilgrim," Doria said, "knew the west-hand comforts." She meant the words Kest had murmured over the wounded. "Nobody says those but the Vow, and nobody but a walked-away Vow knows nobody says them." She let that lie there between the two of them, cook to quartermaster, one deserter to a woman with a war in her third wagon. "I walked away, Sable. There's them that don't. There's them that get sent." She looked toward the meal-cart, toward the small swaddled drover riding silent at Old Ката's head, and then, deliberately, away from her, the way you look away from a thing to tell someone you have seen it. "You'll want to know who else on this string is more than their hire says. I'll not be the one tells you your business. But I've eyes, and I've had them longer than most, and I'd count that girl and that pilgrim on opposite pages if I were the one keeping the book."

"I keep the book," Sable said.

"I know it," said Doria, and got up, and went to see to her fever-boy, and left Sable holding the plain awful weight of being the one who knew.

She went to the drover in the last light, when the caravan had halted dry — no wall this time, no ruin, only the open pan and a doubled watch and Roan's soldiers camped a courteous, watchful bowshot off, their fires an orderly line to the north like a leash laid out to be looked at.

Wren was at Old Ката's head, working brine-sores on the camel's knee with a rag and a patience Sable had stopped being able to explain away. She did not startle when Sable sat down in the salt beside her. She had known, since the third watch two nights gone, exactly what stood between them, and had spent every hour since being no different at all — hauling water, minding the string, ringing no bell because her bell was broken and even broken it kept her secret better than any voice — and Sable understood that this steadiness was not calm. It was discipline. It was the same thing she herself had, worn smooth over years, put on a girl of sixteen by a life that had been trying to kill her since before she could vote.

"I read the last page," Sable said, low, under the camel-noise, watching the northern fires and not the girl. "So you'll know what I know, and we'll not have to pretend at each other, which I haven't the water for." The rag stopped on Old Ката's knee, and started again. "Halloran wants the iron burned and you drowned, and he's a Throne to spend on it, and there's a captain camped a bowshot off with an escort-right that's a noose he hasn't drawn tight yet, and a pilgrim in this caravan who says the west-hand comforts over dying men. I've counted it every way there is. It comes out the same every time. You should be dead six ways before Ninefold."

The girl turned and looked at her, and there was no fear left in it now, only a fierce weighing that Sable recognized because she did it herself in mirrors — the look of someone deciding what a person is worth and whether to spend on them.

"I'm not going to sell you." Sable said it plainly, the way she'd log a true weight. "I want you to hear me say it because I know what it's worth to hear and how little you've had it. I don't do this because it's right — I gave up right in the salt-fleet along with a good deal else. I do it because I've read the count and the count says a girl who could have run laid her hand on the one thing that could hang her and trusted me to carry it, and I have been carrying it two days now and it hasn't put me down, so I expect I'm in it to the end whether I like the arithmetic or not." She held out her hand, her good hand, palm up, quartermaster to ward, the way you close a bargain on the road when a thing is too heavy for a handshake and too true for words. "Here's the pact, and it's the only one I make. You keep your silence and your bell and your camel-work, and you let no one — not Adder, not the captain, not the wool-buyer who'd sell her own crown for a better one, not that gentle murderer of a pilgrim — no one see one grain more of you than the hire. And I'll keep the iron dry and the water counted and the road under us as long as I can count either. We deliver you or we don't. But we don't get you cheaply. Are we counted?"

It was the longest she had spoken to anyone in years without a price fixed to the end of it, and the strangeness of that was not lost on her even as she said it. She dealt in exchange. She had built a whole self out of never being owed and never owing — the clean cold arithmetic of a thing given for a thing received — because the one time in her life she had loved someone past all accounting it had cost her a brother, a commission, and five years of sleeping badly. And here she sat on the salt in the dark, offering a mute stranger a pact with no figure at all on her own side of it, nothing to gain and a war to lose, and finding to her dry disgust that it was the first sum in a long while she did not want to come out even.

Wren looked at the offered hand a long moment. Then she did not take it — she was too careful even now, and Sable respected her the more for it — she reached instead to her own belt and unhooked the broken bell, the drover-bell that had cracked at Dead-Drover's and nearly ended her, the silence she wore like a name, and she pressed it into Sable's open palm and closed Sable's fingers over it with both of her small chapped hands.

Sable understood. It was the girl's whole voice, given for keeping. It was the surer coin than any handclasp, because it said *this is the thing that hides me and I put it in your hand.* Somewhere under the discipline the child in her was betting her life on a reading, again, the way she'd bet it in the third-watch cold, and Sable felt the weight of the little cracked bell in her fist heavier than the whole iron Ledger, because the Ledger was only a war and this was a person.

She had spent her whole life keeping the two from getting confused — the war and the person, the goods and the water, the thing you carried and the thing you were. It was how you crossed the road with your count intact: you did not fall in love with the cargo. But she sat there in the dark with a broken bell still warm from a girl's hands closing inside her fist, and understood that she had already broken the one rule that had kept her alive, and that she was not going to un-break it, and that somewhere back in the third-watch cold two nights gone she had stopped being a quartermaster who happened to be carrying a crate and become something with no name, no wage, and no easy way back.

"Counted," Sable said, and put the bell inside her coat, over the shoulder that hurt, and did not trust her voice past the one word.

They limped west through the small hours toward Ninefold, the crown's fires strung watchful to the north, the wounded ledgered and the dead behind them under salt, and six hundred and one measures of water between the whole strung-out sorry caravan and a cistern-fort that would sell them more at whatever the Salt Guild decided a frightened, burned, escort-shadowed Company was worth — which would be a robbery, because the Guild was neutral the way the scales were neutral, which is to say it weighed you and then took its price and called the taking fair.

She had crossed to Ninefold nine times in her Company years and never once come at it feeling like freight. The fort sold water and neutrality in equal measure and weighed every traveller's worth on the Salt Scales before it named a price, and Sable had always stood those Scales as a quartermaster stands anywhere — knowing her numbers, owing nothing, ready to haggle the Tollwright down a grain. This time she would stand them carrying a thing that could not be weighed and must not be seen, with a crown's captain at her shoulder, a burned caravan at her back, a fever-boy on the meal-cart, and a girl at the lead camel's head whose true worth would have tipped the Scales clean off their pins. She did not know yet what any of it would cost at Ninefold. She knew only, with the flat certainty of long arithmetic, that it would cost, and that she would pay, and that she had somehow stopped minding.

Sable walked the line because she could not have slept. She laid a bare hand on each water-butt for the sweat of a seep. She checked the strapped corner of a crate logged broken and let her palm rest on it a moment in the dark, on the cold worked iron that a girl had trusted her to carry, and she found that the cold of it no longer went into her the way it had that first night. She had grown a callus against it, or grown around it, the way the salt grew around the sinking Widow, the way the pan closed over its dead and kept them.

She was owed nothing. She had agreed to a crate. She carried a war and a crown and a broken bell west toward the toll where everything and everyone got weighed, and she did the last sum of the night and found, without any surprise left in her at all, that she did not want to be anywhere else.

Ahead in the dark, hours off yet, the first grey suggestion of Ninefold's walls stood up out of the Saltreach like a tooth, and the road bent toward it, and the caravan bent with the road, and went on.

ch12.body:
The Saltreach had lied to Sable Coyne for nine days, and then it showed her Ninefold, which was worse, because Ninefold was true and the truth cost salt.

For nine days the desert had laid water along the horizon that was not there — long blue sheets of it, cool and trembling, sliding back as the string walked toward them, the oldest joke the salt knew how to tell. Ninefold did not slide back. It sat where the charts said it would sit, a low black crown of basalt on a swell of white, and it neither shimmered nor promised nor moved, because it had no need to. Everyone came to it in the end. It only had to wait, and weigh.

"There," said Ino from the bed of the tally-wagon, hauling himself up on his good arm to see. "There it is. Nine days, near enough to the hour. I told you." His voice had the thin brightness of a boy trying to prove the fever hadn't taken anything that mattered. Doria pressed him flat again with one broad hand, not looking up from the salt-paste she was working under his bandage.

"You told us for three days it was over the next rise," Sable said.

"A stopped tally's right twice a road." Ino grinned, because she'd said it to him and not past him, and a word from Sable was worth more to the boy than the water she'd have traded for it. She wished he wouldn't spend himself so cheap on her. She had learned in the salt-fleet exactly what it cost to be a thing a seventeen-year-old steered by, and she had left the fleet owing that debt to a grave with her brother's name cut in the headstone.

She walked the string up the last mile herself, on foot, leading Old Ката by the jaw-rope because the old camel-mother would take the gate calmer if a hand she trusted took it with her. Behind Ката came the whole limping order of them — Tallow and Cinder and the yearling they still hadn't named, the freight-camels roped nose to tail, the water-butts riding low and hollow-sounding, the wounded in the wagons. Nine days out of Oststrand and the Company looked it. So did she. She could feel the salt in the creases of her own face like a second skin she'd have to be flensed out of.

Wren walked the drag, where a mute water-drover walked, silent, her broken bell wired shut so it would not ring the lie of her. She did not look at the fort. She looked at the crate lashed amidships in the freight-string, the plain pine box with nothing written on its lid, and then she looked at Sable, once, and Sable looked away first, which she had been doing for a hundred miles now and hated.

The gate of Ninefold was a throat of black stone with a portcullis of iron the desert had not been allowed to rust, and above it, cut deep enough to hold shadow at noon, the only writing the fort offered: WATER IS WEIGHED. Not sold. Weighed. The Salt Guild had a lawyer's love of the exact word.

They weighed the Verdigris Company in the great yard under a canvas gone the grey of old teeth, and the Tollwright of Ninefold weighed them herself, because a caravan was worth her personal attention and a single pilgrim was not.

She was old the way the fort was old, salt-cured past the point where you could put a number to it, and her eyes had gone the flat milk-white of a woman who had looked at too much glare and paid for the looking. It did not seem to hinder her. She stood at the fulcrum of the Salt Scales — two iron pans the size of cartwheels hung on a beam a grown man could not have spanned — and she read the swing of the beam the way Sable read a manifest, with her hands and not her eyes, fingers laid light on the cold iron chain.

"Verdigris," she said. "Adder Voss's outfit. You are lighter than your charter, Voss. You left Oststrand at your full lading and you come to my Scales three butts of water short and a wagon's worth of grief heavier. The desert took a bite of you."

"The desert, and other teeth," Adder said. He stood by the near pan with his hat in his hands, which Sable had seen him do before kings' clerks and never once seen him mean. "We were hit at the second waystation. Ashen riders. We buried two and we've a boy who may make three."

"Ashen." The Tollwright let the word sit. On the Salt Scales, side did not signify; the Guild sold water to Meridian and Coral and the Vow alike and took the same weight from each, and neutrality was the whole of the fort's religion. "The salt belongs to no house," she said, which was the Vow's own creed spoken flat as a toll-clerk's greeting, stripped of its fire. "They tell that to my walls twice a season and then they pay my price for water like everyone with a throat. Bring your salt to the pan, quartermaster. Let us see what the road left you worth."

That was Sable's work, and she came to it the way she came to all her work, which was as if she were being cheated and meant to find out where. The Company's salt was its money — good grey pan-salt in stamped bricks, the coin the road ran on, worth more the deeper into the Saltreach you carried it, which was the one joke the desert told in your favor. She stacked the bricks on the near pan brick by brick and called the count to Ino, who could not hold a pen in his right hand and so held it in his left and cursed his own letters, and against the salt the Tollwright's boy set the Toll-Weight of Ninefold.

It was a plain brass cylinder no bigger than a loaf, green at the seams, and it was the truest thing between the two seas. Every scale on the road was cut to it. It had weighed the passage of two crowns' worth of history and it did not care, and when it settled into the far pan the whole beam sighed and the salt of the Verdigris Company rose to meet it, and Sable watched the iron chains take the strain and thought, not for the first time, that the whole road was only this — a beam, a weight, and the long argument over which pan you belonged in.

The beam levelled. Held. The Tollwright's fingers rode the chain.

"You'll drink," she said. "You've salt to draw against, Voss, though not so much you'll be drinking it deep. I'll fill you eleven butts. Water is weighed at Ninefold and the weight is dear this season — the eastern cisterns are down and the war has drinkers I don't see." She named her price. It was robbery, and it was fair, which was the particular cruelty of the place; there was nowhere else, and so the price was whatever a dying throat would pay, and a dying throat would pay everything.

Sable paid it. She notched the tally-knife across the running board of the wagon, one score for each butt drawn, the way her father had taught her to keep a count no clerk could quietly amend, and the knife was her father's, and every time she used it the way he'd shown her she felt him watching from wherever dead quartermasters went to be sure the sums came out.

It was while she was cutting the ninth score that the freight-string came under the canvas, and the crate came with it, and Sable put her thumb over the knife's edge and stopped counting to watch it weighed.

She should not have let it near the Scales. She'd known that since Oststrand, since a stranger with a soft voice had paid her in salt-iron coin — real salt-iron, cold and heavy and stamped with no mint she knew — to carry one box the length of the road and log it nowhere. Salt-iron did not lie in the hand the way salt lied, growing lighter as you spent it; salt-iron only ever weighed exactly what it was. She had taken the coin. She had taken it broke and blacklisted and allergic to being owed, which was its own kind of debt, and now the thing she had been paid to hide sat on the near pan of the truest scale on the road, and it weighed wrong.

She saw the Tollwright feel it. The old woman's fingers stilled on the chain. Iron reads heavy — the Ledger inside was iron, pages of it, cold succession-iron etched and brined and bound, and no manifest of dried figs and lamp-oil weighed like that. The beam knew. The beam always knew.

"This one," the Tollwright said. "This one is heavier than its lid."

"Ballast," Sable said, which was the first lie in her mouth and a bad one. "River-stone. We pack the fragile freight against—"
