"You pack fragile freight in salt, quartermaster, as your outfit did in the four crates before it, and salt I have weighed a thousand times and know by its swing." The milk eyes turned toward her, and though they could not see her Sable felt seen, weighed, and found to be lying. "I do not sell secrets, Coyne. I sell water and I sell my not-caring, and the second costs more than the first. Shall I put a price on my not-caring?"

It was Adder who priced it, and that was the thing Sable took away from Ninefold and could not set down.

He did it quietly, the way he did everything that mattered, drawing off to the wall of the yard with a Guild factor who had come out from the counting-cell wiping his hands on a cloth as if he'd been at meat — a soft-handed man the fort's roster named Sub-Factor Renn, mid-grade, forgettable, the kind of Guild functionary whose whole worth was that no one remembered his face. Adder remembered it. Adder went to him the way a debtor goes to a window, and Sable, cutting her tenth score into the running board with her father's knife, watched her caravan-master be deferential to a clerk.

Adder Voss was not deferential. Adder had bought Sable out of a Meridian noose with his own name and a bribe he'd never named the size of, and he'd done it leaning against the gallows-post picking his teeth, and in the two years since she had seen him be many things — hard, warm, unreadable, once or twice afraid — but never small, and never before a man three grades down a ladder he did not even climb. Now he stood a half-step too close and a half-inch too low, and whatever passed between his hand and the factor's passed folded and fast, and the Tollwright's beam, forty feet off, went quiet about the heavy crate.

The heavy crate cleared the Scales. No further question. The Tollwright filled their butts.

Sable told herself it was ordinary. The Company greased Guild men at every fort; that was the road; that was the toll under the toll. She had greased them herself, palmed a brick to a water-clerk to get the string filled ahead of a rival string, and thought nothing of it but the arithmetic. This was not that. She knew the shape of a bribe and this had the shape of a payment, which is a different thing — a bribe buys a favor and a payment settles a debt, and you did not settle a debt with a man you had only just met. Adder knew the factor. And the factor, taking whatever Adder gave him, had not looked pleased or bought or ashamed. He had looked like a man receiving something he was owed on a schedule.

And there was the small thing under the small thing, which she had nearly missed. The factor had not written it down. Everything at Ninefold was written down; the Guild logged a spilled cup and the breath you drew to curse it, and the fort ran on ink the way the desert ran on salt. But whatever Adder had folded across, Sub-Factor Renn had folded away into his sleeve and entered in no book, and a Guild man who declined to log a transaction was a Guild man who already understood it was not the kind that went in a ledger. Two men, then, who both knew there was to be no record — and that was not the shape of a bribe. A bribe you wrote up as a gratuity and smiled about. This was the other kind, the kind that lived only in the two heads that made it, because to write it down was to name it, and neither of them wanted it named.

She filed it where she filed the crate, in the cold locked drawer of her head where she kept the things the road would eventually make her open. She had learned that much in the salt-fleet too: you did not confront a wrongness the same day you found it. You weighed it. You let it settle on the beam. You waited to see which pan it rose to.

Adder came back across the yard fitting his hat to his head, and his face was the caravan-master's face again, seamed and dry and sure, and he stopped by her and looked at the ten scores in the running board and the eleventh she had not yet cut.

"Water's dear," he said.

"Water's robbery," Sable said.

"Water's dear," he said again, gently, the way you correct a green drover, "because robbery is a thing a man does to you, and this is a thing the desert does through her. Don't waste your grievance on the Tollwright, Coyne. She's the honest part." He looked at the crate, settled now among the freight with its heavy lie of a lid, and something moved behind his eyes that she could not price. "Get the boy into the shade of the cistern-house and let Doria buy him whatever she thinks he needs off the Guild surgeon. Off the Company's salt. Tonight we water deep and we sleep on stone for the first night in nine, and tomorrow we start the long dry to the Glare." He put two fingers to the wagon-board, over her tally, a small salute to a sum well kept. "You did the count clean. You always do."

She watched him go and thought: I did not count the crate. And you did not ask me to.

She cut the eleventh score. Overhead the Kept Flame burned in its iron cage on the fort's east tower, the Meridian faith's fire that Ninefold kept lit for eastbound pilgrims the same as it kept the Drowned Mother's dish of seawater for the west — two gods sold water at the same window, and the Tollwright's not-caring covered them both. Below the flame, in the yard's long shadow, a pilgrim in dust-grey stood watching the Verdigris string come in off the Scales, watching the wounded carried, watching the drover at the drag with her wired-shut bell, and when Sable's eye crossed him he smiled at her the warm and rueful smile of a man who had shared her road, and lifted one hand, and she nodded back because he was Brother Kest and had ridden with them from the second day, and she had no reason yet to count him among the things she'd have to open.

ch13.body:
Brother Kest loved them, which was the part the world never understood about the work.

He stood in the cistern-house doorway with a wooden cup of Ninefold's dear water going warm in his hands and watched the Verdigris Company make camp on the fort's stone floor, and he loved them, each of them, particularly and by name. He loved the boy Ino, fever-flushed on his pallet, insisting on his tally in a left hand that wouldn't obey, because the boy kept faith with numbers the way a better-taught soul would keep it with the salt itself. He loved the cook Doria, who moved among the wounded with her surgeon's hands and would not meet his eye, and he loved her the more for that, the way you love a sister who has gone to a far country and refused all letters. He even loved the quartermaster Coyne, sharp and closed and sitting apart, cleaning a dead man's knife she thought was only a tool — Coyne, who owed and could not bear it, who was the nearest thing to a soul the Vow could have used and never would, because she had bent her whole life around the one word she could not say, which was *give*.

To love people and still do what the salt required of you — that was the discipline. The soft brethren thought the work was hating well. The work was loving well and not letting the love vote.

The salt belonged to no house. Kest had learned that on his knees at eleven years old in a season the Meridian throne had fenced the eastern pans and priced the water past his family's reach, and he had watched his mother weighed on a scale like this one and found wanting, and turned away from a window that said WATER IS WEIGHED to go home and bury what the weighing cost. No house had made the salt. No crown had cracked the first white pan out of the seabed of the world. Yet here were two thrones and a guild between them, selling a dying man his own inheritance by the butt, and calling the theft *law* and the law *order* and the order *peace*, and the peace was only the quiet a boot makes on a throat. The Ashen Vow would unmake the fences. The salt would run free or it would run over the graves of the ones who fenced it, and Kest had made his peace with graves.

He drank the warm water slowly, because to waste it would be to agree that it was theirs to waste.

They gathered to him after the evening meal, the way they always did, and this too he loved and did not let vote.

It began as it began at every fire — a drover with a burn that wouldn't close, come to Brother Kest because a pilgrim's blessing was free and the Guild surgeon was not; then the drover's friend; then Marsh, the quartermaster's laconic second, who had a gambler's soul and a gambler's hunger for anyone who would tell him the debts could be forgiven. Kest sat on a salt-brick with his back to the cistern's mouth so his voice would carry up off the water, and he did not preach, because a preached word bounces off a road-hard crew like hail off canvas. He asked them things.

"What do you owe?" he asked Marsh, gently, and Marsh laughed and said a number, and the fire laughed with him, and then Kest asked the drover with the burn, and the drover named a smaller number, a season's advance against the Company's salt, and did not laugh. And Kest went around the fire and let each of them name the weight they carried, the debts and the dues, the toll they had paid at the gate and the toll under it, and when he had them all counted he said, softly, into the quiet after:

"And who did the salt owe, before there were men to keep the tally?"

No one answered, because it was not that kind of question. He let it lie on them. Above the fire the Kept Flame burned in its cage and the fort's stone gave back the day's heat and somewhere a camel groaned in her sleep, and Kest looked at their faces going still and thoughtful in the light and felt the old ache of it, the tenderness, because they were so close, all of them, to the one true sum — that a debt you were born already owing was not a debt but a fence, and a fence was a thing a free hand could cut.

"I'll tell you a secret of the road," he said, and smiled, and they leaned in, because he was warm and the desert was cold and a warm man at a fire is believed. "The Scales are honest. Truly. The Tollwright weighs you fair and sells you fair and takes no side, and she is the honest part, and that is the horror of it — that the fairest scale on the earth still asks what a thirsty man is *worth*, and prices his life at what he'll pay, and calls the answer neutral. There is no neutral in a thing that weighs a person. Ask your grief who taught you a soul had a price in salt. It was not the desert. The desert gives its salt to anyone with the back to carry it. It was the men who built the gate."

Marsh shifted on his brick. A gambler cannot sit quiet when the talk turns to debts. "Salt don't owe anybody," he said. "Salt's just salt. It's there or it ain't."

And Kest smiled at him with real affection, because the man had stepped straight onto the hook thinking it was solid ground. "Just so," he said. "Salt's just there. It asks no toll and keeps no tally and belongs to whoever has the back to lift it — and it was so for ten thousand years before the first house drew the first line and said, this white is mine and that white is yours, and here, at the line, you will pay me to pass." He opened his hands to take in the fort, the Scales, the caged Flame burning above them. "Everything you've paid since the Oststrand gate — every score cut in your quartermaster's board, every butt weighed dear tonight — you paid it to a line some dead king drew on ground he never made. And when you're old and dry and they weigh you light, you'll pay the last of it, and they'll call that fair. They'll call it neutral. They'll call it peace." He let his voice go gentle again, gentle as poured water. "I don't ask you to be angry, friend. Anger's only another toll. I ask you to notice whose hand is on the far end of the scale."

He did not say the word *Vow*. He never did, at a fire; the word was a brand and you did not brand a soul you were still courting. He only gave them the ache and let it sit, and watched which faces closed and which opened, and made his small private tally of who might, in a harder season, be brought to cut a fence. Marsh: yes, in debt, in time. The burned drover: perhaps.

And Doria — Doria he did not tally, because her account was closed and had closed itself, years ago and a thousand miles east, when she walked out of Ashfall in the grey before dawn and took the surgeon's road instead of the sword's. She stood now at the meal's edge with her arms folded, watching him lay the old snare she had once helped him set, and he loved her for the watching, the way you love a sister come back from a far country who will not answer your letters but comes, at least, as far as the door. Kest did not hate apostates. Hatred was a toll he refused to pay. He only mourned them — mourned her — the way you mourn a swimmer who has chosen, in sight of the true shore, to turn and stroke back out into the cold dark water, believing the dark to be the kinder. Doria had traded the salt's one great mercy for a caravan's many small ones: soup, and clean bandages, and a boy's fever cooled by hand. She met his eyes across the fire, once, and what passed between them was not enmity. It was two souls who had loved the same terrible truth and now disagreed only on what it was owed. She looked away first. He let her. There would be a reckoning between them somewhere out on the dry — the Vow did not leave a fallen sister to the desert unspoken-to — and he prayed it would be a gentle one, and meant to have a hand in the making of it.

And the drover at the very back, the mute one, the girl with the wired-shut bell who had come to no fire in nine nights and came to this one, drawn against all her training toward the one thing in the desert that promised the fences could fall —

Kest had wondered about her since the fourth day.

He was gentle about the confirming of it, because he was gentle about everything, and because a startled quarry runs.

He rose when the fire burned down, and blessed the burned drover with water and two words, and made his slow pilgrim's round of the settling camp as he did each night, and his round took him past the freight-string where the camels dozed roped nose to tail, and past the plain pine crate that Coyne had sweated over at the Scales and thought no one had marked her sweating. Kest had marked it. Iron reads heavy, and he had stood near the beam and felt it dip and known, the way you know a coin is false by the ring, that the Verdigris Company carried something the shape and weight of the rumor that had put him on this road: a book of iron, and the girl the book was written to crown.

The girl stood by the old camel-mother, Old Ката, with her brow against the beast's great warm neck, saying nothing because she had made silence her whole disguise. Kest came up soft in the dark and stood a respectful drover's distance and looked at the camel and not at her, the way you approach a skittish thing.

"She frets less when you breathe slow," he said, conversational, to the night. "Old Ката. She carried my water-butt the first three days before Coyne moved me back. Good mother. She's lost calves, you can see it in how she counts her string at dusk — she'll not settle till she's touched every nose." He let that sit, warm, true, a thing between two people who loved the same camel. Then, still to the dark, still soft, in the round old vowels of the Meridian court that no water-drover in the world would know to answer to, he said a name. Not *girl*. Not *drover*. He said, gently, as if in blessing, the name the eastern rumor had carried — *Wrenna* — and the old title the Pickle-Yards had etched into iron before her uncle scratched it out — *of the House Sarthe* — and he watched her.

She did not flinch. That was the answer.

A true mute, a true drover, a girl who had never in her life been the name he said, would have turned at a stranger speaking in her ear in the dark — turned at the sound, the intimacy, the wrongness of it — the way any startled animal turns. This one held still. Held perfectly, beautifully, trained-to-the-bone still, the way you are only still when stillness is a thing you have been taught costs your life to lose. She kept her brow against the camel and her breath slow and her hand easy on the jaw-rope, and the discipline of her not-turning was louder than any cry. He had asked the desert a question and the desert's silence had answered *yes*.

"Peace of the salt on you, drover," Kest said, warmly, and moved on, and did not let his heart show her the grief in it. For he did love her too, now that he was sure of her — this fierce still girl who had done nothing but be born the wrong blood into the wrong fence, and who would be, at the crossing home, the thing the Highwarden burned to prove the fences could fall. He touched the knife at his belt through his robe, the plain short pilgrim's knife with the good edge, and he made her, privately, a promise. When it came — and it would come, at the Glare's far throat where the Vow would be waiting — he would see to it himself that she went by the blade and not the brand. Quick. Clean. A mercy the soft brethren would call weakness and he called love. He would not let them give her to the fire alive. That much he could carry for her.

He passed the quartermaster on his way out, where she sat apart with her father's knife and her closed hard face, and he gave her a pilgrim's nod and got back the flat wary nothing she gave everyone, and he thought, with the particular respect you keep for the one piece on the board that can still surprise you: *her.* Coyne was the danger. Not the wool-buyer, who would only ever do the profitable thing, and the profitable thing could be predicted and shaped. Not the caravan-master, whose price the Vow already owned. Coyne. Because Coyne had looked at the crate and gone quiet, and Coyne guarded the drover against her own flinching nature, and a woman who could not bear to be owed might, given long enough, decide that a debt of the heart was the one debt she would ruin herself to pay. If any soul in the Saltreach chose the girl and meant it, it would be the one who priced everything and had just met the single thing she could not sell. That was why the signal could not wait for the morning. Give Coyne a week and a reason and she might become a wall. Kest went out to be sure the fire reached the dunes before she did.

Then he walked out past the last of the fort's light, out onto the open dune where a pilgrim might go to pray to no house and no flame, and he knelt in the cooling salt with his face to the deep dark of the west, and he built his small fire the way the Highwarden's watchers were taught to read it — not a beacon, nothing the fort's wall would question of a praying man, only three handfuls of dry brush and a pinch of the grey ash he carried in a twist of cloth, so the smoke would carry the Vow's own smell to a nose that knew it. He fed it in the count they used. Long. Long. Short. *The book is here. The heir is here. Both, together, confirmed.* Not a raid now. Not the crate alone. The whole prize, walking west into the Glare on the Verdigris string, toward the crossing where Ottlength waited.

He knelt and watched the small flame eat the dark, and far off, past the third dune-crest where no fort's eye could reach, a spark answered him — once, and gone, a struck light shielded and shown and hidden again, the Highwarden's hand saying *heard*.

Kest smothered his fire with a slow palm and knelt a while longer in the true dark with the ash cooling under his hand, and he prayed, sincerely, for all of them by name — for Ino's fever and Doria's lost faith and Coyne's unpayable debt and for Wrenna Sarthe of the fenced blood, whom he would love enough to kill well — and then he rose, and dusted the salt from his knees, and went back in to the fire to be warm among them, because the work was loving well, and not letting the love vote.

ch14.body:
Ysolde Marrin had crossed half a desert to buy wool she did not want, and she flattered herself that she was doing it beautifully.

She held court, such as it was, from the tail of her wagon under a striped awning the color of a Lowmarch tide-market, with a jug of watered wine she had no intention of finishing and a bolt of grey Saltreach fleece across her knees that she fingered as she talked, exactly as a wool-buyer would, exactly, because the whole art of being a spymaster in a place with no shadows was to be so precisely what you claimed that no one thought to ask what else you were. The Drowned Mother taught that the deepest water looked the stillest. Ysolde had built a career in the still.

She had learned the trade young, in the tide-markets under the reef where a merchant's daughter with a good ear could sell three secrets before breakfast and never once be caught holding one, and she had refined it across nineteen years in the Coral Seat's service until the refining was very nearly the only self she had left. Her masters named her a wool-buyer in their letters because the joke pleased them, and because a joke repeated in enough ledgers becomes a fact. She did not mind. A spy who looked like a spy was a corpse with better posture. The whole art was to be so exactly the harmless thing you claimed to be that the harm went unweighed — and the Saltreach, which flensed every other kind of cover down to the bone, suited her better than the courts did, because in a country with no shadows the only place left to hide was in the plain white light of being precisely what you said.

"It's coarse," she told the Guild wool-agent, sorrowfully, letting the fleece run through her fingers. "Look at the crimp. My weavers in Lowmarch will weep. I'll give you half your asking and consider myself robbed by a professional." She smiled to take the sting out, and the agent smiled back, and neither of them cared about the wool, and that suited Ysolde precisely, because the wool was never the point. The point was that a wool-buyer had reason to talk to every soul who came through Ninefold with a bolt to sell or a rumor to trade, and rumor, unlike fleece, Ysolde would pay top price for and never haggle.

It came to her, as she'd arranged for everything to come to her, over the wagon-tail before the fort's own criers had it.

The Tollwright's fast-riders had run in at dusk from the east with the Guild's mail — the road's true bloodstream, water one way and word the other — and Ysolde had a standing arrangement with a particular saddle-sore courier that a certain wool-buyer heard the eastern news before the eastern news was strictly the fort's to give, in exchange for coin the courier's Guild wages did not stretch to. He came to her awning with his hat low and took his coin and gave her the sentence, and then Ysolde sat a while with the coarse grey fleece in her lap and did not say anything witty at all, which for her was the truest measure of alarm.

The Regent had moved.

Halloran Sarthe had, the courier's sentence said, *settled the succession*. The words were a coffin with a lace lining. In the plain of it: the Meridian throne had convened its Kept-Flame priests and its compliant council and had the old law read aloud and had it declared — solemnly, lawfully, with every seal the Pickle-Yards could press in hot wax — that the line of the elder branch was extinct, the child Wrenna Sarthe confirmed dead these three years past of the coughing sickness, may the Flame keep her, and the regency dissolved into a reign. Halloran was not Regent now. Halloran was King, in trust of no one, by a law that said there was no one left to hold the trust for.

It was, Ysolde thought, beautifully done. She could admire it the way she admired the fleece's crimp — coldly, professionally, as a thing well made by hands she meant to defeat. You did not seize a throne in Oststrand; the Kept Flame would burn a usurper and the salt-fleets would sail against him. You *inherited* it, lawfully, by first making very certain there was no one else the law could point to, and then having the law point to you. Three years he'd waited. Three years of the girl declared dead, so the declaration would have the mellow patina of an old grief and not the raw look of a fresh crime. And now, the mourning decently aged, he closed his hand.

She found she was not surprised, and being unsurprised frightened her more than shock would have, because it meant some patient back room of her mind had been expecting exactly this and had only been waiting on the courier. Halloran Sarthe was not a hot-blooded usurper she could bait into a blunder. He was a careful man who had done a monstrous thing so slowly it looked like weather, and careful men were the hardest of all to unseat, because they left no seam. Ysolde had spent her whole career prising at seams — a council bribed here, a fleet becalmed there, a treaty patiently starved — and you could not prise at a man who had made his crime lawful and then let it age like good salt-fish until the smell was just the smell of the larder. Unless. Unless somewhere the same account survived in a harder hand than wax, in a metal that took no amendment and answered to no council, cut by a grandmother's grief into pages a fire could not read and a lie could not out-argue.

And somewhere in the Verdigris string, Ysolde was all but certain, sat the one thing in the world that could reach into Oststrand and unmake every seal Halloran had pressed.

She had known the Company carried a secret since the fourth day — you did not spend a career reading the still water and fail to notice a quartermaster who guarded one plain crate the way a mother guards a sick child. She had probed it over dinner and been fenced off by Coyne with a dry skill that had, inconveniently, made Ysolde like her. She had thought it contraband, or unbonded salt, or somebody's smuggled god. She had been thinking too small. She sat under her striped awning with the news cooling in her and let the pieces settle through the water, and they settled into a shape she should have seen from Oststrand's gate.

An iron book. It had to be an iron book. Lowmarch's own agents in the Pickle-Yards had whispered for two years of a succession-ledger the old Dowager had etched and brined and then spirited out of the workshop the night before Halloran's men came to melt it — the Salt-Iron Ledger, unforgeable, cold as truth, on whose pages the real order of the House Sarthe was cut into metal that could not be quietly amended the way a paper roll could be amended, the way a *law* could be amended by a council that wanted its water-rights renewed. Halloran had spent three years and a false death and every seal he owned to write a lie in wax. And the counter to it — the heavy, patient, literal iron *fact* of it — was riding west across the Saltreach on a disgraced Company's freight-string, four wagons from where Ysolde sat pretending to hate the crimp of a fleece.

And if the Ledger was here, then the drover was not a drover.

Ysolde had noticed the mute girl the way she noticed everything — filed her, a watchful stray with too much stillness and a dead bell, and moved on. Now she took the file out and read it in the new light and felt something close to vertigo, the deep-water lurch of a diver who looks down and sees not the bottom she expected but a further, colder dark. The child declared dead of the coughing sickness. A ward the Company had hired the same morning it took an unlisted crate. A girl who walked the drag in silence and let a quartermaster guard her. *Wrenna Sarthe, alive, walking my caravan in a drover's coat.* Not a proof only. A claimant. The proof and the person to press it, together, on the road, in reach.

Her masters at the Coral Seat had sent her out to buy leverage. She had thought she'd come home with a treaty clause, a river-toll wrung out of some Company indiscretion, a middling season's advantage in the endless slow tide-war between the reef and the throne. She had, instead, blundered into the whole board. A living Meridian heir who owed her crown to no one, and the one document on earth that could seat her, both of them dependent for their very water on a caravan Ysolde could reach, flatter, buy — this was not leverage. This was the hinge of the age, and Lowmarch's hand was nearest it, and Ysolde Marrin's hand was Lowmarch's.

She thought, with the part of her that never went off duty: *If the Coral Seat holds the Ledger, the Coral Seat crowns the Meridian.* You did not war with Oststrand; you spent lives against black basalt and the Kept Flame and came home lighter. But you could *seat a grateful queen*, and a queen who owed you her iron proof and her living breath would sign a tide-treaty her council would call ruin and call it gratitude. No fleet. No siege. A wool-buyer, a fortune, and a frightened girl's whole future held in the reef's soft hand. It was the most beautiful trade Ysolde had ever been near, and she had spent her life near beautiful trades.

And yet. She turned the coarse grey fleece over in her hands and made herself say the cold part, the part her masters would never write and would expect her to have weighed regardless. A trade this beautiful carried a beautiful cost, and the cost was a girl. To seat Wrenna Sarthe as Lowmarch's grateful queen, Ysolde would first have to take her — take the Ledger, take the claimant, lift the two of them out of the fragile keeping of a caravan that had already bled to carry them this far, and bear them west into the reef's soft, patient, acquisitive hand. The girl would be crowned. The girl would also be owned, as surely as the fleece in Ysolde's lap, a queen who signed what the Coral Seat set before her because the Coral Seat held the cold iron that said she was real. It was a mercy and a theft in a single motion, and Ysolde had made a long career of not being able to tell her mercies from her thefts, and had slept well enough, mostly, on the not-knowing.

She went to weigh it against the honest part, which was the Tollwright, because Ysolde made a practice of testing her best ideas on the one person in any room who could not be charmed.

She found her at the Scales in the last light, alone, running the great cold chains through her ruined-eyed hands as another woman might tell beads. Ysolde brought her no wine and no flattery, because the Tollwright had milk-white eyes and a nose for the shape of a lie the way Ysolde had for the shape of a truth, and they knew each other, in the professional way of two people who sell the intangible for coin.

"You've had the eastern mail," Ysolde said. "So have I. The throne is *settled*."

"The throne is settled," the Tollwright agreed. "I'll sell more water for it. Wars are thirsty and grief is thirstier." Her fingers rode the chain. "You'll want to buy my not-caring, wool-buyer, the way the caravan-master bought it this afternoon. I'll tell you what I told my Scales when his heavy crate came over them and rang wrong. I do not sell secrets. I sell water, and I sell the space around a thing where I decline to look. The looking, you must do yourself, and the carrying of what you see."

"I only want to know the price of the space," Ysolde said, "around one wagon, going west, for the length of your not-looking."

The Tollwright named a number. It was robbery, and it was fair, and Ysolde paid it gladly, because it bought her the one thing the fort could sell that mattered: the certainty that when she made her move on the Verdigris Company's crate, the truest scale on the road would decline, professionally, to weigh it against her.

"You buy a great deal of not-looking, of late," the Tollwright observed, folding the coin away somewhere in her salt-stiff robes. "The caravan-master this afternoon. The wool-buyer at dusk. My Scales grow fat on one plain crate that everybody swears to me is figs." She turned her ruined eyes toward Ysolde, and though they could not see, Ysolde had the distinct discomfort of being weighed all the same, chain and beam and brass. "I'll tell you the thing I don't tell the ones who pay me less. Whatever rides in that box, it is heavier than the box — and a thing that weighs more than it looks will always, in the end, sink the one who carries it or the one who reaches for it. Salt-iron does not float, wool-buyer. Be certain, before you reach, that you can swim while holding it down."

"I'm Lowmarch-born," Ysolde said. "We're taught to swim before we're taught to lie."

"Then you were taught in the wrong order," the Tollwright said, and went back to telling her cold chains over like beads, done with her.

Ysolde did not go straight back to her wagon. A wool-buyer's feet were permitted to wander, and no one wondered at it, so hers wandered along the freight-string where the camels dozed roped nose to tail, and she looked — properly, for the first time, with the eastern news gone cold in her chest — at the mute drover asleep against the old camel-mother's flank. A slight girl, road-burned, unremarkable, precisely as she was built to be. But Ysolde had spent nineteen years learning to read what a person did with their stillness, and this girl's stillness was not a drover's. A drover slept like a dropped rope. This one slept like a held breath: one hand loose but ready on the jaw-line, her face turned from the fire, the sleep of someone who had learned in the cradle that safety was a story other people were told. Ysolde had met that stillness before, in the reef-courts, in hostages and heirs and the children of the newly fallen. *There you are,* she thought, with something that was almost tenderness and almost hunger and, being Ysolde, was exactly the both of them at once. *There you are — the whole age asleep on a camel, and you don't even know your own weight.*

Then she went back to her wagon in the dark, past the Verdigris fires, and she saw the quartermaster sitting apart with a dead man's knife across her knee, sharp and closed and guarding, and Ysolde felt the two things she always felt at the top of a great trade and had long ago stopped pretending were only one thing. The clean cold joy of the board laid bare. And, inconveniently, warmly, treacherously — a genuine reluctance to be the one who cheated Sable Coyne, who fenced so well, and liked her back, and did not yet know she was standing on the hinge of the age with a dead brother's knife and no idea what her one plain crate was worth.

"I'm going to have to offer her a fortune," Ysolde said to the fleece in her arms, ruefully, in the dark, "and I'm rather afraid I'm going to mean the rest of it too." The Drowned Mother taught that the deepest water looked the stillest. Ysolde had never in her life been so still, or felt so far from the bottom.

ch15.body:
The summons came the way everything came from Ysolde Marrin — beautifully, and with a joke folded inside it, so you could not be sure whether you'd been invited or outmaneuvered.

It came by way of Ino, who had bullied Doria into letting him sit propped at the cistern-house door "to keep the tally of who comes and goes, since no one else here can count," and who delivered the wool-buyer's message with the enormous gravity of a boy entrusted with intrigue. "The Lowmarch lady says," he reported, "that she has a proposition regarding fleece, and that you are the only soul in this caravan with the wit to appreciate a coarse crimp, and that you should bring your own opinion of her wine because she knows you'll have one." He paused, delighted. "Are you going to buy wool, Sable? We don't have room for wool."

"We have room for whatever pays the water," Sable said, and did not tell him that no one who watched the crate the way the wool-buyer watched the crate had ever, once, meant the wool.

Marrin's wool-wagon was a lie so comfortable you wanted to lie down in it.

From the outside it was a trader's box like any other, canvas over ribs, but Ysolde had made the inside into a small floating embassy of the Coral Seat — a hanging lamp of pierced brass that threw the Drowned Mother's wave-patterns across the canvas, a folding chair with actual cushions, real glass, and everywhere the bolts of grey fleece stacked to shoulder height, so that you conducted your treason in a room that smelled honestly of sheep. Sable had been in it once before, on the night the mirage-storm took the west butt and stranded the two of them together in the white until dawn, and she had told herself since that she remembered the wagon and not the night, and she was lying, and she knew the shape of that lie because it weighed wrong in her hand the way the crate weighed wrong on the Scales.

Ysolde poured two glasses of the wine Sable was meant to have an opinion of, and Sable had one, and said it, and Ysolde laughed with her whole face, and for a moment it was only the fencing, which Sable was good at and enjoyed and trusted, because a fence you can see is not the one that cuts you.

"You said coarse crimp," Sable said. "This is the good clip and you know it. You've been overpaying these Guild men on purpose so they'll talk to you, which means you're not here for wool, which means I'm not here for wool, which means you may as well pour the second glass now."

"I do like you," Ysolde said, and poured it. "It's the great inconvenience of my working life. Most people make me do all the fencing myself; it's exhausting, being the only clever soul in a wagon. You spare me the labor and then have the poor manners to enjoy it." She folded back into the cushions. "Tell me honestly. That boy of yours at the door — Ino — will he keep the arm?"

It was a real question, folded into the play of it, and it went in under Sable's guard exactly the way Ysolde meant it to, because the surest road past a good fence is to ask, kindly, after the thing on the other side of it the fencer actually loves.

"Doria thinks so," Sable said, before she'd decided to answer. "If it stays clean to the Glare." And then, hearing herself, hating how easily it had come: "That's not a thing you get to ask me and have for free."

"No," Ysolde agreed gently. "Nothing here is free. That's rather the subject I asked you over to discuss."

Then Ysolde set down her glass, and folded her elegant hands, and stopped being funny, which frightened Sable more than a drawn knife.

"The throne is settled," Ysolde said. "You'll have heard. The whole fort's heard by now — the Regent's a King, the elder line's extinct by law, the poor lost child three years dead of a cough, may the Flame keep her." She watched Sable over the lamp. "It's a very good lie. I do admire a good lie; it's the only art form both my crowns agree on. But a lie in wax has one weakness, Sable, and it's this: somewhere there could always be the same account written in a harder hand. Iron, say. Something a council can't quietly re-read." She let that sit, the way the Tollwright let the beam settle. "You're carrying it. I've known you were carrying *something* since the fourth day. Tonight I know what."

Sable drank, slowly, to buy the half-second, and thought: *she doesn't know. She's guessing, and guessing well, and if I twitch she'll know she guessed right.* She kept her face the quartermaster's face, the one she'd learned across a hundred manifests, and said, "You've bought a lot of wool to end up talking about crates."

"I've bought a lot of wool," Ysolde agreed pleasantly, "to be a woman who talks to everyone. And I'll buy your crate, Sable. That's the proposition. Not smuggle it, not steal it — the Ashen Vow will try to steal it, and I imagine the throne will try to burn it, and I am neither, I'm a *buyer*, it's the one honest thing about me." She reached into the fleece behind her and set on the little folding table between them a purse, and did not open it with a flourish, because she was too good for flourishes; she simply set it down and let its own weight speak, and it settled onto the wood with the flat dead heaviness that only ever meant one thing.

Salt-iron.

Sable knew the sound the way she knew her father's knife. Salt-iron did not shift or chime; it only ever weighed exactly what it was. There was a small fortune's worth of it in that purse, cold and honest and stamped, and it sat on the table between them radiating the one quality Sable had organized her whole ruined life around chasing and never once caught: *enough*. Enough to clear the Company's marks against her. Enough to buy off the Meridian blacklist that had kept her off every honest deck between the seas. Enough to never again take a stranger's coin to hide a stranger's crate because she was too broke to say no. Enough to be, for the first time since a noose and a brother's grave, a woman who owed nothing to anyone.

"And there's more," Ysolde said, quieter, "when it's in Lowmarch hands. I won't insult you by pretending it's a small thing I'm asking or a small thing I'm paying. It's the largest thing either of us will ever touch. Which is why it should be touched by someone with the wit to appreciate a coarse crimp, and not left to zealots and kings." She turned her glass by the stem. "The Coral Seat doesn't want a war, Sable. Wars are for people who've run out of cleverness. We want a treaty. And it happens — it merely happens — that the same iron that buys us a treaty also buys a certain living girl a throne, instead of a burning. I'm offering to make everyone's worst outcome a great deal better. Including yours. That's not a thing I get to say in my trade very often. Usually I only get to make one side better." She looked up, and for once there was nothing folded inside the look. "I'd like it to be you. Both because you're the one carrying it, and because— well. You know the *because*. We agreed not to speak of the night we don't speak of."

The trouble with the offer was that it was good, and the trouble with Ysolde was that Sable believed her, and the trouble with both was Wren.

She had not said Wren's name in her own head as *Wren* in front of Ysolde; she'd kept the girl in the locked cold drawer with the crate, because Ysolde read faces the way Sable read weights. But she thought of her now, whether she would or no — the fierce still girl with the wired-shut bell, standing in the wreck of the crate the night it cracked and Sable read the iron pages by starlight and understood; the girl who had looked at her across a hundred miles and trusted her with nothing, which was the only currency the girl had left to spend, and had spent it on Sable anyway because there was no one else. A fragile pact, made quiet in the dark after the ambush, that Sable had not signed with a knife-score because some debts you can't tally. *I'll not sell you.* She hadn't even said it. She'd only stopped looking away.

And that was the trap of it, the true one, worse than the purse — that the stopping had cost her nothing at the time and might cost her everything now, and she had never once agreed to that exchange. She had not chosen the girl. The road had handed her the girl the way it handed her weather. A wiser quartermaster, the woman she'd been at the Oststrand gate, broke and clean of any tie, would take the salt-iron and sleep like a stone, because that woman knew to the grain what a stranger was worth — a stranger was worth exactly what someone would pay for her, and here was Ysolde Marrin, paying a fortune. That was the market. That was the one law Sable had ever fully trusted, the law her father cut into wagon-boards and her brother had gone on believing right down into the water. *Everything has a price, and the only fool is the one who won't name his. Name it, then, Coyne. Name the girl's. Say the number back across the table and be free.*

She thought of Petar. She didn't want to and she did, the way the tongue goes back to a bad tooth. Her brother had named his price once — had let the salt-fleet buy his silence over a rotten manifest, because the coin was good and the risk was somebody else's and everything, after all, has a price. The manifest had been rotten in the way that drowns eleven men. Petar had gone over the side after the eleventh, trying to un-spend a thing that would not be un-spent, and Sable had left the fleet because she could not draw breath in a service that had taught her brother his sums so well. *Everything has a price.* She had watched, with her own eyes, what became of a man who believed it all the way to the bottom.

And here was a purse of salt-iron on a folding table that would make her free, and all it cost was a girl she had never promised anything and owed nothing to and had guarded, against her own hard instinct, the whole white length of the road.

"Say a number," Sable heard herself say, because a quartermaster's tongue negotiates while her soul catches up, and she watched Ysolde's face and hated that she watched it hoping for two different things at once.

Ysolde said a number.

It was obscene. It was freedom. It was the largest sum Sable had ever heard aimed at her own two hands, and it landed in the wool-smelling dark and sat there being enough, and Sable felt the whole beam of her tilt toward it the way the Company's salt had risen to the Toll-Weight, honest iron drawn to honest iron, worth answering worth. She thought about Oststrand and the blacklist and her brother's grave that she'd not had the coin to raise a proper stone over. She thought about being a woman who owed nothing. She thought, for one long ugly clean second, *yes.*

Then she thought about the Salt Scales, and the sentence cut over the gate. WATER IS WEIGHED. And under it the truth Adder had named her without knowing what he named: *she's the honest part — the horror is that the fairest scale still asks what a person is worth.* Ysolde was the honest part too. That was the horror of *her*. She had put a fair price on the girl and it was a true price and it was a great deal better than a burning, and it was still a price on a person, weighed out in salt-iron on a folding table, and Sable had spent her whole life on the wrong side of scales that priced people, and had told herself the difference between her and the men who worked them was that she, at least, only weighed salt.

"That's a real offer," Sable said. Her voice came out level, which surprised her. "That's the realest offer anyone's made me in my life, and I want you to know I heard every part of it, including the part you folded in and think I missed." She saw that land; saw Ysolde, for once, not certain. "So I'll answer it like a real offer and not a fence. I'm not going to say yes tonight, and I'm not going to say no, because a quartermaster who answers a number that size the same hour she hears it is a quartermaster who's about to be robbed by her own wanting. I'm going to weigh it. Properly. On stone. And I'm going to give you a straight answer before we make the Glare, and it'll be *straight*, Ysolde, whichever way it falls, because you've paid me the courtesy of an honest price and I'll pay you the courtesy of an honest scale."

She stood. The purse sat on the table between them, enough and cold and waiting, and she did not touch it, because to touch it was to have started spending it in her head, and she'd spent too many things in her head already tonight.

Ysolde looked up at her a moment, and then she smiled — not the whole-face laugh, but a smaller, realer thing, rueful and a little rueful at herself. "Do you know," she said, "I believe that's the first time anyone's ever left this wagon with the purse still on the table. You're going to be very bad for my reputation, Sable Coyne." She lifted her wine. "Go and weigh it, then. On stone. I'll be here selling wool I don't want to a fort that doesn't need it, being precisely what I claim to be." A beat, softer, the folded thing showing its edge. "I did mean the rest of it. That's the part you should weigh heaviest, and I'm furious with myself for saying so."

Sable went out into the cold and stood a moment under the fort's black wall, under the Kept Flame in its iron cage and the sweep of desert stars the Saltreach hung so cruelly close, and she breathed the clean nothing-smell of the salt and let the wagon's warmth boil off her. Four wagons down, the freight-string dozed, and among it the plain pine crate held its cold iron and its buried truth, and somewhere near it a fierce still girl slept with her brow against a camel's neck, trusting a woman who had just been offered a fortune to stop.

She had not lied to Ysolde. She was going to weigh it, properly, on stone. That was the whole trouble. Sable Coyne had spent her life being certain that everything had a price and that the only fools were the ones who didn't know theirs — and now, four days short of the Glare, with a purse of enough sitting on a folding table behind her, she stood in the dark and was terribly, unprofitably afraid that she had finally found the one weight her father's scales could not read.

She went to find a flat stone to sleep on, and did not sleep, and in the morning the Verdigris Company would turn its string toward the long dry and the Glare beyond it, and Sable would carry west, unspent and unspoken, the heaviest thing she had ever refused to weigh.

ch16.body:
Ninefold sold its water by the swallow and called the price mercy.

Sable Coyne stood in the cistern-fort's weighing-yard at first light and watched a Guild boy tip a bright measure of well-water into the Company's third butt, and she counted it the way she counted everything now — not in cups but in what a cup cost. Two fingers of loose salt to the cup at Ninefold's rate, and the rate had climbed a third since the eastern road brought news the Regent had moved and the succession was, in the Tollwright's careful phrasing, *settled*. Thirst travelled faster than any rider. The Guild knew it. The brass Toll-Weight sat on the Salt Scales' near pan, cold and honest and utterly without pity, and against it the whole road was measured and found wanting.

She had done this sum a hundred times since the crate cracked open on a night three weeks behind them. She did it again. To cross the Glare a caravan wanted eleven days of water for beasts and crew, and prudence added two, and Ninefold would sell her nine at a price that would empty the Company's salt to the staves. Nine days for a thirteen-day want. The arithmetic did not care that she was tired. Arithmetic never did.

"You're frowning at good water," said Ino, at her elbow. The boy had no business being upright — Doria had dug an Ashen arrowhead out of his shoulder at the last ruin and stitched him with sailmaker's thread — but he carried the tally-ledger against his good side like a shield, and he would sooner have died than let another hand keep the count. Seventeen, and grey under the eyes, and proud as a cat.

"I'm frowning at the sum," Sable said. "Mark it: three butts topped, two short. Note the rate."

He noted it. His numerals had gone shaky with the wound and he formed them slowly, ashamed of the slowness, and she pretended not to watch him do it. A tally in a clean hand was the only prayer she trusted. Everything true in the Saltreach could be weighed, written, and made to answer for itself. That was the whole of her faith, such as it was, and it had never once asked her for more than she had.

Which was the trouble. Because last night, in the lamp-light of a wool-wagon that smelled of cedar and expensive patience, a Coral-Seat wool-buyer named Ysolde Marrin had asked her for exactly what she had, and offered a number for it.

Sable had not slept for turning the number over.

It was not vulgar of Ysolde to have named a figure; it was the most honest thing anyone had done for her in a year. *Four hundred bricks of white,* she'd said, in that unhurried voice that made a bribe sound like a courtesy, *paid in Lowmarch on delivery, and a letter that strikes your name from the fleet's black list.* Four hundred bricks. Sable had stood in a debtor's dock in Oststrand once and heard herself valued, boots and commission and brother's grave and all, at eleven. Ysolde had offered her thirty-six times what a court had said she was worth, for a single cold iron book she did not own and had sworn to no one to keep.

She knew what a life fetched, priced against a cargo. She had watched it done. Eleven years back a captain-of-fleets had driven the salt-barges through a black squall off Oststrand rather than lose three days and the bonus that rode on them, and forty salt-hands had gone down with the water still tallied full in the butts they were lashed beside — forty lives set against a delivery date and found the lighter, logged as weather, mourned by no one who could sign a paper. Her brother Petar had been thirty-one of the forty. She had stood at the court-martial and said the sum aloud — *forty against three days* — and been broke and blacklisted and near-hanged for the saying of it, because the one crime the priced world could not forgive was a quartermaster who insisted a life was not a line-item you could carry down to the far column. She had left the fleet owing Petar a debt she could never pay, since you cannot pay the dead; you can only refuse, ever after, to work the sum that drowned them.

That was the shape of the thing. She owed the Ledger nothing. She had not asked for it. A stranger had paid her in salt-iron coin to carry an unlisted crate and log no questions, and questions had come anyway, the way they did, uninvited and armed. She could hand the crate to Ysolde and be quit of the road with her name back and her purse full and no debt owed to any living soul, which was the only kind of freedom Sable Coyne had ever wanted.

Nobody would even blame her. That was the poison of it. Adder would call it good sense. The crew would eat for a winter. Wren —

Wren would say nothing. Wren said nothing about everything. That was the point of Wren.

Sable capped her thinking off the way she capped a butt, hard, and went to find the girl before the sum could finish itself without her.

The water-string was picketed in the fort's north shade, and Wren was working down it with a horn cup and a rag, wetting the beasts' nostrils against the dust, and the old lead camel-mother stood over her like a grey cliff with opinions.

Old Ката had chosen the girl on the first day out and never unchosen her. The camel took water from Wren's hand that she would spit at a grown drover for offering, and knelt to the bell that would not have moved her for the Tollwright himself. That bell hung at Wren's belt now, mended — Marsh had brazed the crack at Dead-Drover's and it rang a half-tone flat, which the camels seemed to prefer. It was the girl's whole voice. A mute water-drover spoke in bells: one for *come*, two for *hold*, a long shiver of the wrist for *down*. Sable had watched her learn the grammar of it out of pure necessity and get good enough that the crew forgot she couldn't talk. Sable had not forgotten. Sable was paid to remember what everyone else was glad to lose.

The girl looked up as her shadow fell across the picket. Watchful. Always that first, before anything else — the flat assessing flick of the eyes that took in your hands, your weight, the fall of your coat where a knife might be. A hunted thing's manners. Sable knew them from the inside.

"They're watered short," Sable said, because it was true and because it was the kind of thing you could say to a person you were about to betray or not betray, and the words wouldn't know the difference. "We buy nine days here. The Glare wants thirteen. Do you understand what that means."

It was not a question and Wren did not answer it as one. She set the cup down. She held up one hand, fingers spread — *nine* — and then folded two down, slow, deliberate, and turned the closed fist so the two missing fingers faced the western horizon, toward the white. *Nine, and two we won't have, out there.* Then she touched two fingers to her own throat, and to Old Ката's, and swept them low along the whole picketed string.

*The short falls on the beasts first. And then on us.*

"On the beasts first," Sable agreed. "Then the youngest. Then whoever's carrying wounded." She heard herself. "Then the drovers, who walk."

Wren watched her say it. And here was the thing that Sable had not been able to sleep through, the thing that Ysolde with all her cedar cleverness would never understand because Ysolde had never once in her life been for sale: the girl did not use it. She had every lever. She knew Sable knew who she was — that pact had been struck quietly at the last ruin, over Ino's bleeding, *I know what you are and I haven't sold you yet* — and a girl with a claim to a throne and a book that proved it might have leaned on that, might have promised, might have named a court and a reward and a future the way everyone from the Regent's coin to the Coral Seat's wool had named one. Wren named nothing. She had nothing to offer and she knew it and she did not pretend otherwise. She only stood in the short water with the camels and told Sable the truth of the arithmetic with her hands, because Sable had asked, and the truth was owed.

That was it. That was the whole of it. Sable had spent her life allergic to being owed and here was the one person on the road who had never tried to put her in the ledger at all.

*Four hundred bricks,* said the sum, one last time.

*No,* said Sable, to no one, in the place where she kept the accounts that never got written down. *Not her. Not for that.*

It was not a noble feeling. She wanted that on record, if only her own record. It was closer to spite — spite at the whole priced world, at the dock that said eleven and the wool-wagon that said four hundred, at everyone who had ever handed her a number and called it her. For once she would refuse the number and keep the thing, not because the thing was worth more but because refusing was the only wealth she had left that no one had priced.

Provisional. She made herself say the word inside, quartermaster to quartermaster. *Provisional.* The road was long and the Glare was thirsty and a woman could revise a tally. But for today, and out loud to nobody, she chose the girl over the fortune, and told the sum to close.

She reached into the crate-cart on her way past — a habit now, a wound she kept probing — and laid two fingers on the iron through the straw. Even in the risen sun the Salt-Iron Ledger was cold, colder than the shade had any right to make it, cold like well-water, like a coin from the bottom of a purse. Heavy in a way that had nothing to do with weight. She had read four of its brined pages by lamplight and understood the fifth without reading it, and she took her hand back the way you take it back from a stove: quickly, and pretending you hadn't.

"Come on," she told the girl, and did not tell her anything else. Some choices you keep the way Ninefold kept its water. By the swallow. To yourself.

Adder Voss wanted to be gone by noon, and that was the second thing that kept her awake.

She found him at the fort's west sally-port with the caravan-master's slate, striking the order of march, and he had the look he'd worn since Ninefold — a man doing sums of his own and not liking the total. He had bought her off a Meridian noose eleven years ago with his own name as surety, and Sable owed him a life for it, an actual life, the only debt she'd ever accepted because refusing it would have meant refusing to be alive to refuse. It made her watch him more closely than she watched anyone. You watched what you owed. That was only prudent.

"We're short nine to thirteen on water," she said, "and you want the deep road."

"I want the road while it's still ours to want." He didn't look up. "You saw the factor."

She had. The Guild factor at Ninefold, a soft grey man with clean hands, to whom Adder had spoken with a deference that fit him like another man's coat. Adder Voss deferred to weather and to arithmetic and to nothing that walked on two legs, and yet twice now she'd seen him drop his eyes to that clean grey man and take instruction like a corporal. She filed it. She did not know yet what the file was for.

"The Weeping Rocks are two days on," Adder said. "Salt-spring, cold and clean, no Guild, no toll. We top the butts there for free and go into the Glare full. That's your thirteen. That's why we don't buy Ninefold's ninth day at Ninefold's ninth-day price." Now he did look at her, and there was something under the pragmatism, something she'd have called fear in a lesser man. "We don't stay here, Sable. Whatever the wool-buyer's offering — and I know she's offering — we don't sit at a Guild well and haggle over the cargo while the Regent's cavalry closes the distance behind us. We move. We keep moving. On the road we're a caravan. Sitting still we're a target with a manifest."

It was good sense. It was, in fact, exactly her own sense, handed back to her by the man who'd taught it to her, and that was what made her uneasy — that Adder wanted the free water at the Weeping Rocks so badly, and named the reason so well, and would not quite hold her eye while he did it.

"The Weeping Rocks," she said, testing the shape of it.

"Free water and a night's rest." He struck the last line on the slate. "Cheapest thing on the whole road. When did you ever turn down cheap?"

Never. That was the answer, and he knew it, and she gave it to him because she had made one expensive choice already this morning and did not have another in her yet. She went and put the caravan in its order — the crate-cart mid-string where a quartermaster could see it, Ino in the sick-wagon over his protests, Ysolde's cedar-and-secrets wool-wagon riding under escort-right two beasts back, the water-string with the girl and the old grey mother at its head. The Salt Scales dwindled behind them as they filed out the west gate and the brass Toll-Weight caught the sun one last time, weighing nothing, weighing everyone.

Sable took her place at the crate-cart and did not look at the wool-wagon, which was its own kind of message and would be read as one. She had stalled Ysolde with a woman's whole art of stalling and would go on stalling until the stall itself became the answer. Let the Coral Seat think the door still stood ajar. She had shut it this morning in the north shade, quietly, over short water, and told no one, and the only witness was a camel who couldn't testify and a girl who wouldn't.

The white opened ahead of them, flat to the rim of the world, and somewhere out in it a spring wept clean cold water for free. *Cheapest thing on the whole road.* She rode toward it with the iron cold at her back and the number refused in her pocket, and told herself, quartermaster to quartermaster, that a thing offered free in the Saltreach had never once in the history of the road been anything of the kind.

ch17.body:
Wren smelled the water a full hour before she saw it, and did not believe it, because the Saltreach had lied to her every day of the road.

The desert lied in mirrors — false lakes laid flat and silver along the noon, false towers, once a whole false city with gulls over it that had turned out to be a salt-pan and three vultures. She had learned to disbelieve her eyes out here the way she had learned, long before the road, to disbelieve a kind voice in a marble hall. But the nose was harder to fool. This was green under the white, wet stone and crushed reed and the particular cold mineral breath of water that had never seen the sky until now, and Old Ката lifted her great head and groaned low in her chest and quickened without being told, and the whole water-string quickened behind her like a rope pulled taut, and Wren let herself, at last, believe.

The Weeping Rocks were not much to a stranger's eye and were everything to a thirsty one: a knuckle of dark stone shouldering up out of the flat, veined and seeping, so that the whole low face of it *wept* — beads and threads of water sliding down the rock to gather in a stone basin some patient century had worn, and below that a green apron of reed and salt-grass and three stunted date-palms leaning together like old men sharing a secret. No wall. No toll-house. No brass weight, no Guild boy with a horn cup and a price. Just water, coming out of the ground because it wanted to, more than a caravan could drink.

The crew went a little mad with it, in the quiet way of road-worn people. Marsh put his whole head in the basin and came up blowing. Doria Fenn, who fed them and stitched them and forgave them and judged them all in the same flat voice, filled her largest pot and did not put it on the fire — she simply looked at a pot full of clean water she had not had to ration, and something in her hard cook's face loosened. Even Sable, who Wren had never once seen want a thing where anyone could watch, knelt at the seep and drank from her cupped hand slow, with her eyes shut, the way you did a thing you didn't want measured.

Ino got himself carried to the water in his blanket and made them prop him at the basin's lip so he could put his own bandaged hand in it and keep his own count of the free butts as they filled, because a thing unmeasured, he informed the whole camp in his reedy convalescent's voice, had a way of walking off. Doria threatened to weigh *him* if he didn't lie back. Marsh, who owed money to half the caravan and worry to the other half, laughed for the first time since Ninefold. It was a small camp at a small spring in a large dead land, and for one evening it forgot to be afraid, and Wren, watching them forget, loved them and feared for them in the same breath, because she had learned in a marble hall that the forgetting was always when the hand came down.

Wren watered the beasts first. That was the drover's law and it was also her own — the short falls on the beasts first, and so the plenty should reach them first too; the arithmetic ran both directions if you were honest. She rang Old Ката down to the basin, two fingers of the bell and a long shiver for *drink your fill*, and the old mother drank and drank and then stood dripping and pressed her whiskered lip to Wren's hair, which was the closest thing to being called *daughter* that Wren had felt since Oststrand. She stood in the wet reed with the camel's breath in her hair and was, for the length of a held moment, simply a girl at a spring, owed nothing and owing nothing, nameless in the good way instead of the frightened way.

She had not always been nameless. That was the mercy the road had given her that the marble hall never could — the mercy of being no one. In Oststrand she had been a name before she was a girl, *Wrenna Sarthe* stitched into her collars and carried ahead of her into every room, a name her uncle smiled at across the Counting-Hall the way a man smiles at a debt he means to call. She had learned young that a name could be a leash. The night they smuggled her out — a drover's coat thrown over her good linen, a bell pressed into her hand, her grandmother's ink-stained fingers hard on her jaw, *say nothing, ring for what you need, live* — she had wept for the losing of it all, and only out here, a year deep in the white, had she come to understand that the old woman had not stripped her name away to punish her. She had stripped it away to hide her in the one place a name could not follow: silence, and salt, and a string of camels who did not care whose daughter you were so long as you brought the water on time.

It could not last. She knew that the way she knew the desert lied. But she let it last as long as it would.

Sable found her at dusk mending tack, and sat down across the saddle-frame without asking, which from Sable was a kind of asking, and a kind of trust.

They had reached a thing, the two of them, that Wren did not have a bell for and would not have had a word for even if she'd let herself use words. At the last ruin, over Ino's blood, the quartermaster had said *I know what you are* and had not sold her, and every day since had guarded her against Wren's own instinct to bolt, to hide deeper, to trust no hand at all. It was not warmth. Sable had no warmth to spare and made no pretense of it. It was something drier and more durable — the regard of one hunted thing for another, and under that, lately, something that had started to look like it might survive the road. Wren had learned to read the woman the way she read weather. Tonight Sable was clear. Tonight, for once, nothing was coming off her but the ordinary tiredness of a person who had carried something heavy a long way and not put it down.

Doria came into the firelight with Wren's own drover-saddle over her arm and a needle in her teeth. "Girth's frayed to threads and the tree's cracked," the cook said around the needle, dropping the saddle by the fire. "You've been riding on faith and a prayer, drover. Sit. This wants restuffing before the Glare or it'll gall your beast to the bone."

It was Wren's saddle — the one she'd been given the night they smuggled her out of Oststrand in a drover's coat with a bell at her belt and a dead girl's name, if the Regent's proclamation was to be believed, since he had told two crowns and a continent that Wrenna Sarthe was in the ground. She'd ridden it the whole road. She had slept with her head on it. She knew its every lump and had never once wondered at the lumps, because a road-saddle was all lumps, that was what a saddle *was*.

Doria opened the seam along the cantle to pull the old packing, and her flat cook's voice stopped flat.

She drew out a packet. Oilcloth, waxed at the folds, sewn shut with a fine close hand that was not a saddler's hand — too even, too patient, the stitching of someone who had all the time in the world and meant every stitch to hold. Doria turned it in the firelight and Wren, watching, felt the ground of herself tilt, because she knew that stitching. She had been taught that stitching. In a marble hall by a woman with ink-stained fingers who said a stitch, child, is a promise you make with your hands, and only a fool breaks a promise she can see.

Sable had gone very still. "Doria. Cut it."

The cook cut the outer stitches with her surgeon's care and unfolded the oilcloth, and inside were letters — a thin sheaf, close-written both sides in a hand gone spidery with age but still upright, still refusing to lean — and the topmost sheet was headed in a script Wren's fingers moved to trace before her eyes had finished it.

*To my granddaughter, on the road, if the road has kept her.*

Wren did not make a sound. She had spent a year not making sounds; her whole life now was the muscle of not making sounds. But Doria looked at her once, quick and knowing, the look of a woman who had half-guessed weeks ago and now had the whole of it in her hands, and passed her the letters without a word, and turned her broad back to the rest of the camp so that Wren could read her grandmother in the firelight with only a cook and a quartermaster to witness it.

*If you are reading this,* the Dowager had written, *then you are alive, and the men who told me you were dead are liars, which I knew, though it is a comfort to be proved right at my age when so little else obliges. They hold me kindly. They hold me. Do not grieve it; I am old and the Pickle-Yards taught my hands a stubbornness the Regent has not the patience to break. I have work yet.*

And below, in the driest voice, a voice Wren could hear as if the old woman sat across the fire and not a continent away in a guarded room: *The book is true, child. I made it true myself, iron and brine, and no forger living can lie in iron the way they lie so easily in paper. But iron is a stubborn witness and a silent one, and silence — you of all souls now know — is too easily called guilt. So I have made these papers to speak for the iron. Names, dates, the midwife's mark, your mother's own hand, the false grave and who dug it. Read together, iron and paper answer each other, and no counting-hall in Oststrand can pretend the sum does not come out to you.*

Wren read it twice. Her hands did not shake — she had trained the shake out of them along with the voice — but something behind her ribs shook that she had no muscle to still, and she let it, because there was no one here to sell her the letting.

The last lines were not law. They were only an old woman to a child. *I am sorry. I sewed you a saddle and a road and a company of strangers and I could not sew you a childhood, and that is the debt I will die owing you. When you come to your throne — and you will come to it, for the salt is stubborn and so are we — do not take it because the iron says you must. Take it because you have seen the road, and know what water costs, and will not sell the thirsty a swallow and call it mercy. That is the only right to rule I believe in anymore. The rest is bookkeeping.*

For a year Wren had carried the Ledger the way you carry a stone that someone else has told you is precious — a weight assigned, a thing she guarded because Sable guarded it and the crew's lives had knotted themselves to it, but not, in her secret heart, a thing she had believed was *hers*. Iron was cold. Iron was the Regent's own word turned back against him, a legal engine, a proof. It had never once felt like her grandmother's hand on her jaw. But paper did. Paper in that spidery upright hand felt exactly like the old woman, and reading it, Wren felt the claim stop being a thing done *to* her — a name, a leash, a warrant, a pretender's death cried in the squares — and become, for the first time, a thing she might one day choose to pick up. *Take it because you have seen the road.* She had seen the road. She had watered the beasts short and known in her own hands who the shortfall fell on. Perhaps that was where a right to anything began.

Wren lowered the letters. Across the fire Sable Coyne was watching her with a face carefully emptied of everything, and Wren understood that the quartermaster had heard, in *do not sell the thirsty a swallow*, the exact accusation she leveled at the whole priced world, spoken in a dead woman's stubborn hand from inside a saddle Wren had slept on for a thousand miles. Two hunted things by a fire, and a third voice between them now, patient and iron-backed and unafraid.

"She's alive," Wren mouthed — no breath in it, just the shape — and Sable, who had learned to read her, nodded once.

"Then we've a delivery," the quartermaster said, low, "and now I've read the manifest." And that was as close as Sable Coyne would ever come to swearing an oath, and Wren, who had been offered oaths by liars her whole life, believed this one precisely because it came dressed as a shipping term.

The peace held until the second watch, and then Old Ката broke it.

The old mother came up off her knees in the picket with a groan that was not a water-groan, head swung east, ears pinned, and every camel in the string caught it off her the way the string had caught her thirst that morning. Wren was on her feet before she'd decided to be. She had learned the desert's lies; she had also learned, harder, the desert's rare truths, and a lead camel-mother staring east into the dark with her nostrils working was a truth.

She rang the bell once — sharp, a single hard note, the note that in a year of the road she had never yet had cause to ring, the note the crew had taught her for the thing no one wanted named. *Watch. Something comes.*

The camp came awake around her, low and fast, road-people who slept with one hand on a picket-line. Sable was there in a breath, tally-knife already loose in her fist, following the old mother's stare out to where the last light bled off the eastern rim. And Wren, whose eyes had learned to disbelieve, made herself believe what she saw: not a mirage, because mirages died with the sun and this was the true dark — a smudge of paler dark low on the flat, and above it, catching the risen edge of the moon, the small cold flash of metal that no reed or rock or weeping stone would ever make. Riders. Many. Coming straight for the one green place in a hundred miles of white as if they had known, all along, exactly where the thirsty would kneel.

Nobody had followed a trail here. You could not track a caravan across salt-flats in the dark. They had come *to* the Weeping Rocks — to this spring, this night, this rest — the way you came to a place you'd been told of. And Wren stood in the free clean water that had felt, for one whole afternoon, like a thing owed to no one, and understood with the cold understanding of the hunted that it had been the most expensive water on the road all along, and that somewhere among the sleeping crew who had drunk it laughing, a mouth had already spoken the price.

ch18.body:
Captain Roan Ferrough smelled the water before his outriders sighted the fires, and hated it, because it meant the thing was real and close and would have to be done tonight.

He had let himself half-hope, through the long dry chase off Ninefold, that the caravan would slip him — go north to the salt-pans, or scatter, or simply be the wrong caravan, so that he might ride back to the Regent's counting-clerks and report the trail gone cold and mean it. A soldier was permitted to fail. A soldier was not permitted to disobey, and the daylight between those two had been the only shade Roan had found to ride in for a fortnight. But here was the green smell of the Weeping Rocks coming up out of the dark, and here on the flat were the picket-fires of a Verdigris string bedded down for the night, right where the water was, exactly as the grey Guild message had promised they would be. No failing to be had. Only obeying.

He raised a fist and his troop drew rein behind him, forty dune-cavalry in road-dun with their lances cased, good men, his men, who had followed him up out of nothing because he had never once spent them cheap. That was the whole of his craft and his whole pride — Roan Ferrough spent his men dear or not at all. He looked at the warrant in his glove, though he had it by heart, and by heart was the trouble.

*By the hand of Halloran Sarthe, Regent-in-Trust of the Meridian Throne, keeper of the Kept Flame:* the seizure of the Verdigris caravan and all its cargo, the arrest of one Adder Voss and his quartermaster and crew for smuggling against the Throne, and — the line his eye kept catching on like a nail in cloth — *the taking, alive if compliant and by any needful means if not, of the pretender styling herself Wrenna Sarthe, a dead girl walking under a false name to the ruin of the peace.*

A dead girl. The Regent's own proclamation, six weeks old and cried in every square of Oststrand, said Wrenna Sarthe lay in the crypt under the Kept Flame, mourned by her uncle, may the Flame keep her. And now a warrant in the same hand called her a pretender to be taken alive-if-compliant. Roan had served the Throne for nineteen years and had made his peace with a great many orders he did not like, because an army that debated its orders was a mob with good boots. But he had never before been handed a paper that lied about a corpse in one line and demanded its arrest in the next, and asked him to hold both true at once, and call the holding duty.

The Kept Flame did not lie. That was the whole of the faith he had been raised in — that the Flame burning in the Throne-annex ran on true oil and true wick and would gutter the instant a false word was sworn beside it, so that a man of Oststrand measured his own honesty against a fire that could not be bribed. Roan had knelt to it as a boy and taken his commission by it as a man and believed, in the plain unclever way he believed most things, that the Throne kept the Flame and the Flame kept the Throne honest, each the other's witness.
