He did not know, riding down on the Weeping Rocks with a lie folded in his glove, when he had lost the ability to picture that Flame without also picturing it guttering. Somewhere east of Ninefold, he thought. Somewhere in the reading of a warrant that mourned a girl and hunted her in the very same breath.

He was not a clever man and did not pretend to be. He was a man who kept the Flame, said his oaths plain, and slept sound because he never made himself agree to two things that could not both be so. That sleep was gone now. He'd not had it since Ninefold.

"Captain?" His sergeant, at his shoulder, quiet. "We take them at first light? Cavalry's poor work in the dark, and they've the water at their backs."

"At first light," Roan said, and was ashamed of the relief in it, that he had bought himself a night before he'd known he was buying it. "We ring the camp. No lances uncased unless they run. And hear me — no man of ours goes near the water-string or the drovers till I've stood in that camp myself. Am I heard."

"Heard, Captain."

He rode down onto the flat alone under a flag of parley, into the light of another company's fires, to arrest a dead girl.

They met him standing, which he respected, and armed, which he'd expected, and unsurprised, which told him something — that they'd seen him coming, that the caravan-master ran a real night-watch, that these were not the fat smugglers the warrant painted.

The quartermaster came to the edge of the firelight to meet the flag, and Roan knew her before she spoke, and the knowing went through him like cold water. He had never met her. He had heard of her the way every officer of the Meridian service had heard of her: Coyne, of the salt-fleet, the one who'd stood at a court-martial and told a captain-of-fleets to his gilded face that he'd drowned a crew of forty for a cargo bonus and let it be logged as weather — and had been broke and blacklisted and near-hanged for the telling, because the captain-of-fleets was cousin to a duke and the forty were only salt-hands. Her brother among the forty, men said. Roan had been a lieutenant then. He remembered thinking, in the safe cheap way of a man whose own conscience had not yet been billed: *there goes a fool who could not keep two things true at once.*

He was not thinking it cheaply now.

"Captain of dune-cavalry," Sable Coyne said, reading his collar-flashes, "riding down on a licensed caravan under parley. You'll have a paper."

"I have a paper." He did not dismount; a man delivered a warrant from the saddle, that was form, and form was the last dry ground he had. He read it out plain, all of it, the smuggling and the seizure and the arrest — and then, because he would not be a man who hid a line, the last line too, the pretender, the dead girl, the alive-if-compliant. He watched the caravan-master's face while he read it, a big grey pragmatic man named Voss who had gone the colour of ash at *seizure* and stayed ashen, and he watched the quartermaster's face, which did not change at all, which was its own kind of confession — you did not go still as stone at a warrant for a pretender you'd never heard of; you went loud.

The caravan-master found his tongue first, which Roan noted, because it was the wrong man's tongue to find first. Voss talked — fast, reasonable, a licensed Company, papers all in order, a misunderstanding surely, the cargo bonded at Oststrand, names that could be sent to and would vouch — and the whole while his eyes went not to Roan's warrant but past Roan's shoulder, east, into the dark off the flat, the way a man watches a door he is expecting someone to come through. Roan had questioned enough frightened men to know the two kinds apart: the ones afraid of what you will do to them, and the ones afraid of what they have already done. Voss was the second kind. Roan filed it, the way he filed everything he could not yet use, and turned back to the quartermaster, who had not talked at all.

And he watched, at the back of the firelight, a slight figure in a drover's coat with a bell at her belt, who had come three steps closer than a mute water-drover had any reason to, and stood there in the light with her chin up and her hands open at her sides, looking at him — at *him*, Roan Ferrough, the man come to arrest her — with a steadiness he had seen in exactly one other place in his life: on the Regent himself, across the Counting-Hall, the day Halloran Sarthe took the Throne in trust and dared the room to say the word *usurper*. The same bones. The same refusal to drop the eyes.

*A dead girl walking under a false name.* The warrant lied about the corpse. He had known that since Ninefold. He had not known, until he looked at her face in the firelight, that it lied about the *pretender* too — that this was no player got up in a claim, but the thing itself, the true blood the proclamation had buried alive on paper. And a warrant that called the true heir a pretender and ordered her taken *by any needful means* was not an arrest. Roan had escorted arrests. He had escorted executions, and knew the difference in his hands, and this warrant was the second thing wearing the first thing's coat.

"You're Coyne," he heard himself say, low, only to her. "Of the fleet."

"I was a lot of things." The tally-knife did not move in her hand, but it did not go away either. "You've come a long way to take a girl who's already dead, Captain. Your own Regent buried her. It was cried in the squares. I heard it cried at Ninefold six days ago. So either your paper's a forgery" — and here she smiled, thin and without any warmth at all, a fleet-officer's smile, the smile of someone who had once told a gilded man the truth and paid for it — "or the man who signed it is."

It was the exact shape of the thing he had not let himself say. She had said it standing in her own firelight with forty lances in the dark around her camp, the way she'd said the other thing in the court-martial, because some people could not hold two untrue things at once no matter what it cost them, and God help him, God and the Kept Flame help him, he was one of them and always had been and had only lately been sent somewhere the cost came due.

He made himself look at the girl once more before he turned his horse. She had not moved from her three steps forward. She watched him the way her blood watched the Counting-Hall, level and unhurried, and Roan Ferrough, who kept the Flame and did not lie and could not hold two untrue things at once, found that he could not make his mouth shape the word *pretender* to her face. The word was in the warrant. It was not in him. He inclined his head to her — a fraction, the bow you gave a rank and not a prisoner — before he had decided to, and saw her mark it, and saw the quartermaster mark him marking it, and rode back up the flat carrying the shame of a man who has just shown two companies and forty of his own lances exactly where his oath had cracked.

He gave them the night.

He told himself it was form. He told his sergeant it was tactics — cavalry was poor work in the dark, the beasts wanted rest, a camp against water would only bleed his men if rushed by moonlight, and all of that was true, every word, and none of it was why. He rode back up to his troop on the flat and set the ring and posted the watch and gave the order that would have been given by any careful captain: *first light. Not before.* And then he sat his horse a little apart from his men in the cold, with the warrant a dead weight in his glove, and did the sum he had been refusing since Ninefold, the way she'd made him do it — out loud, to the dark, two things held up side by side to see if they could both be true.

*I keep the Flame,* he said to the dark. *I keep my oath to the Throne.*

*The man on the Throne buried a living girl and signed her death twice, once as mourning and once as a warrant, and calls it keeping the peace.*

They would not both stand. He had known since the water came up green out of the night that they would not both stand, and that a night was all he had to give while he decided which one he was — a soldier who did as the paper said and slept no more, or an oath-breaker who kept faith with the Flame by breaking faith with the hand that held it. He did not decide it that night. He was not a quick man. But he had given them the hours, the small mercy of a slow soldier, and he told himself that whatever came at first light, he had at least not spent them cheap.

He thought of his men rolled in their cloaks on the cold flat, forty who had ridden into a dead land on his word because his word had always been good, and he wondered what he would ask of them at first light and by what right. To charge a licensed caravan for the crime of carrying a truth the Throne had outlawed. To take a girl alive-if-compliant and hand her back to men who had already killed her once on paper and would want the paper made honest. His men would do it if he ordered it — that was the horror folded up inside the comfort of command. They trusted him not to spend them cheap, and he no longer knew whether obeying this warrant or breaking it was the cheaper spending; only that one of the two would cost him the sleep he had already lost, and the other would cost him everything that was left.

He should have known better than to think the night was his to give.

The Weeping Rocks lay below him in the moonlight, green and quiet, the two companies bedded a bowshot apart around the one good water in a dead land, and out past both of them the Saltreach ran east to a rim of dark that Roan's tired eyes took, at first, for the ordinary dark of the deep desert — until a point of it kindled orange, low and small and wrong, and then another, and another, strung along the eastern flat like beads on a wire, coming on. Not campfires. Moving. Fire that moved was carried, and fire carried across the Saltreach at the dead of night, toward the only water for a hundred miles, was carried by men who did not mean to drink it.

His sergeant's voice came up sharp from the picket. "*Captain —*"

"I see them," Roan said, and his hand went to his sword out of nineteen years of habit before his mind had finished naming the thing his eyes had already known: that the choice he had thought was his to make slow, in his own honest time, had just been taken out of his hands by someone who kept neither Flame nor Throne nor any faith but ash.

ch19.body:
Sable had watered nine days into the butts and meant to steal the Weeping Rocks' free four before dawn, and the arithmetic was very clean and very good and lasted exactly until the wind changed and brought her the smell of lamp-oil where no lamp was lit.

She'd not slept. A quartermaster with a warrant ringed around her camp and a captain's grudging night ticking away did not sleep; she'd spent the dark hours doing the only thing she trusted, which was counting — counting butts, counting beasts, counting the odds of running west into the Glare against the odds of the cavalry's lances, and hating every column, because both totals came out in blood and the only question was whose. She was at the crate-cart with her hand on the cold iron through the straw, doing the sum again, when the wind backed round out of the east and laid across the camp the thick sweet reek of oil.

For one breath she thought: *the cavalry's fired the reeds, to smoke us.* Then she thought, colder: *no. Roan Ferrough gave us the night. That man wouldn't cheat a clock.* And then she was running for the spring, tally-knife out, shouting the camp awake, because there was only one thing at the Weeping Rocks worth pouring oil on, and it was not the reeds.

It was the water.

She reached the basin as the first torch came down into it — flung from the dark of the eastern rocks in a long slow arc, trailing flame — and the surface of the seep, the clean cold century-worn basin that had wept them a day of mercy, went up in a low blue sheet of burning oil. Someone had spent the dark hours too. Someone had come down off the flat and poured the whole reeking cargo of it across the one good water in a hundred miles and up the weeping face of the rock, into the seams the spring ran through, and now they lit it, and the Weeping Rocks burned. Not to take the water. To *end* it. To make sure that when the fire died there would be a poisoned, oil-fouled, ash-choked basin that no crown and no caravan and no cavalry would drink from ever again.

"*Off the water!*" Doria Fenn had Sable's arm, hauling her back from the heat, and the cook's flat face in the fire-light was not flat now; it was the face of a woman looking at a thing she had walked a thousand miles to stop looking at. "That's not war, Sable, that's *scripture*. They'd rather no one drink than the wrong one drink. I *know* this. I *did* this, once — Flame forgive me, I've carried the oil —"

And she stopped, because there was no time to confess a whole life over a burning spring, and Sable watched the cook shut the past like a firebox and turn the key on it. Doria Fenn had walked out of the Ashen Vow across this same desert years ago with nothing but a needle and the plain certainty that a creed which burned water to keep it pure had mistaken purity for love. She never spoke of it. She spoke of it now only in what her hands did — and her hands, Sable saw, had already quit reaching for the cleaver and started reaching for the wounded, for Ino's blanket, for the beasts, because that was the whole of the scripture Doria had left herself: fix what you can reach, feed who you can feed, and let the sure men sing.

Up on the dark rim the beads of fire were moving, resolving, becoming what they were: riders, dune-riders, a long ragged line of them coming down onto the flat with torches high and their faces wrapped, and over them, unhurried, a big man on a pale camel who did not carry a torch because he did not need to — Highwarden Ottlength, come to watch his creed made real, the salt kept for no house by the simple method of making it worth no house's taking. And they were singing. That was the part Sable would keep. Coming down out of the dark to burn a spring, the Ashen Vow were *singing*, low and glad, a hymn to no crown and no water and no debt, and it was the most frightened she had been on the whole road, more than the lances, because you could bargain with lances.

They branded what they burned. That was the Vow's signature, and Sable saw it now, high on the weeping face of the rock where the oil-fire had climbed: the ash-brand, a hand's-width of iron seared black into the stone above the ruined spring, the mark they burned into everything they *freed* — a well, a granary, a temple, a caravan — so that all who came after would read it and know the Ashen Vow had passed here and made this thing belong to no one by the plain method of making it good to no one. Highwarden Ottlength sat his pale camel below it, unhurried, watching his riders work, and did not trouble to look at the caravan at all. He did not need the caravan yet. He had the book's whole delivery cornered against a poisoned spring with a dead land at its back, and he could let the desert do his pressing for him. That was the part that frightened Sable worse than the singing: the patience of it. A man in a hurry made mistakes a quartermaster could sell him. Ottlength was in no hurry whatever.

She found Kest by the crate-cart, and understood everything, too late, in the space of a single step.

Brother Kest — the pilgrim, the gentle one, who had shared his water at Dead-Drover's and blessed Ino's wound in a warm sincere voice and argued with her by the fire about what a soul owed to whom, and lost the argument kindly, and gone on liking her — was standing at the crate-cart with the straw pulled back and both hands laid flat on the cold iron of the Salt-Iron Ledger. Not stealing it. She saw at once he wasn't stealing it. He had a skin of oil open at his hip and he was anointing it, wetting the iron pages down with the same lamp-oil that burned the spring, his lips moving, his good warm face lit from the side by the fire he'd let in, and when he looked up at her there was no guilt in it at all, which was the terrible thing, which was worse than any guilt could have been.

"I signalled them from Ninefold," he said, gently, the way he said everything. "You should know it was me, and not one of your own. I'd not have a innocent carry it." He pressed the oil into the iron with real tenderness. "I've walked with you a long way, Sable Coyne, and I've come to love this crew, and I want you to understand I do this *because* of that, not despite it. This book will make a girl a queen. A queen makes a throne, and a throne makes a hundred years of men like your captain out there riding down the thirsty on paper. The salt belongs to no house. Better it drink oil than crown one more owner." He almost smiled. "You of all people. You who won't be owned. How can you carry a book whose whole purpose is to *own* the road?"

And there it was — her own argument, the argument she'd made to herself in Ninefold's north shade over short water, handed back to her out of a zealot's warm mouth with a torch in the other hand, and she hated that it fit, she hated that Kest of all of them had heard her truly, that the man setting fire to the world had understood her better than the wool-buyer or the caravan-master or anyone who wished her well.

"You forgot the arithmetic," Sable said, and put the tally-knife to his throat. "You'd burn the water so no house owns it. But the crew that dies of the thirst you're making tonight — Ino, who's seventeen, and never owned a thing but a tally-ledger — they don't die free of a house, Brother. They just die. You didn't refuse the debt. You just made sure somebody else pays it."

She did not cut him. She wanted that on record too. Doria came up beside her out of the burning light with a cook's cleaver and her whole terrible past in her face, and it was Doria, not Sable, that Kest looked at — Doria, who had carried the oil once and set it down, the one apostate in the world whose eyes he could not meet with all that warm certainty intact. Something in him flinched from her that had not flinched from a knife. "Doria," he said, softer. "You know I'm right. You knew it when you walked."

"I knew you were *sure*," Doria said. "I stopped being able to tell the difference between sure and right, so I left. Get your hands off the girl's book, Kest, or I'll take them off at the wrist and stitch you after, because that's *my* scripture now — I fix what I can reach." And Kest, who would have died on Sable's knife singing, took his oiled hands off the cold iron and stepped back from a cook, because the only thing a zealot cannot bear is the calm face of the one who used to believe.

He went, into the smoke and the singing and his Highwarden's line, and Sable let him go, because chasing him meant leaving the crate, and the crate was cold and heavy and iron in her hands as she and Doria dragged the straw back over the oil-slicked Ledger — it had not caught; iron does not catch; that was the whole grim joke of it, that the one thing at the Weeping Rocks that could not be burned was the book, and the one thing that could was the water they all needed to live long enough to deliver it.

There was no choosing left. That was almost a mercy.

The spring was burning and would be poison by dawn. Behind them east came the Ashen Vow, singing, forty torches and a Highwarden who wanted the Ledger and the girl turned to ash on principle. Between the Vow and the caravan sat Roan Ferrough's forty lances, awake now, a ring of cavalry that had come to arrest them and now stood between them and a worse thing — and Sable saw, in one clean flash across the burning flat, the captain on his horse with his sword out, not charging the caravan, *turning*, wheeling his troop east to face the torches, because whatever else Roan Ferrough was he was a man who would not let a spring be murdered in front of him no matter whose warrant was in his glove. His night's mercy had become a shield by accident, and he'd have the whole reckoning of that later, if any of them lived to reckon.

For one heartbeat the whole burning flat hung in a kind of terrible balance — the Vow coming down out of the east singing, the cavalry wheeling to meet them, the caravan caught between two companies of armed men and one dying spring — and every soul on the Weeping Rocks was suddenly, absurdly, on the same side of exactly one question, which was whether the water lived. It did not live. The blue fire had it. Whoever won the fight about to break across the flat would win a poisoned basin and a branded rock and a hundred miles of white in every direction, and Sable Coyne, who had spent a life reading which way to run off a bad manifest, read this one at a glance and knew there was only one door in the whole burning room that led anywhere but a grave.

West. The only clean direction on the whole compass was west, into the dark, into the Glare — the deep waterless belly of the Saltreach that wanted thirteen days of water and would get the nine in the butts and not one swallow more, because the free four they'd meant to steal were burning blue behind them.

Sable did the sum one last time, standing at the crate-cart with the reek of oil and the sound of hymns and the small hard note of a drover's bell cutting across all of it — Wren, up at the head of the water-string, ringing the beasts to their feet, ringing them to march, doing the one thing she could do without a voice, holding the string together with a flat half-tone of brazed bronze while the world burned. Nine days for a thirteen-day crossing. The arithmetic did not care that she was tired, or afraid, or that a gentle man had just told her the truest lie she'd ever heard. It only came out the way it came out.

"Marsh — cut the pickets, string them tight, we walk in a dark march." Her voice went out over the camp flat and steady, the quartermaster's voice, the only faith she had. "Doria, Ino in the sick-wagon and lash him down. Ката leads. Everybody drinks now, everybody drinks their fill *now* while there's water to lose, because after tonight the tally starts and the tally is short." She swung up beside the crate-cart with the cold iron at her knee and the burning spring at her back and the whole priced world reduced, at last, to a single clean unpriced fact: they would go into the Glare with too little water, and either come out the far side or not, and there was no fourth thing anyone could offer her for the book that was worth more than the next swallow now.

She looked west, into the flat black nothing where the Glare waited, and gave the order she'd been dreading since Ninefold, since the crate cracked, since a stranger paid her in salt-iron coin a lifetime ago to carry one cold heavy thing and ask no questions.

"Walk them on," Sable said. "Into the white. We'll see what we're worth by the far side."

And the Verdigris Company turned its back on the burning water and walked the girl and the iron and the short tally out into the dark, toward the Glare, while behind them the Weeping Rocks wept fire instead of water, and the Ashen Vow sang, and Roan Ferrough's lances came down to meet the torches, and the last free water on the whole salt road went to ash and oil under a moon that weighed nothing and witnessed everyone.

ch20.body:
The Glare began as a color before it was a place. All the last day the white had been climbing out of the west like a second noon, a brightness with no sun in it, until by dusk the far edge of the Saltreach was not a horizon at all but a wound in the eye — a rim of pure salt-shine that swallowed distance and gave nothing back. Wren had watched it come on from her place at Old Ката's shoulder, and she had understood, without anyone telling her, that this was the thing the drovers meant when they lowered their voices and would not name it straight. The Glare. Even the word was a flinch.

They had halted a bowshot short of it because no one had the courage to be the first to step in with the light going.

Wren kept her hand on the camel-mother's neck and did not take it away, because the warmth there was the only ordinary thing left. Behind them, a day and a half behind, the Weeping Rocks still smoked. She could not see the smoke anymore but she carried the smell of it in her clothes, in the wet-ash reek of a spring poisoned on purpose, and she thought she would carry it the rest of her life however long or short that turned out to be. The one good water for eighty leagues, salted with something worse than salt and set alight, so that the crew had filled what butts they could from the fouled runoff and boiled it and strained it through Doria's charcoal and still it tasted of the hand that had ruined it. Too little. Everyone knew it was too little. The knowing sat over the camp like the white sat over the west.

Ino should have been calling the tally. It was his voice she listened for at every halt, the water-clerk's sing-song — so many measures drawn, so many kept, mark it, Coyne, mark it — but Ino had ridden the whole afternoon slumped in Sorrel's shadow with his eyes bright and wrong, and it was Sable who had gone up and down the string counting butts with her own mouth pressed thin. Wren had watched that too. She watched everything. It was the one skill her silence had left her: three months mute at the tail of a caravan had made her a reader of shoulders and hands and the small betrayals of the back of a neck, and what she read now, up and down the halted line, was a crew doing the arithmetic of their own dying and not liking the sum.

She had a bell. She had worn it the whole road at her collar — the drover's bell that marked her as one of the voiceless, the deaf-and-dumb water-hands the Company hired cheap because they could not gossip a cargo — and it had cracked against a doorframe at the Dead-Drover ruin weeks ago and gone dull, so that now it did not ring so much as knock, a small wooden knock at her throat when she moved. A broken bell for a false silence. She had grown to hate it and to need it in the same breath, the way you need the lie that is keeping you alive.

The argument started at the fire, if you could call a pit of smouldering camel-dung a fire, and it started the way these things always did, sideways, from a man too frightened to say the true thing.

"We go back to the Rocks." That was Marsh, Sable's own second, hunched with his forearms on his knees and not looking up. "Boil it another day. There's more water in a burnt spring than in that." He tipped his chin at the white. "There's no water in that at all. That's the whole point of it. It's got a name because it kills people."

"The Rocks are burning," someone said.

"The Rocks were burning. Fire goes out. Salt-Iron warrant doesn't." He meant Roan's cavalry, somewhere behind, riding under the Regent's seal to take the caravan and the pretender both. "We're between a fire and a noose and you all want to walk into the one place that's neither because it's got nothing at all. That's not a plan. That's just choosing the slow way."

No one answered him for a moment, and in the silence Wren felt the whole camp begin to lean his direction, not because he was right but because he was afraid out loud and fear is contagious as a yawn. She looked for Sable and found her at the edge of the light with the firm set to her jaw that Wren had learned meant she was choosing her words like coin, but before Sable could spend any of them Adder spoke from the dark.

"West," the caravan-master said. Only that. He did not raise his voice. He never did. "We rest till the moon's up, and we go west by the cool, and we don't stop till we're through." And there was something in how he said it, some flatness under the certainty, that snagged in Wren's ear like a thread on a nail — a man ordering a thing he already knew the shape of, the way you speak of a room you have walked in the dark. She could not have said why it troubled her. She filed it, the way she filed everything, in the wordless ledger behind her teeth.

But west or back, it did not matter to Marsh's fear, and the fear was winning. Two of the teamsters had stood. Someone was already talking about how many butts a fast string could carry back to the Rocks if they cut the sick and the slow loose, and no one said whose names those were, but everyone's eyes went, once, quick and ashamed, to the place where Ino lay in the camel's shadow with the fever making him beautiful and doomed.

Wren felt it then — the moment the caravan stopped being a caravan and became eleven people and forty camels each doing sums for one. She felt it the way you feel a floor give.

And she understood that no one at that fire could stop it. Sable could give an order and be obeyed and hated, and the hatred would do the Vow's work for it, splitting them before the salt even started. Adder's flatness would not hold them; they could hear the wrongness in it same as she could, even if they couldn't name it. There was no voice in that camp with the standing to make frightened people brave, because standing on the road was bought with water and salt and years, and everyone there had spent theirs down to the rim.

Except that there was one person whose standing had nothing to do with the road at all, and she had been keeping it in her mouth for three months, and she was so afraid of it that her hands had gone cold in the desert heat.

She took the bell off first.

Afterward she could never explain why that had to come first, except that she could not do the one thing while wearing the sign of the other. Her fingers found the knot at her nape, the greasy leather she had tied and retied a hundred nights, and she worked it loose and drew the cord over her head and held the broken bell in her fist where it could not even knock. The small motion drew no eyes. She was the mute water-drover; no one watched what she did with her own collar.

Then Wren stood up into the firelight and said, in a voice rusted from disuse and steadier than she had any right to expect, "You won't make it back to the Rocks."

It was not loud. That was the thing she got right without knowing she was getting anything right — she did not shout it, she said it, the way you state a weight or a distance, a fact of the road. But a mute speaking is louder than any shout. The camp went so still she could hear the camels grinding cud and the tick of cooling salt. Marsh's head came up. Doria, at the fire's far side with her surgeon's hands full of Ino's wrist, went absolutely rigid, and her eyes came to Wren's face with a recognition in them that was three months late arriving and arrived all at once.

"You're a fast string," Wren went on, into that terrible attention, and she made herself keep going because to stop now was to drown. "Say you are. Say you cut loose everything that slows you — the sick, the spare butts, the Ledger-crate, all of it. You ride hard for a spring that's fouled and burning, with a Meridian warrant closing the road behind you. And say you even reach it." She turned the fact over so they could see its underside. "You've spent half your water getting there. To drink poison. With Captain Ferrough's cavalry between you and the only other water on the eastern road. That's not the slow way out, Marsh. That's the fast one. West is the slow way. West is the way where slow is the whole idea, because slow is how you live through it."

"And what would you know about it." Marsh's voice cracked in the middle, half fury and half a drowning man's need to be argued out of the water. "You've never said a word the whole road. You've never carried the tally. You don't even —" He stopped, because he had been about to say you don't even know what's in the crate, and some animal part of him had felt the ground there and shied.

Wren looked at him and let the silence do a little of her work, the way silence had done her work for three months, and then she spent the truth she had been saving, not all of it, but enough.

"I know what's in the crate," she said. "I know what it's worth. I know exactly how far men will ride to burn it, because they burned a spring to make us carry it into the Glare thirsty, and it worked, look at us. And I am telling you that the crate crosses. Not because it's mine to command." That was a lie and everyone would learn it was a lie and she said it anyway, because the truth was not ready and the crew was. "Because I have crossed worse than this on less than this, and I am telling you it can be done, and I will tell you every measure of how while we do it. Doria. How many days of water, drawn tight, one measure a soul, half for the camels?"

A beat. Doria's clever eyes moved over her, doing their own arithmetic, and the surgeon chose — Wren saw her choose — to answer the drover as if the drover had the right to ask.

"Five," Doria said. "Four if it stays this hot. Three if we're fools with it."

"Then we won't be fools with it." Wren turned to the white, so that when she spoke next she was speaking to the thing itself and letting them hear her do it. "Four days of Glare. We march the cool and lie up the heat under whatever shade we can rig. No standing rations — the tally comes to me and Coyne every dawn and every dusk and it comes true, no man drinks ahead, no man drinks behind, and any butt that goes short between dusk and dawn, we all answer for, because in there a stolen mouthful is a stolen life and it might be yours." She did not look at Marsh when she said it. She did not have to. She felt him flinch as though she had, and she filed that, too, and did not yet understand what she had filed. "Camels first at the worst of it. Old Ката leads. She's crossed it before and she'll smell the far side before any of us. You follow her nose and you follow the tally and you do not follow the water you'll see out there that isn't there. Four days. Then reef and shade and the west and we're through."

The quiet after was different from the quiet before. It was not agreement, exactly. It was the particular hush of frightened people who have been handed a rope to hold and have found, to their surprise, that it holds their weight.

Sable moved first. Of course it was Sable. She came off the edge of the dark into the firelight and she looked at Wren for a long moment with an expression Wren had never once seen on that guarded face — not the wariness she'd worn since the crate cracked open, not the flat quartermaster's assessment, but something closer to a soldier recognizing rank. Then she pulled the tally-knife from her belt, her father's knife, the one she notched the water-count into, and she held it up so the fire caught the worn blade, and she said to the crew, loud and dry and final:

"You heard the drover. Strike the camp. We march on the moon." And then, lower, only for the space between the two of them, as she passed close: "Whatever you are — I'll follow it. But God help you, you'll tell me the rest before the far side."

Wren put the broken bell in her pocket. She did not tie it back on. She went to Old Ката and set her forehead against the great warm neck for one breath, one, the last privacy she thought she might have for four days, and the camel-mother huffed at her and lipped her hair as though she were an ordinary girl and not the thing the whole road wanted to burn.

Then she turned the string to face the white, and by the time the moon came up hard and cold over the salt she was at its head, walking first, so that when the caravan followed Old Ката into the Glare it was following a girl as well, and neither the girl nor the crew let themselves think too long about which of the two of them the road would spend to get the other across.

ch21.body:
By the second dawn Sable had stopped believing in the far side.

She knew it was still there. She could have told you the leagues, more or less, the way she could tell you the weight of a salt-block by the ache in her shoulders — the quartermaster's arithmetic ran on under everything, tallying, always tallying, it was the last thing in her that would die. But belief was a different animal than knowledge, and belief needed something to feed on, a landmark, a shadow, a line where the world stopped being white, and the Glare gave it nothing. The Glare gave you a floor of cracked salt so bright it came up through the soles of your boots as heat and through the slits of your salt-veil as pain, and a sky bleached to the color of an old bone, and between them a shimmer where the two met and lied to you about water. That was all. From the first hour it was all, and by the second dawn Sable's eyes had gone from aching to a dull ringing brightness she couldn't blink out, and the far side was a rumor she paid into like a debt she no longer expected to collect.

She marched at the rear where a quartermaster belonged, watching the string the way you watch a rope under load, for the strand about to go.

They had gone tight on the water the way Wren said. Dawn tally and dusk tally, one measure a soul, and Sable ran it herself now because Ino couldn't. That was the first strand gone. The boy had kept the Company's water-ledger since he was fifteen and idolized her for reasons she'd never deserved and never corrected, and now he rode lashed upright in Sorrel's panniers with a fever cooking the old arrow-graze in his shoulder — the wound from the ruin, the one Doria had cleaned and closed and that had waited all these weeks in the meat of him for a hot enough day to bloom. It had found one. He talked in the heat. He called the tally in his sleep, so-many-drawn, so-many-kept, mark it, Coyne, and the crew had stopped being able to bear the sound of it, that cheerful ghost of the ledger coming out of a slack gray face, and Sable had ordered him gagged loose with a wet cloth as much to spare them as to spare his cracking lips. Doria said the fever would break or it wouldn't by the third night. Doria did not say which she thought. Doria's face when she looked at Ino was the face of a woman spending the last of something.

The mirages started with the light and got worse as it climbed.

Sable had crossed salt before — she'd been a Meridian salt-fleet officer once, before the noose, before Adder, she knew the tricks the Saltreach played on a starved eye — but the Glare was a different order of liar. It didn't just paint water. It painted whole cool blue lakes with reeds at their margins, it painted the black-basalt sea-walls of Oststrand rising out of the shimmer with the tide-bells ringing, it painted the road behind you as an ocean so that turning back meant drowning. It painted people. That was the cruelty of it, that was the thing the drovers wouldn't say at the fire: on the second day, when the salt was ringing in her skull and her tongue had gone to leather, Sable looked out along the blazing floor and saw her brother walking parallel to the string, a stone's throw off, Petar in his salt-fleet blues with the collar she'd last seen soaked black, keeping easy pace with her, not looking over, the way he'd walked beside her their whole childhood. She knew it was the Glare. She knew it the way you know a thing and disbelieve it at once. She watched Petar walk beside her for the better part of an hour and did not call out to him because she was a quartermaster and calling out cost water, and because if she called and he turned and had her father's tally-knife wound in his belly where she'd last really seen it, she thought the last strong strand in her might go. So she marched, and her dead brother marched, and neither of them spoke, and that was the closest thing to company she got in the Glare.

The camel went in the middle of the second afternoon.

It was Sorrel — of course it was Sorrel, it was always the one carrying the most that the salt wanted — a good steady water-cow eleven years on the road, and she had been favoring a foot since noon and no one had the water to spare for stopping. They came to a place where the salt-crust had a sheen to it, a faint wet gleam that the drovers knew to skirt because under the crust the Glare hid brine-sinks, pockets of heavy dead water thick as syrup and hungry, and Old Ката at the head swung them wide of it and every camel followed her nose the way Wren had said. Every camel but Sorrel. The fever-boy was on her back. Something spooked her — a mirage, a smell, the plain end of her patience — and she broke the line at a shambling run straight across the sheen, and the crust held for three strides and took her on the fourth.

Sable was already running. Everyone was already running, and running in the Glare is a way of spending your life you don't get back, and it didn't matter. The brine had Sorrel to the belly before they reached her and to the chest by the time they got a line on her, and she screamed — camels do not often make a sound you'll carry to your grave, but Sorrel made it, a sound like a gate — and Marsh and two teamsters and Sable herself hauled on the line until the rope cut the meat of their salt-cracked hands and the sink hauled back, patient, and won. They saved the boy. Doria and Wren dragged Ino off the pannier-frame as it went under, dragged him across the groaning crust by his fever-slack arms, and they saved him, and the water-butts lashed to Sorrel's off-side they did not save, two full butts and a half, gone into the brine in the time it takes to say a name.

Sable knelt on the singing salt with the rope-burn welling on her palms and watched the last of the water she was responsible for slide under, and she did the arithmetic, because she could not not do it, and the arithmetic said they had crossed the line from tight into not enough somewhere between one breath and the next, and she was the quartermaster and it was her tally and she had not seen it coming.

Except that when she made herself run the numbers back — later, at the dusk halt, with her hands wrapped in the rags Doria could spare — the numbers did not come out to Sorrel.

She kept the dusk tally by feel because her eyes were done for the day.

Every butt in the string, she put her hands on it, unstoppered it, weighed the slosh, and where she couldn't trust the weight she dipped a measure and looked at it against what the ledger in her head said should be there. And what the ledger in her head said, over and over, butt after butt, was more than her hands were finding. Not by Sorrel's two-and-a-half. By more. A finger's depth here. Two fingers there. A butt she'd have swown was near full down to two-thirds and no leak in the staves to show for it. Small thefts, spread wide and old, the kind of skimming a man does when he's careful and frightened and has been at it long enough to know exactly how much won't be noticed by a tally kept by a fevered boy who worshipped the crew that was robbing him.

She sat with it a long time in the cold that came down on the Glare at dusk hard as the heat had come down at noon, two extremes and nothing kind between them, and she watched the camp and did the other arithmetic, the ugly one, the who.

Marsh was mending the line where Sorrel had cut it. He'd been quiet since the sink. Quieter than a man is from grief for a camel. He worked with his back to the fire and his shoulders had the particular set she'd been reading off frightened men since she was a water-hand herself, the set of a man waiting for a hand on his collar, and she remembered — the salt shook it loose in her, the way exhaustion sometimes shakes loose the thing you should have seen weeks back — she remembered that Marsh had a debt. Everyone knew Marsh had a debt; it was practically his second name, Marsh-who-owes, a gambling rope around his neck that had followed him onto the caravan the way such things do. She'd never asked to whom. On the road you didn't. You covered a man's debt with your silence the way you covered his water with the tally, and you trusted the tally to keep him honest, and the tally had been kept by a boy who was now dying in a pannier.

She got up. Her knees told her what they thought of it. She crossed the camp and crouched by Marsh at the cut line, and she didn't say anything at first, just put her two rag-wrapped hands out and took a turn of the rope to help him splice, the way they'd spliced a thousand lines together on a dozen roads, and after a while Marsh said, without looking up, in a voice gone to gravel, "How short."

So he already knew she'd know. That was almost a mercy.

"Enough that it wasn't Sorrel," Sable said. "Enough that it's been going out the bottom of my string for weeks and I was too busy watching the horizon for the Vow to watch the water at my own feet." She kept her voice flat. The tally-voice. "I'm not going to ask you was it you, Marsh, because you'd tell me and then I'd have to do something about it in front of the crew, and we can't afford what I'd have to do. So I'm going to ask you a different thing, and you're going to answer it true, because Ino's dying of a wound he took covering your retreat at the ruin and you owe him a true answer if you never pay another debt in your life." She felt him go still under the rope. "Who did you owe."

The splice sagged forgotten between their hands. Marsh looked up, and in the last of the light his face was the face of a man who has been carrying something up a hill for a very long time and has just been told he can put it down, and doesn't believe it, and wants to so badly it's a kind of pain.

"You're going to wish you'd let me answer the first question," he said.

"Marsh."

"It wasn't gambling. Not — not only." He wet his cracked lips with a tongue that had no water to give them. "The debt was real, at the start. But a man came to me at the Verdigris Yards, before we ever loaded, and he bought it up. The whole rope. Bought me a clean slate for one thing — keep the water-tally soft on a butt or two, put a little by against a hard stretch, don't ask what it's for. I thought it was pilfering. Everybody pilfers. I swear on the boy I thought it was just a man skimming his own caravan, and I've done worse things than help a man rob a company that hanged better people than me." His voice dropped so low she had to lean into the cold to catch it, and the whole white world seemed to lean in with her. "And then at the Rocks I saw who he signaled to. Across the water. Before it burned. I saw who he was talking to with a shade-lamp in the dark, and it wasn't a Guild factor, Coyne, it was a dune-rider, and I put the water together with the route together with every ambush that ever found us on the open salt where no one should've known to look, and I've been carrying it for two days and I'd have carried it to the far side and never said, except you asked me true and Ino's dying, so." He stopped. He made himself say the name. "It was Adder. It's been Adder the whole road. He's the leak. He's been the leak for years."

Sable did not drop the rope. She was proud of that afterward, in the small cold way you're proud of a thing that cost you everything to do — she did not drop the rope and she did not make a sound, and her face, she was fairly sure, did not move at all. The tally-voice held. It was the only thing that held.

Because Adder Voss had cut her down from a Meridian gibbet with his own knife when the salt-fleet was three breaths from hanging her for her brother's death, and had paid her price to the Company out of his own purse, and had given her a berth and a name and a road back to being a person when she had decided to stop being one. She owed Adder her life. It was the one debt she had never resented, the single rope around her own neck she had chosen to keep on, because Adder Voss was the nearest thing to honest that a bought life could point at, and she had built the whole of who she was now on that being true.

Out on the salt, at the edge of the firelight, her dead brother stood watching her with his black collar, and for once she thought he might be real, because only the dead should get to look at a thing this cleanly.

"Splice the line," she told Marsh, and her voice did not shake, and that was a lie of a kind, and she'd learned lies from a girl who'd kept one for three months and made it look like mercy. "Splice the line and say nothing and drink your measure and no more. We cross first. We cross the crew first, and Ino, and the crate." She stood, and the Glare rang white and empty in every direction, all of it worth a fortune in salt and none of it worth a mouthful of water, and somewhere ahead in the dark her caravan-master was leading them, sure and flat, down a route he had sold. "And then Adder and I are going to have a reckoning about what he thinks he's owed."

ch22.body:
She let him have the third dawn. It was the cruelest thing she had it in her to do and she did it on purpose, the way she did everything now, by tally.

She let Adder call the morning march and set the string and check Old Ката's nose against the far white, all his ordinary certain motions, the caravan-master husbanding his people across the killing floor, and she watched him do it knowing what she knew and she made herself watch, because she wanted to be sure. Not of Marsh — Marsh had no reason to lie that cost him less than the truth had. She wanted to be sure of herself, that when she opened this she was opening it because it was true and not because the salt had cooked her judgment to the same leather as her tongue. So she watched Adder be good at his work, be kind to Ino in passing, lay his broad scarred hand on the Ledger-crate as he went by it the way a man lays a hand on cargo he's responsible for, and she catalogued each of these against the shade-lamp signaling a dune-rider across a spring he was about to let them burn, and by the time the sun cleared the flat she was sure, and being sure was worse than doubting had been.

She had rehearsed a hundred openings across the cold hours and thrown every one away. There was no clever way to ask a man why he had sold you. There was no quartermaster's ledger that balanced this — she had tried to make one in her head, the way she made one of everything, life against life, the gibbet-debt against the burned spring against Doria's charcoal-strained water against a fever-boy calling the tally in his sleep, and the columns would not add, because the thing Adder had spent was not a thing you could enter in a column. You could not tally trust. That was the whole trouble with it. You banked it without counting, and then one day you found the vault had been empty for years and you had been living off the memory of a sum.

She thought of Petar while she watched Adder work; she could not help it. The Glare had put her dead brother at her shoulder for two days and he was still half-there, a smear at the edge of the ringing white, and she found herself telling him things the way she had when they were water-hands together and the night-watch ran long. Look at him, she told Petar. Look how good he is at it. That was the part she could not forgive and could not stop admiring — that a man could be genuinely, decently good at the keeping of people and sell them anyway, and mean the kindness while he did it. She had thought those were opposite things. The road was teaching her they lived in the same man, cheek to cheek, and that the teaching was going to cost her the last clean thing she had let herself believe.

She waited until the mid-morning halt, when the heat drove them to rig the shade-cloths and lie up, because she wanted witnesses and she wanted them still. She wanted Wren there. She had thought about that a long while in the cold and decided the girl had earned the right to see the man who'd been selling her to the fire, and had earned, too, the harder thing — to see how Sable handled a betrayal, because Wren was going to spend a life among betrayals if she lived to claim what the crate said was hers, and she might as well learn the shape of one from someone who loved her.

That word had come to Sable in the night, unbidden and unwelcome, and she had not been able to put it back.

"Adder." She said it across the rigged shade, into the exhausted quiet of eleven people and one fever-boy and the camels couched in their own thin shadows. "How long have you been feeding us to the Vow?"

The camp did not react at first, because half of them thought they'd misheard and the other half hoped they had. Adder looked up from the strap he was mending. His weathered face did the thing she'd been afraid it would do, which was not to flinch, not to whiten, not to reach for a weapon or a denial — it simply arranged itself, slowly, into a kind of tiredness, as though a weight he'd been holding level for years had finally been allowed to sag. He set the strap down. He looked at her with something that in a better man she'd have called sorrow, and in this moment she made herself refuse to call anything, because she could not afford the arithmetic of his feelings, only of his acts.

"Years," Adder said. He didn't ask how she knew. That was the worst of it, that he gave her the truth like a man paying a bill he'd always known would come due. "Since before you. Since the winter the Company nearly went under and the Vow's coin was the only coin that came, and I told myself it was routes, just routes, the road belongs to no house so what's a route worth to the men who believe that hardest. I told myself a lot of things across a lot of years, Sable. You get good at it." His eyes went, once, to the crate, and back. "And then this run they wanted more than a route. They wanted to know the day and the water and the weak stretch, and I gave it to them, and I told myself the same lie one more time, that it was cargo and coin and none of my crew would be the ones the salt kept." He spread his scarred hands. "That was the lie I couldn't make hold. I knew it wouldn't hold when I made it. I made it anyway. There's the whole of me, if you want it. I'm a man who'll do a thing he knows he can't forgive so he doesn't have to feel it happening yet."

"You burned the Rocks." That was Doria, from beside Ino, in a voice Sable had never heard the surgeon use — the flat of it, the ash of it. "You let Kest burn the one water, knowing we'd have to run the Glare short. You did the sum on us. You knew what four days short would cost and you spent it."

"I didn't burn it." Adder's jaw worked. "But I knew it would be burned, and I didn't warn you, and there's no daylight between those, Doria, I know it. You of all people know it." Something passed between the caravan-master and the cook then, some freight of a shared old country, the Vow they'd both come out of by different doors, and it was the first Sable understood how deep this went, that the rot had roots older than the road they were standing on.

"Where were you handing us over," Sable said. "You steered us west by the cool three nights running. You've been walking us somewhere. Where."

Adder was quiet for a moment, and in the quiet Sable heard it — the thing under the shade-cloth's flap, out on the ringing white, that she'd been half-hearing since the halt and telling herself was the wind: a bell. Not a camel-bell. A shade-lamp's little wind-clapper, the kind a dune-rider hangs to be found by, the kind that says here, come to me, close now. Kest's bell. Kest, who had ghosted them since the Rocks, warm and patient and murdering, waiting out on the salt for the master to deliver what he'd sold.

"Here," Adder said simply. "About here. Ottlength's riders are a half-day off and closing, and they've had the water and the route from me the whole road, and the arrangement was I bring the caravan slack and thirsty into the deep Glare where you'd be too spent to fight, and they take the crate and the girl, and the rest of you they'd have let walk to the far side because dead crew makes noise and live crew makes excuses." He looked, finally, at Wren, who had come to her feet at the edge of the shade with her broken bell in her fist and her face gone to something older than her years. "I'm sorry, girl. That's a coin I can't pay back and I won't insult you pretending I mean to try. I only mean to tell you it was never you. It was never even the crown. It was that I owed a debt in the one currency I let myself believe was clean, and I paid it with everyone I was supposed to keep."

For a moment no one moved, and then — this was the thing Sable had braced for and hated to be right about — someone did. One of the teamsters, a salt-cracked man everyone called Ledger-Tom for a reason no one remembered, got half to his feet at the shade's edge with his eyes going from the crate to the white and back, doing the arithmetic Adder had counted on him doing: that the master knew the road, that the master surely had water cached out there with the riders, that a man who wanted to live might do worse than walk out of the deep Glare beside the one person who had arranged to survive it. Two others shifted their weight. The caravan hung on the edge of coming apart along that seam, the seam Adder had always known was there, because a bought crew is only ever loyal to the next payment.

"Sit down, Tom," Marsh said. He did not stand to say it. He said it from the ground, hoarse and gray, with the particular authority of a man who has just told the worst truth of his own life out loud and found the sky did not fall. "He's got no water cached that isn't a lie to get you walking. I know. I kept his skim the whole road. There's nothing out there but riders who'll take the crate off his hands and leave the rest of us for the salt to keep. You want to trust the sums of the man who's been cooking them since the Yards, go ahead. I did." He looked at his own cracked hands. "Look where it put me." Ledger-Tom looked at him a long moment, and sat, and the seam held — not because anyone had bought it shut, but because one shamed man had chosen, out loud, in front of them all, and choosing turned out to be the one thing that could hold a caravan when the salt and the coin could not.

And here was the place, Sable knew, where a story wanted a knife. Her father's tally-knife was on her belt and her rag-wrapped hand was near it and the whole broken camp was watching to see what the quartermaster did with a man who'd sold them to the salt. She thought about Petar. She thought about the gibbet and the knife that had cut her down. She did the arithmetic one more time, the ugliest yet, life against life, debt against debt, and she found — to her own surprise, to the cold clean surprise of it — that it came out even, and that even was not the same as paid.

"I owe you my life," Sable said. "You know I do. You've never once spent it, and I always waited for you to, and now I understand you were never going to, because you were spending everyone else's instead and mine was the one you kept clean so you could look at it. Well. Here's what your loan buys." She drew the tally-knife. The camp flinched. She turned it in her fist and drove it point-down through the strap he'd been mending, into the salt, so it stood there quivering between them, and she stepped back from it. "It buys you walking. Your life for mine, even, and even's the best you get. Take water for two days — two, I've tallied it, and if you take a mouthful more Marsh will know and I'll know and the Glare can settle the rest. Take the bull Ropewalk and go to your riders. Tell Ottlength the caravan he was promised split on him in the deep Glare and there's no crate to take because the crate walks with people who'll die on it first, and that includes a fever-clerk and a cook and a drover-girl and me, so he can spend his water chasing us into the west or he can spend it getting his own men home, and I'd think hard on the sums if I were him." She heard her own voice, and it was steady, and steady was a mercy she was giving the crew and not the man. "That's the whole of what I'll pay, Adder. I won't kill you and I won't keep you. You wanted the road to belong to no house? Have it. Walk it alone."

For a moment she thought he might argue, or beg, or — worst — thank her. He did none of it. He pulled the tally-knife out of the salt and cleaned it on his sleeve, an old drover's habit, tending a tool, and he handed it back to her hilt-first, and she took it because to refuse it would have been a smaller thing than she wanted to be, and their hands did not touch. Then Adder Voss got up off the salt and coiled two days of water onto the bull Ropewalk with his own hands under the tally of the whole crew watching, not a mouthful over, and he walked out from under the shade-cloth into the white toward the far small sound of Kest's bell, and the caravan split there, in the deep Glare, without another word, the way a rope splits — not clean, never clean, a long fraying and then the sudden give.

He did not look back, and Sable made herself watch him not do it, because she'd told Wren there was a shape to this and a person ought to see the shape whole.

The crew watched with her. That was the second cruelty and she chose it too — she would not let them turn away, would not let it become a private shame between master and quartermaster, because they had all been sold and they had all been kept alive by the same tally, and they had earned the right to see the ledger closed. Ino, propped against Old Ката with the fever still bright in him, watched Adder go with tears cutting clean tracks through the salt-crust on his young face and said nothing, because there was nothing a water-clerk could enter for this, no column for a man walking into the white you would have died for a week ago. Sable put her hand once on the boy's good shoulder and left it there until the figure was gone.

When he was a wavering figure in the shimmer and then a mirage among mirages and then nothing, Wren came and stood at Sable's shoulder and looked out at the nothing with her.

"You let him live," the girl said. Not a question. Working something out.

"I paid what I owed and not a measure more." Sable slid the knife home. Her hands, she noticed, had finally stopped shaking; they'd shaken for two days and now, with the worst of it done, they were still. "That's the only kind of debt worth keeping, Wren. The kind you close to the last coin and never carry again. Remember it. You're going to be owed a great deal by a great many people who'll want you to forgive them cheap so it costs them nothing." She turned the string west, toward the killing light, toward whatever water was left in the world. "Don't. Make them pay it even. Even's the only mercy the road respects."

ch23.body:
Doria had buried men in every ground the two crowns owned — reef-sand at Lowmarch, black basalt-grit at Oststrand, the good brown dirt of the marches where things could rot and become other things — and she had come to believe, over a life of it, that you could read a country by what it did to its dead. The salt did the truest thing of all. The salt kept them.

She sat the fourth night's watch over Ino because no one else could bear to and because she had decided, somewhere in the last day, that if the boy was going to die she was not going to let him do it among people too frightened of losing him to hold his hand. His fever had climbed all day and now, in the killing cold that came down on the Glare when the sun quit, it had gone strange and quiet, the loud delirium burned off, and he lay in the lee of couched Old Ката with his eyes half open on the hard white stars and called the tally so softly you had to lean in to catch it. So-many-drawn. So-many-kept. Mark it. She wet his lips from her own measure, which was against Sable's law and which Sable, catching her at it, had said nothing about, and she thought about faith, because there was nothing else out here big enough to think about.

She had been Ashen Vow once. The crew knew it and didn't speak of it, the way you don't speak of a scar on a friend. She had believed it the way you believe a thing when you are young and furious and have watched a crown price your mother's water out of her reach until she died of a thirst a king could have quenched with the sweepings of his salt-cellar — she had believed that the road belonged to no house, that the salt was no man's to sell, that the Drowned Mother and the Kept Flame were only two purses wearing the faces of gods, and that the Vow's cold creed was the one clean thing in a bought world. She had believed it enough to burn things. She had the ash-brand's mark on the inside of her own wrist where she'd put it herself, a girl proving her faith, and she had walked away from all of it the year she understood that the Vow priced a human life exactly the way the crowns did — cheaper, if anything, because the crowns at least pretended, and the Vow was proud of the arithmetic. She had walked into the Verdigris Yards with a surgeon's kit she'd taught herself out of and a cook's hands and the mark on her wrist, and Adder Voss had hired her without asking a single question, and she'd loved him a little for that, and now she knew why he hadn't asked. You don't ask a fellow-drowning-swimmer how they came to be in the water.

She wet Ino's lips again and thought about what she had told herself, all those years — that faith was the thing that priced you and mercy was the thing that didn't, and that she had left the Vow when she could no longer tell them apart. It was not the whole truth. The whole truth was smaller and worse. She had left because a man she had loved in the Vow had died of a wound she could have dressed, and the Highwarden had forbidden the water to clean it, because water spent on the wounded was water the crowns had not earned, and Doria had stood over him with her surgeon's hands full of a bandage she was not allowed to wet and understood, all at once, that she had joined a thing that would let a man rot to make a point. That was the ground the Vow made of its dead. She had read the country by it, the way she read every country, and she had walked out the next dawn and never looked back, and she had been reading countries by their dead ever since, and had never yet found one whose god she could keep.

She was thinking that — of Adder walking out into the white toward the bell, of the two of them and the one door they'd each found out of the same dark — when she saw the shape at the water-butts.

It should not have been there. The butts were lashed at the center of the couched camels where the cold was least and a thief was most seen, and the watch was hers, and there was no one on the salt tonight but the crew and forty camels and a dying boy. But there was a shape, low and patient, moving among the lashed butts with the unhurried care of a man who has all the time faith gives, and when it turned its head the starlight caught the mild broad planes of a face she had loved across a thousand miles of shared bread, and she understood, with the particular sick lurch of recognizing your own younger self, exactly what Brother Kest was doing at the water.

He had a small horn vial in his hand. She knew the vial. She'd carried its brother once. Salt-of-lead and the crushed root that went with it, the Vow's quiet unmaker, a few drops to a butt and the water stayed sweet to the tongue and killed by the third day, so that a caravan died walking and blamed the Glare and no one ever found the hand. Deny the water. The salt belongs to no house. If a crown can't be crowned without water in the desert, then let the desert keep its water and its crowns both. She had helped write that logic into her own bones once. She could have finished the sentence he was writing in the dark.

"Kest," Doria said, very quietly, so as not to wake the crew, so as not to wake the boy. "Come away from the water."

He did not startle. Of course he didn't. He looked over at her with that warmth that had frightened her longest of all his qualities — Kest was never more terrible than when he was being kind — and he said, in his low pleasant sermon-voice, "Doria Fenn. Sister. I hoped it would be you on the watch. I've been dreading it would be the girl." He didn't stop what he was doing. His hands went on, unhurried, working the stopper of the nearest butt. "You know what this is. You know it's mercy. Better the whole road ends here in the clean salt than one more house buys one more crown with our thirst. You knew that once truer than I did. You taught it to men who taught it to me."

"I did." She got up off the cold ground slow, her old knees, her surgeon's care with her own body. "That's how I know it's a lie. I taught it and I watched what it cost and I did the sum you never let yourself do, Kest — I priced it, the way they price everything, and do you know what I found? The Vow charges the same coin the crowns do. Lives. It just tells you they're free." She moved between him and the butts, not fast, an old woman putting herself in a doorway. "There's a boy behind me calling the water-tally in his sleep because he loved a crew enough to take an arrow for the worst of them. You'd have him die walking and call it clean. That's not the salt belonging to no house. That's just you, deciding you get to keep him. Same as any king."

Kest's hands paused on the stopper. Just for a breath. That was the thing about him she had always known and always feared — he listened, truly listened; he was not a fanatic who had stopped his ears, he heard you and weighed you and killed you anyway, and the listening was the horror of it. "You were the best of us," he said, and there was real grief in it. "When they sent me to the Company, they told me: if it goes hard, find Fenn — she'll remember what it was for. I've spent the whole road not finding you, because I knew what you'd say, and I knew you'd be right, and I would have to do it anyway."

"Then you already know the sermon," Doria said. "You only wanted to hear it in a voice that meant it once. The Vow isn't the clean thing left when the crowns fail, Kest. It's the same knife the crowns hold, and it tells a man the thirst is his own fault for having a throat."

"Step aside, sister." Still gentle. Gentler. The vial was open in his hand. "I don't want to spend you. You're the last of us that ever meant it."

"No," Doria said. "You're the last of you that ever meant it. I stopped being us a long time ago." And she did the thing she had been deciding to do since the fire at the Glare's edge, since a mute girl stood up and made frightened people brave, since she'd chosen — quietly, days back, without telling anyone, the way she'd chosen everything that mattered — the caravan. She got her hand around the horn vial and she would not let go of it, an old cook's grip, a grip that had wrung necks and set bones and held down screaming men for the saw, and she turned it away from the water and toward the salt, toward the ground, spilling it out into the one place its poison couldn't matter, and she shouted — she who never raised her voice — she shouted the camp awake with the whole of her cracked and precious breath, "The water! To the water, the water's fouled, wake up, TO THE WATER —"

The knife she felt more than saw. She'd taught men how to use one in close where there's no room to swing; she recognized the short economical drive of it, up under the ribs, the Vow's way, quiet and sure and merciful in its own arithmetic. Kest did it the way he did everything, with sorrow and without hesitation, and he caught her as she folded so that she went down soft, cradled, and for a moment his warm terrible face was the whole of the sky.

"I know," he told her, low, only for her, as the camp erupted behind him into shouting and Sable's voice cutting through it and the ring of steel. "I know you meant it. I'll carry that you meant it." And then he was up and gone, out into the white dark, a shape and then a rumor and then nothing, still loose, still faithful, carrying her the way you carry a debt you've decided not to pay.

She did not die at once. The salt is patient; it let her have a little while.

They got her turned over and Sable's rag-wrapped hands were pressing the wound and Wren was there with her broken bell somehow ringing its dull knock against Doria's collarbone as the girl bent close, and Doria wanted to tell them the water was safe, she'd spilled it, he hadn't reached the butts, the tally still held — the last thing she had it in her to give them was a number that came out right — and she got enough of it out that she saw Sable understand, saw the quartermaster's terrible arithmetic register safe and take one weight off the pile, and that was worth the breath it cost.

"The boy," Doria said. Her voice was going. "Break the fever tonight. It'll break tonight or not. Willow bark's in the — the green tin, not the gray, you always take the gray. Sable. The green tin."

"Green tin," Sable said. Her flat voice had a crack straight through it now and she wasn't troubling to hide it. "I've got it. Doria. Hold on. We're through tomorrow, the far side's tomorrow, you don't get to —"

"I chose it," Doria said, because it seemed important that they know she'd chosen, that this was not the road spending her but her spending herself, the one wealth the Vow and the crowns both had always tried to price and never quite could. "I chose the caravan. Long time back. Tell — tell the girl that's how you do it. Not the crate. Not the crown. You choose the people and then you pay whatever it comes to." She found Wren's face in the starlight and it was the face she'd half-recognized at the fire weeks ago and fully known the night the drover spoke, and she was glad, she found, absurdly glad, to be one of the few who'd gotten to see the girl become herself before the end. "Cross them over," Doria told her. "All of them. To the last coin."

They buried her in the salt at dawn, at the edge of the far white, because you cannot carry a body across the last of the Glare and you would not want to, the salt being the truest ground there is.

There was no soil to give her and no flame to keep — the Kept Flame was a crown's god and the Drowned Mother a crown's god and Doria had been done with crowns since before most of them were born — so the crew gave her the road's own rite, the one that belongs to no house because it belongs to the salt: they laid her straight with her surgeon's hands folded, and each of them poured out a measure of their own tallied water onto the white beside her, the dearest thing any of them owned, water in the Glare, spent on the dead who could not drink it, because that was the whole point, that was the only prayer the road believed — that a life is worth more than the water it costs, and here is the water to prove we know it. Then they heaped the salt over her by hand, and the salt took her and would keep her, sweet and unrotting and whole, for as long as the Saltreach was white, which was to say forever, which was to say until the last crown fell and the road belonged, at last, to no house.

Wren stood at the foot of it when the salt was heaped, and she took the broken drover-bell out of her pocket — the false silence she had worn the whole road, the lie that had kept her alive — and she set it down in the white beside the grave, its dull cracked knock stilled for good, a small wooden weight given to the salt. No one asked her why. Sable thought she understood it: the girl was burying a silence beside the woman who had told her how to spend herself, and keeping only the voice. Ino, too weak to stand, poured out his measure from where he lay, and the water ran down the salt and was gone, and he watched it go with the grave face of a boy learning the one sum that never comes out even.

Sable notched the tally-knife once, for the count, because Doria would have wanted the number kept.

Then they turned the string west into the last day of the Glare, one measure lighter and one soul short and the water clean, and behind them the low white grave already indistinguishable from the salt that was everywhere, that was money and weather and ground and now was Doria too, kept.

ch24.body:
They came off the Glare a little before the fourth dusk, and the world had edges again.

Sable didn't trust them at first — a low dark line in the west that could have been one more mirage tuning up for the evening's lies — but it stayed put when she blinked, and then it resolved into the broken hills that skirted the deep salt on the Lowmarch side, real rock, gray-brown and honest, with a smear of something green in the folds of it that meant the marches, that meant water in the ground where the ground could hold it, that meant the far side was not a rumor she'd been paying into after all. The crew made no noise about it. They were past noise. They came down off the ringing white onto the first honest gravel any of them had stood on in four days and several of them simply sat down where the salt ended, at the exact line where white became gray, and put their cracked hands flat on the cool stone as though on a living thing.

Sable let them have it. A quartermaster learns when a halt is worth more than the water it costs, and this one was — a few breaths of grief and gravel and the plain animal fact of having lived, to be spent later against the days when they would need to believe they could do it again. She counted heads while they sat, because counting was how she prayed. Ten souls, where twelve had come onto the far edge of the Glare: Adder walked out by his own choosing, and Doria into the salt by hers, a different kind of choosing that the tally-knife wore a fresh notch for, a notch she had caught her thumb finding a dozen times since dawn. The rest of them had crossed. She made herself count it as a number that came out, because Doria would have, and because the only other thing to count was what it had cost, and she was not ready for that sum and thought she might never be.

Ino was alive. The fever had broken in the black middle of the night — the green tin, the willow bark, Doria's last order carried out by Sable's own unsteady hands — broken and left him gray and hollow and blinking and asking, in a thread of the old sing-song, whether anyone had kept the tally while he was under. Someone had laughed. It had come out wrong, wetter than a laugh, but he'd taken it for one and been comforted, and Sable had gone off behind a camel and stood with her forehead against Old Ката's flank for the length of ten breaths and then come back and been the quartermaster again, because that was the job and the job was the only thing that had gotten any of them across.

She was doing the arithmetic of the marches — how far to the first honest spring, how many days on the water they had left, whether Ino could ride or must be carried — when Ysolde Marrin came and sat down beside her on the last of the salt, elegant even now, even here, and Sable knew before the woman said a word that the wool-buyer had chosen this moment on purpose, and knew, with a weariness that had nothing to do with thirst, exactly why.

"Don't," Sable said.

"You don't know what I'm going to say."

"I've known what you were going to say since Ninefold. You've just been waiting for the price to be right." Sable didn't look at her. She looked west, at the green in the folds of the hills. "And the price is right now, isn't it. You're a professional.
